title: Sepsis, Infection & Anaphylaxis
note: Set 4: Learn chapters (Sepsis, Infection & Anaphylaxis notes, structured for easy reading), learning outcomes, landmark trials and a linked reading list. Speak, Retrieve and SAQ content to follow.

items.title: 1. From infection to sepsis: the host response and organ failure
items.priority: P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO) + P4 LOW (2 parent LOs) + P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 1.1 Start with normal host defence

- The distinction between colonisation, infection, inflammation and sepsis matters because an organ-dysfunction syndrome cannot be diagnosed from a positive culture, fever or raised C-reactive protein alone.
- Colonisation means organisms are present without tissue invasion or a harmful host response
- Infection means organisms invade or proliferate with a local or systemic response
- Inflammation is a response to injury that may be sterile (pancreatitis, burns or major trauma) or caused by infection.
- Sepsis occurs only when the response to infection becomes dysregulated and threatens organ function.
- Conversely, an elderly, neutropenic or immunosuppressed patient may develop fulminant infection without fever or leukocytosis.

- The first line of defence is intact skin, mucosa, ciliary clearance, gastric acidity, commensal flora and endogenous antimicrobial peptides.
- When bacteria breach these barriers, macrophages, neutrophils and dendritic cells recognise conserved pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), such as endotoxin/lipopolysaccharide and peptidoglycan, through pattern-recognition receptors including Toll-like receptors.
- Damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) from injured host cells amplify the response even if organisms are subsequently controlled.
- Complement activation produces opsonisation (C3b), chemotaxis (C5a) and membrane attack complexes; coagulation and platelets also contribute to innate immune containment.

- A well-regulated response recruits neutrophils, enhances phagocytosis, produces local vascular permeability and then resolves.
- In sepsis, inflammatory and counter-regulatory pathways are both profoundly altered.
- Cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β and IL-6 promote endothelial activation, nitric oxide production and vasodilatation; IL-10 and immune-checkpoint pathways suppress antigen presentation and adaptive immunity.
- The syndrome is not simply ‘too much inflammation’: profound immune suppression may coexist with hyperinflammation, increasing vulnerability to secondary bacterial, fungal and viral infection.
- This explains why a septic patient can be simultaneously vasoplegic, prothrombotic and immunocompromised.

**Why surgery and anaesthesia alter immune competence:**

- Major surgical tissue injury releases DAMPs and activates complement, coagulation and neutrophils even without infection.
- The neuroendocrine stress response increases catecholamines and cortisol, producing lymphocyte redistribution, impaired cell-mediated responses, insulin resistance and a transient systemic pro- and anti-inflammatory state.
- Neutrophil dysfunction, local tissue hypoperfusion, hypothermia, hyperglycaemia, blood loss and transfusion may impair wound defence.
- Volatile agents, opioids and regional techniques influence immune pathways in experimental models, but clinical evidence does not justify selecting propofol or a regional technique solely to prevent cancer recurrence or sepsis.
- What does translate reliably to practice is avoiding unnecessary hypothermia, prolonged tissue hypoxaemia, poor glycaemic control, excessive transfusion, undertreated infection and disruption of the sterile barrier.
- Persistent postoperative fever may represent sterile inflammation, but new organ dysfunction must trigger evaluation for infection, myocardial injury, pulmonary embolism and other complications rather than being dismissed as a normal response to surgery.

**Clinical connection.** An isolated high CRP does not prove sepsis; a patient with pneumonia, new confusion, creatinine rise and hypoxaemia may have sepsis despite modest inflammatory markers. Empirical antibiotics treat the pathogen, while resuscitation and organ support treat consequences of the host response. Neither replaces source control.

## 1.2 Definitions, historical language and bedside tools

- The 2016 Sepsis-3 consensus defines **sepsis** as life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection.
- Its operational criterion is a new rise of **at least two SOFA points** attributable to infection.
- A septic shock subset requires vasopressors to maintain MAP **at least 65 mmHg** and a blood lactate **above 2 mmol/L** despite adequate fluid resuscitation, in the absence of another predominant explanation.
- This identifies a high-risk phenotype; a patient who is hypotensive from infection but has not yet received fluids or vasopressors should nevertheless be treated urgently.
- Sepsis is primarily a clinical diagnosis; criteria are not reasons to delay treatment.

- Older curricula retain terms that still appear in examination questions.
- **SIRS** is two or more of temperature >38°C or <36°C; heart rate >90/min; respiratory rate >20/min or PaCO₂ <32 mmHg; white cell count >12 or <4 ×10⁹/L or >10% immature forms.
- SIRS can reflect non-infective injury.
- **Severe sepsis** meant sepsis with organ dysfunction in older definitions but is redundant under Sepsis-3, because organ dysfunction is intrinsic to the modern definition.
- Be able to state both meanings and explain which terminology is current.

- The full SOFA score comprises oxygenation (PaO₂/FiO₂), coagulation (platelets), liver (bilirubin), cardiovascular support (MAP/vasopressors), consciousness (GCS) and renal function (creatinine/urine output).
- It is useful for tracking organ dysfunction, not as the sole screening tool. qSOFA is altered mentation, respiratory rate ≥22/min and systolic pressure ≤100 mmHg; two or more suggests increased risk outside ICU but **its low sensitivity means it must not be the sole screen**.
- The 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) recommends NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS rather than qSOFA alone as a single screening tool.
- The bedside question is: is this patient infected, developing acute organ dysfunction, and deteriorating in a way that requires treatment now?

| **Framework** | **What it is good for** | **Critical limitation** |
|---|---|---|
| SIRS | Physiological warning signs; historical terminology | Very non-specific; sterile inflammation may satisfy it |
| NEWS2/MEWS | Early recognition and escalation on wards | Screens for deterioration, not infection or causation |
| qSOFA | Recognising especially high-risk infected patients | Insensitive as a stand-alone screen |
| SOFA | Defining and monitoring organ dysfunction | Needs laboratory data and an attributed change from baseline |
| Sepsis-3 shock criteria | Identifying vasopressor-dependent, hyperlactataemic shock | A research/clinical phenotype, not an instruction to await lactate or vasopressors before acting |

## 1.3 How inflammation causes circulatory failure

- Arterial vasodilatation reduces systemic vascular resistance through excess nitric oxide signalling, vasopressin deficiency, abnormal potassium-channel activity and reduced vascular responsiveness to endogenous catecholamines.
- Venodilatation increases **unstressed volume**, reducing the pressure driving venous return even when total intravascular volume has not changed.
- Simultaneous glycocalyx degradation, endothelial injury and capillary leak move protein-rich fluid into interstitial spaces; fever, reduced intake and gastrointestinal losses add true hypovolaemia.
- Septic shock is therefore a mixture of **relative hypovolaemia, absolute hypovolaemia and distributive vasoplegia**, sometimes with cardiac dysfunction.

- Coronary flow and myocardial contractility are also altered.
- Sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy may produce reversible global biventricular systolic depression, abnormal relaxation or predominantly right ventricular failure, particularly in ARDS with high pulmonary vascular resistance.
- Early cardiac output may be high because low afterload permits a hyperdynamic circulation; a later low cardiac output is not mandatory for tissue hypoxia.
- Bedside echo distinguishes a small hyperdynamic, fluid-depleted ventricle from a dilated poorly contracting ventricle, RV dysfunction or obstructive shock.
- This changes whether additional fluid, vasopressors or an inotrope is appropriate.

- Endothelial injury causes heterogeneous microvascular flow: some capillaries are well perfused while adjacent units are poorly perfused despite an apparently normal MAP or cardiac output.
- Leukocyte adhesion, platelet microthrombi, tissue oedema and reduced capillary density increase oxygen diffusion distance.
- Impaired mitochondrial oxygen utilisation and altered metabolic signalling further uncouple global oxygen delivery from cellular ATP production.
- The key specialist insight is that restoring systemic pressure is **necessary but may be insufficient** for tissue perfusion; giving additional fluid merely because the lactate has not normalised can worsen pulmonary, renal and intestinal oedema.

- Oxygen delivery is **DO₂ = CO × CaO₂**; arterial oxygen content is approximately **CaO₂ = 1.34 × Hb(g/dL) × SaO₂ + 0.003 × PaO₂(mmHg)**.
- Thus global delivery depends primarily on cardiac output, haemoglobin and saturation; raising PaO₂ above adequate saturation contributes little dissolved oxygen.
- In normal physiology extraction increases if delivery falls.
- In septic microvascular dysfunction, extraction may fail regionally; mixed venous saturation can be normal or high while organs remain hypoxic.
- Interpret SvO₂/ScvO₂ in context, not as a stand-alone endpoint.

## 1.4 Lactate: a marker of severity, not a synonym for anaerobic metabolism

- Lactate is generated when pyruvate is reduced by lactate dehydrogenase.
- In shock, impaired oxygen delivery can increase anaerobic lactate production, but adrenergic stimulation accelerates aerobic glycolysis and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity; inflammatory signalling, altered hepatic clearance, seizures and exogenous adrenaline also elevate lactate.
- Hepatic and renal dysfunction reduce clearance.
- A high lactate therefore warrants urgent evaluation but does not always imply ongoing fluid-responsive hypovolaemia.
- A normal lactate does not exclude regional ischaemia or early sepsis.

- Serial lactate is useful to judge the overall direction of resuscitation; combine it with mentation, capillary refill, temperature and mottling, urine output, echocardiography, blood pressure and acid–base status.
- A persistent rise should prompt a search for inadequately treated infection/source, hypoxaemia, low output, mesenteric ischaemia, severe adrenergic drive, haemorrhage or an alternative diagnosis.
- The 2026 SSC suggests serial lactate in septic shock or raised lactate, and explicitly advises against continuing IV fluids solely to force lactate normalisation.

## 1.5 How sepsis injures individual organs

**Lungs:**

- Endothelial and alveolar epithelial injury causes protein-rich permeability oedema and neutrophilic inflammation, reducing compliance and creating shunt.
- Sepsis is a major cause of ARDS.
- Ventilation–perfusion mismatch initially causes type 1 respiratory failure; increased dead space and fatigue can later produce hypercapnia.
- Positive-pressure ventilation may improve oxygenation but increase RV afterload and reduce venous return; excessive tidal volume or driving pressure creates ventilator-induced injury.

**Kidneys:**

- Sepsis-associated AKI can occur without sustained global renal hypoperfusion.
- Intrarenal microcirculatory redistribution, tubular stress, inflammatory and mitochondrial changes coexist with reduced filtration.
- Low urine output may indicate hypoperfusion, neurohormonal water retention or intrinsic AKI; it must not reflexively trigger more crystalloid.
- Assess volume responsiveness, obstruction, nephrotoxic drugs, electrolytes and acid–base status.
- Initiate renal replacement for conventional indications (refractory hyperkalaemia, dangerous acidemia, fluid overload, uraemic complications), not creatinine alone.

**Brain:**

- Sepsis-associated encephalopathy ranges from delirium and inattention to coma without direct CNS infection.
- Mechanisms include cytokine signalling, disturbed blood–brain barrier, microvascular dysfunction, hypoxaemia, metabolic derangements, drug accumulation and impaired cerebral autoregulation.
- Focal signs, meningism, seizures or persistent unexplained impairment demand investigation for stroke, encephalitis, meningitis or another pathology.

**Coagulation:**

- Tissue factor expression and endothelial activation accelerate thrombin generation; reduced natural anticoagulants, impaired fibrinolysis and platelet consumption can progress from microthrombosis to sepsis-induced coagulopathy and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC).
- Expect falling platelets, prolonging PT/INR, rising D-dimer and, in overt DIC, falling fibrinogen.
- Early fibrinogen can be normal/high as an acute-phase reactant.
- Treat the source and shock, give VTE prophylaxis unless contraindicated, and reserve component replacement for bleeding/procedures guided by results rather than correcting laboratory numbers indiscriminately.

**Heart, liver and gut:**

- Myocardial depression and atrial arrhythmias aggravate low output.
- Cholestasis and hepatocellular injury impair drug clearance and lactate metabolism.
- Gut barrier dysfunction, ileus and intestinal oedema reduce tolerance of enteral nutrition, while mesenteric hypoperfusion can progress to ischaemia.
- Adrenal and thyroid hormone alterations are often adaptive critical-illness responses rather than primary endocrine failure.
- Coexisting hypoglycaemia or high glucose, temperature dysregulation and catabolism reflect systemic physiological stress.

Sepsis survivors may develop critical illness polyneuromyopathy, cognitive impairment, depression, reduced exercise tolerance, recurrent infection and prolonged organ dysfunction. Post-sepsis follow-up and rehabilitation are therefore part of adequate care, not an optional afterthought.

items.title: 2. Recognition, investigation and resuscitation of sepsis and septic shock
items.body:
## 2.1 Clinical recognition: act on physiology while testing the hypothesis

- The unwell patient with suspected infection needs concurrent **resuscitation and diagnosis**.
- Assess airway protection, respiratory work, pulse oximetry, respiratory rate, perfusion and mental status.
- Record temperature, blood pressure (including MAP), pulse, capillary refill, mottling, urine output and volume status; look for a purpuric rash, cellulitis, indwelling devices and signs of peritonitis.
- Establish the course of illness and immunosuppression, recent surgery, travel, antibiotic exposure, previous multidrug-resistant isolates and possible healthcare-associated infection.
- Elderly or neutropenic patients may be hypothermic, normotensive or afebrile despite serious infection.

- The differential diagnosis of vasodilatory shock includes anaphylaxis, neurogenic shock, adrenal crisis, pancreatitis, liver failure and drug-induced vasoplegia.
- Septic physiology can coexist with haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism, cardiogenic shock or bowel ischaemia.
- In a ventilated patient, acute hypotension and tachycardia require exclusion of tension pneumothorax, anaesthetic effects and acute blood loss.
- An ultrasound assessment of biventricular size/function, IVC in context, lungs and abdomen may rapidly reveal a competing explanation; no single echo view measures total intravascular volume reliably.

## 2.2 Investigations: obtain what will change a decision

- **Blood cultures** (commonly two sets from separate venepuncture sites, with adequate volume) should be taken promptly, ideally before antibiotics **provided this causes no material delay**; draw paired peripheral and line cultures when catheter infection is suspected.
- Microbiological samples are source-specific: urine microscopy/culture, sputum or tracheal aspirate, CSF where safe, wound/operative tissue, drain fluid, pleural fluid, biliary sampling or stool testing for C. difficile as relevant.
- Avoid superficial swabs that misrepresent a deep infection.
- Obtain recent local antibiograms and prior culture records.

- Baseline blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, glucose, liver tests, coagulation including fibrinogen as indicated, lactate, blood gas, CRP and, where relevant, procalcitonin establish severity and organ dysfunction.
- ABG assesses hypoxaemia, ventilation and mixed acid–base disturbance; interpret serum lactate along with perfusion.
- Procalcitonin can support decisions about stopping antibiotics when duration is uncertain, **not** determine on its own whether to commence treatment.
- ECG and troponin are appropriate for arrhythmias/ischaemia or myocardial dysfunction, but troponin elevation in sepsis is not automatically type 1 MI.

Image the suspected focus promptly:

- Chest radiograph or CT for pneumonia/complication.
- Ultrasound of kidneys/biliary tract for obstruction.
- Contrast CT abdomen/pelvis for perforation, collections or ischaemic bowel.
- Ultrasound/CT for abscesses.
- Echocardiography when infective endocarditis or cardiac dysfunction is suspected.

- Contrast is often justified in unstable patients when imaging reveals a surgically reversible problem; the harm of missed diagnosis can outweigh contrast-associated kidney risk.
- Stabilise enough for transfer and arrange an immediate pathway to drainage or theatre where indicated.

## 2.3 First-hour priorities and the meaning of antibiotic timing

- The 2026 SSC distinguishes diagnostic certainty and haemodynamic severity.
- In **septic shock**, administer appropriate IV antimicrobials immediately, ideally within **1 hour of recognition**.
- The same applies to probable or definite sepsis without shock.
- In **possible sepsis without shock**, undertake a rapid time-limited evaluation; if concern persists, give antibiotics within **3 hours of first suspicion**.
- When infection is unlikely and no shock is present, continue observation and investigate alternative causes rather than automatically prescribing broad-spectrum agents.
- This balances harm from treatment delay with antimicrobial toxicity and resistance.

- Do not interpret ‘one-hour antibiotics’ as an isolated bundle that neglects source control, sampling, oxygenation or circulation.
- Within the first minutes: call for help/escalate to ICU or theatre, secure vascular access, obtain cultures and lactate, begin empiric treatment, assess whether fluids are likely to help, start vasopressors when necessary, and actively organise source control.
- The overall aim is to restore organ perfusion **without worsening oedema** while eliminating infection.

## 2.4 Initial fluid therapy: what the guideline says and what the physiology requires

- A balanced crystalloid is generally first-line, because its chloride concentration and buffer anions reduce the risk of hyperchloraemic acidosis compared with large saline volumes; saline can be appropriate in traumatic brain injury and specific electrolyte situations.
- Starch solutions should not be used; gelatin is discouraged.
- The 2026 SSC **conditionally suggests at least 30 mL/kg of IV crystalloid within the first 3 hours** for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock, with explicit attention to cardiac/renal comorbidity and frequent reassessment.
- Use actual weight, or adjusted/ideal weight when BMI >30 kg/m², for the weight-based calculation.
- This is not evidence that every patient must receive an unassessed 30 mL/kg bolus before noradrenaline, nor a reason to ignore pulmonary oedema.

- A sensible bedside approach is to deliver an initial bolus such as 250–500 mL rapidly in a frail or cardiac-compromised adult (larger boluses may be appropriate in others), reassess BP, capillary refill, echo, pulmonary congestion, stroke volume and symptoms, and repeat while benefit exceeds harm.
- Identify fluid tolerance independently of fluid responsiveness: a ventricle may increase stroke volume after a bolus yet the patient may already have severe extravascular lung water.
- Consider bedside ultrasound for biventricular dysfunction and B-lines, elevated filling pressures and abdominal distension.
- A passive-leg-raise manoeuvre transiently transfers approximately 150–300 mL of venous blood into the thorax and is reversible; measure the change in stroke volume or cardiac output rather than BP alone.
- An increase in stroke volume of around **≥10%** usually supports fluid responsiveness, subject to measurement method.

- Pulse-pressure variation and stroke-volume variation are most useful with sinus rhythm, controlled mechanical ventilation, adequate tidal volumes, closed chest and absence of major RV dysfunction; they are unreliable in spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia and high intra-abdominal pressure.
- A mini-fluid challenge or end-expiratory occlusion with real-time cardiac output measurement can be useful alternatives.
- Static CVP values poorly predict responsiveness; a low CVP can be supportive context but not a therapeutic target.
- The physiological question after each bolus is: did systemic flow and tissue perfusion improve, and did the patient’s lungs or venous pressures become less tolerant of further fluid?

## 2.5 Start vasopressors early when vasoplegia predominates

- Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) is first-line in septic shock.
- By activating α1 receptors it restores arterial resistance and venous stressed volume; modest β1 activity supports contractility.
- A practical adult infusion may begin around **0.02–0.1 microgram/kg/min**, titrated rapidly to perfusion and MAP; local dilution and prescribing practices vary.
- The 2026 SSC recommends an initial MAP target **65 mmHg** rather than routinely higher pressures.
- In patients **aged 65 or older**, it conditionally suggests an initial **60–65 mmHg** range rather than higher.
- A patient with chronic severe hypertension, poor capillary refill or acute neurological injury may require individualised goals.
- Avoid treating MAP as the sole endpoint.

- Noradrenaline can be started through a well-sited, monitored peripheral cannula rather than waiting for central access, particularly when delaying vasopressors would prolong dangerous hypotension.
- Inspect the site frequently, use a dedicated line, and transition to central access if ongoing/escalating support is needed.
- An arterial line is useful for unstable readings, rapid titration and repeated ABGs, but should not delay initial treatment.
- If noradrenaline needs continue to increase, evaluate source control, volume status, myocardial function and alternative shock causes, then **add vasopressin**, commonly **0.03 units/min** (a fixed low dose) rather than simply escalating catecholamine indefinitely.
- If MAP remains inadequate despite noradrenaline and vasopressin, add adrenaline.
- Vasopressin causes V1-mediated vasoconstriction and reduces catecholamine dose; risks include ischaemia of digits/gut at high doses.
- Dopamine carries more arrhythmia risk and is not first line.

- If hypoperfusion persists despite an adequate MAP and fluid status and echo shows low cardiac output, the problem is **pump failure**, not simply inadequate arterial tone.
- Consider dobutamine (for example **2.5–10 microgram/kg/min**, titrated to CO and tolerance) added to noradrenaline or use adrenaline as an alternative inotrope/vasopressor.
- Dobutamine can induce tachycardia and hypotension through β2 effects; adrenaline can increase lactate without tissue hypoxia.
- Reassess rhythm, RV afterload, ischaemia and oxygen delivery rather than pursuing an arbitrary cardiac-index target.

## 2.6 What goal-directed therapy means after the major trials

- The original Rivers early goal-directed therapy protocol mandated CVP, ScvO₂, transfusion and dobutamine thresholds.
- Later large trials—ProCESS, ARISE and ProMISe—found no survival advantage of that rigid invasive protocol over contemporary high-quality usual care in early septic shock.
- This does **not** mean resuscitation goals are unimportant: it means that automatically targeting CVP 8–12 mmHg or ScvO₂ 70% and transfusing to haematocrit 30% is not justified.
- The modern approach is personalised, repeated assessment using BP, perfusion, dynamic flow measures, lactate trajectory and echo.
- The CLASSIC and CLOVERS trials likewise do not justify either extreme of fluid strategy for every patient; distinguish early rescue from subsequent avoidance of fluid accumulation.
- The Australia/New Zealand-led **ARISE FLUIDS trial (2026)** compared early vasopressors with restricted fluids against more generous early fluids and later vasopressors in 963 analysed patients with septic shock.
- The median days alive and out of hospital at 90 days was **76 in each group** (difference 0.0 days; P=1.00): early vasopressors reduced administered fluid by a median of about 1.1 L and pulmonary oedema (0.6% versus 5.0%) but did not improve its primary outcome.
- Patients had already received early fluid before randomisation, and urgent theatre transfer was excluded, so the trial cannot establish that all fluids should be avoided from presentation or prescribe the optimal strategy for emergency laparotomy.
- It strengthens the case for selecting fluids and vasopressors according to a patient’s physiological response.

- Capillary refill (usually reassessed after firm fingertip pressure for several seconds) and mottling provide rapid markers of skin microcirculatory perfusion; the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK trial suggested a potentially useful capillary-refill–guided strategy, though its primary mortality comparison did not meet conventional statistical significance.
- The subsequent **ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 trial (2025)** evaluated a personalised capillary-refill-targeted protocol incorporating diastolic arterial pressure, fluid responsiveness and echo against usual care.
- Its hierarchical composite of death, duration of organ support and hospital stay modestly favoured the intervention (win ratio **1.16**, 95% CI **1.02–1.33**), largely through shorter organ-support duration; it did not demonstrate an isolated definitive mortality reduction.
- The clinical insight is that capillary refill becomes more useful when embedded in a **structured individual haemodynamic algorithm**, not treated as another magic threshold.
- Peripheral perfusion can deteriorate with hypothermia and vasoconstriction, so it is supportive information rather than a complete haemodynamic assessment.
- A clinically meaningful response integrates multiple domains, rather than one ‘normal number’.

## 2.7 Management once the patient reaches ICU

**Airway and ventilation:**

- Intubate when oxygenation or ventilation fails, airway protection is compromised, work of breathing is unsustainable, or urgent source control requires general anaesthesia.
- Preoxygenation may be limited by shunt, and induction can precipitate profound circulatory collapse through reduced sympathetic tone and positive-pressure ventilation.
- Prepare noradrenaline, fluid if responsive, meticulous drug titration and the haemodynamically safest available induction plan (often small aliquots of ketamine or etomidate where appropriate rather than a full hypotensive propofol bolus).
- Anticipate rapid desaturation, aspiration and altered drug clearance.
- After intubation, screen for ARDS and use lung-protective ventilation.
- For ARDS, start around **6 mL/kg predicted body weight**, keep **plateau pressure ≤30 cmH₂O**, consider higher PEEP in moderate–severe ARDS and prone ventilation **>12 hours/day** where indicated.
- Adjust PEEP with attention to preload and RV performance.
- Avoid excessive oxygen after stabilisation; the 2026 SSC allows patient-tailored conservative or liberal oxygen targets rather than one compulsory SpO₂ number.
- High-flow nasal oxygen is generally preferred to conventional oxygen in significant acute hypoxaemia when suitable and monitored.

**Corticosteroids:**

- The 2026 SSC conditionally suggests IV corticosteroids in septic shock.
- A common evidence-based regimen is **hydrocortisone 200 mg/day**, for example 50 mg IV every 6 hours or continuous infusion, particularly for persistent vasopressor requirement.
- It accelerates shock resolution; survival findings differ between ADRENAL (no statistically significant 90-day mortality reduction) and APROCCHSS (hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduced mortality).
- Monitor glucose, secondary infection and neuromuscular weakness; avoid assuming corticosteroids replace fluid, vasopressor or source control.
- Do not extend routine stress-dose therapy to uncomplicated sepsis without shock.

**Renal, metabolic and haematological support:**

- Monitor fluid balance, creatinine, potassium, acid–base status and nephrotoxic exposure.
- Do not start renal replacement therapy for AKI without conventional indications; choose continuous therapy when haemodynamic instability makes intermittent shifts poorly tolerated.
- For profound acidemia, sodium bicarbonate is not indicated solely to improve vasopressor response in lactic acidosis; the 2026 SSC conditionally supports its use when **pH ≤7.2 plus AKI stage 2–3**.
- Start insulin when glucose is **≥10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL)** and avoid hypoglycaemia.
- Restrictive red-cell transfusion is generally appropriate (often Hb around 70 g/L threshold in stable ICU patients), individualised for bleeding, myocardial ischaemia and oxygen delivery.
- Use LMWH VTE prophylaxis unless contraindicated, with renal adjustment as required.
- Initiate enteral nutrition when feasible, commonly within 72 hours, with careful tolerance and aspiration assessment.

**Infection and line stewardship:**

- Review the suspected source, culture results and antibiotic therapy daily.
- Remove unnecessary central lines, urinary catheters and invasive devices.
- Assess whether the patient remains fluid responsive, and stop maintenance/resuscitation infusions that no longer provide benefit.
- Once acute shock is stabilised, actively manage accumulated fluid using diuretics or ultrafiltration where appropriate.
- Review delirium, mobilisation, nutrition, pressure injury, family communication, goals of care and long-term post-ICU needs.
- Routine IV vitamin C, immunoglobulin and extracorporeal blood purification are not recommended to improve sepsis outcomes.

## 2.8 Anaesthesia for the septic patient: a perioperative sequence

**Preoperative:**

- Identify source and urgency of control; assess degree of shock, oxygenation, altered consciousness, coagulation, cardiomyopathy, acute kidney injury and metabolic derangement.
- Determine whether the operation is source control (should generally proceed with simultaneous resuscitation) or truly elective (usually postpone while active sepsis is treated).
- Culture and administer empiric antibiotics before incision when feasible without delaying lifesaving surgery.
- Discuss resuscitation ceilings, organ support and postoperative ICU requirements.
- Optimise access, crossmatch, point-of-care ultrasound, arterial monitoring and noradrenaline; aspiration risk is frequently high because of ileus or bowel obstruction.

**Intraoperative:**

- Plan a controlled haemodynamically prepared induction and rapid secure airway.
- Even etomidate and ketamine can cause hypotension in catecholamine-depleted patients; no induction agent removes the need for resuscitation.
- Titrate anaesthetic depth to markedly reduced requirements, maintain source-specific haemodynamic targets and avoid both prolonged hypotension and indiscriminate fluid loading.
- Use arterial blood gases and lactate trends with a logical interval, rather than chasing small fluctuations.
- Correct calcium, potassium and severe acid–base abnormalities where clinically important.
- Communicate when the abdomen will be opened, collections drained or ischaemic bowel resected, because release of inflammatory mediators and abrupt changes in venous return can transiently worsen shock.
- Neuraxial techniques are generally unsuitable during uncontrolled shock or coagulation abnormalities and must be considered against the risk of infection at the intended site.

**Postoperative:**

- A functioning source-control procedure may not immediately reverse vasoplegia.
- Plan continued ventilation when oxygenation, physiological reserve or haemodynamic support is inadequate; reassess perfusion and vasopressors after surgical correction.
- Handover operative findings, residual source uncertainty, cultures, antibiotics/next dose, administered fluids, blood products, coagulopathy, vasopressor doses, urine output, lactate trajectory and the next planned review.
- Resume feeds, VTE prevention, physiotherapy and device removal when safe.

## 2.9 Special applications: maternal sepsis and safe intrahospital transfer

**Maternal sepsis and pneumonia:**

- Pregnancy increases circulating blood volume and resting cardiac output, lowers systemic vascular resistance, increases minute ventilation and oxygen consumption, and reduces functional residual capacity.
- Consequently, a pregnant patient with pneumonia may become hypoxaemic rapidly, while the physiological tachycardia and lower blood pressure of pregnancy can complicate recognition of deterioration.
- Maternal resuscitation must take priority because oxygen delivery to the fetus depends on maternal perfusion.
- Use multidisciplinary obstetric, ICU, anaesthesia, respiratory and neonatal input early; consider fetal gestation, viability, monitoring and the effect of maternal hypoxaemia/acidosis, while still treating her pneumonia and septic physiology decisively.
- Blood cultures, appropriate chest imaging and prompt pregnancy-compatible antimicrobial therapy should not be withheld through unfounded radiation or drug concerns.
- Control maternal oxygenation and ventilation; when invasive ventilation is necessary, use lung-protective targets appropriate to predicted body weight and ARDS physiology while accounting for normal pregnancy PaCO₂ (often around **28–32 mmHg**) and avoiding severe respiratory acidosis.
- Apply manual left uterine displacement in later pregnancy to prevent aortocaval compression, titrate fluids to perfusion rather than indiscriminate volume, and start noradrenaline for sustained vasoplegia when required.
- Major maternal physiological instability and fetal monitoring decisions must not distract from antibiotics, source control and supportive treatment.
- The **2025.1 Final examiner report** specifically criticised answers about severe maternal pneumonia that discussed neonatal or obstetric planning at length while neglecting maternal oxygenation, ventilation, haemodynamics and antimicrobials.

**Transfer of a deteriorating septic patient:**

- Intra-hospital transport from ED, ward or ICU to CT, theatre, intervention or a specialist unit is itself a high-risk intervention.
- Movement removes the patient from the equipment, personnel and ready assistance available at the bedside; a septic patient requiring escalating vasopressors may arrest during supine positioning, transfer or induction.
- Before departure, ask whether the planned investigation will change treatment and whether bedside ultrasound or immediate surgery is more appropriate.
- Stabilise airway/ventilation, oxygenation, arterial pressure and vascular access **to a clinically acceptable minimum**; secure infusions with adequate remaining volume, check pumps/battery/oxygen supply, establish transport monitor/defibrillator access, bring appropriate emergency drugs and assign a trained escort.
- A patient unable to maintain airway protection or oxygenation during transfer should generally have definitive airway management before travel when the balance of urgency and risk supports it.
- Use an agreed SBAR-style handover describing source concern, sepsis severity, ventilator settings, fluids/vasopressors, IV access, drug timing, contingency for deterioration and receiving-team readiness.
- The **2026.1 Final examiner report** explicitly examined risk assessment, stabilisation and airway decisions for transfer as well as physiological optimisation before emergency surgery in severe sepsis.

items.title: 3. Source control and life-threatening intra-abdominal infection
items.body:
## 3.1 Why antibiotics alone cannot cure an uncontrolled source

- Antimicrobials are effective only when they reach a susceptible organism in sufficient concentration.
- A mature abscess has an avascular centre, high bacterial burden, low pH and impaired host immune access.
- Obstructed systems (an infected ureter, biliary tree or bowel) remain infected because pressure and stagnant contents drive tissue injury and bacteraemia.
- Necrotic tissue has lost perfusion entirely.
- When infection has produced these physical abnormalities, definitive management is to **drain pus, relieve obstruction, excise dead tissue, repair leakage, remove infected foreign material or re-establish organ perfusion**.
- Antibiotic escalation cannot compensate for a missed perforation or undrained collection.

- Source control is therefore a form of resuscitation.
- The 2026 SSC conditionally suggests **early source control, ideally within six hours of diagnosing sepsis or septic shock requiring source control**.
- That is an urgency target rather than a guarantee of safety at six hours: a patient with diffuse peritonitis, mesenteric ischaemia or necrotising fasciitis may need intervention immediately, with resuscitation undertaken in parallel.
- The decision must take account of procedural feasibility and the competing danger of transferring an unresuscitated patient.
- When uncertainty remains, repeated joint review by surgeon, anaesthetist, interventional radiologist and intensivist is essential.

- **Four questions organise decisions:** What anatomical process is driving infection? Can it be drained or corrected without open surgery? What physiological instability should be treated before/during the intervention? What features would indicate that the first procedure failed and further source control is needed?

## 3.2 The anatomy determines the microbiology

- The upper gastrointestinal tract and proximal small bowel have comparatively low organism concentrations, whereas distal ileal and colonic contents contain dense Gram-negative facultative bacteria and obligate anaerobes.
- Biliary infection is usually caused by enteric Gram-negatives and, in selected healthcare-associated disease, enterococci; infected necrotic pancreas, post-operative leaks and prolonged hospitalisation raise the probability of resistant organisms or Candida.
- This is why the same empirical antibiotic regimen is not adequate for every abdominal source.
- Coverage must reflect **organisms likely at that site, contamination severity, community versus hospital acquisition, earlier microbiology and host susceptibility**, then be narrowed once the source and cultures are known.

- Uncomplicated appendicitis or community-acquired diverticular perforation in an otherwise well patient differs substantially from a day-seven oesophagojejunal anastomotic leak in a neutropenic patient already exposed to carbapenems.
- The latter needs urgent surgical reassessment, possible coverage of resistant Gram-negatives, enterococci and fungi depending on risks, and explicit attention to antifungal stewardship.
- A positive Candida culture from a sterile intra-abdominal operative specimen may be meaningful; Candida from a long-standing drain is often colonisation and requires clinical interpretation.

## 3.3 Recognising abdominal catastrophe

- Clinical markers are imperfect: fever, abdominal pain, guarding, distension, ileus, vomiting, diarrhoea or absent bowel sounds may occur, but a sedated, paralysed, elderly or immunocompromised patient may lack peritoneal signs.
- Examine the surgical wound and stoma, review drain output for faeces, pus or bile, assess rising lactate, organ support, fluid balance and repeated abdominal findings.
- After recent surgery, an unexpectedly persistent inflammatory response, ongoing catecholamines, failure to tolerate feeds or a new organ failure should trigger a search for anastomotic leak or intra-abdominal collection, even if the first CT was reassuring.

**Imaging:**

- Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is often the most useful test to locate perforation, collections, free intraperitoneal gas, devascularised bowel, portal venous gas or pneumatosis.
- Ultrasound is fast and avoids transfer for biliary dilatation, cholecystitis, free fluid or hydronephrosis but misses many deep collections.
- Bedside focused ultrasound cannot confidently exclude mesenteric ischaemia.
- In haemodynamically stable patients with suspected acute mesenteric ischaemia, CT angiography is the preferred initial vascular investigation; diagnostic delay is more dangerous than a theoretical contrast-associated renal insult.
- A negative study early in disease does not replace reassessment when clinical concern remains high.

## 3.4 Common sources: understand the definitive treatment

| **Condition** | **Pathophysiology and clues** | **Source control and specialist implications** |
|---|---|---|
| Perforated hollow viscus | Enteric spillage → polymicrobial peritonitis; may cause rapid vasoplegia and ileus | Urgent surgery to close/resect perforation, lavage where appropriate, drain collections; treat both Gram-negative aerobes and anaerobes |
| Complicated appendicitis/diverticulitis | Contained abscess versus diffuse faecal peritonitis | Percutaneous drainage may be possible for suitable abscess; diffuse peritonitis or uncontrolled perforation usually needs operative control |
| Acute ascending cholangitis | Biliary obstruction raises ductal pressure and seeds bloodstream; jaundice may be absent | Biliary decompression (usually ERCP; percutaneous if unsuitable), antibiotics and haemodynamic support; do not substitute antibiotics for decompression |
| Acute cholecystitis/empyema | Gallbladder obstruction and ischaemia, sometimes bacterial infection | Cholecystectomy when feasible; percutaneous cholecystostomy can bridge unstable/high-risk patients |
| Infected obstructed urinary tract | Ureteric blockage + infected urine → pyonephrosis/urosepsis | Urgent ureteric stent or nephrostomy; do not wait for culture or fever resolution |
| Acute mesenteric ischaemia | Perfusion deficit (embolism, thrombosis, low-flow non-occlusive ischaemia) → mucosal injury, necrosis and secondary sepsis | Early vascular/surgical consultation, revascularisation when possible, resection of non-viable bowel, planned second look where viability uncertain |
| Infected pancreatic necrosis | Necrotic avascular pancreatic tissue; often later in course of pancreatitis | Prefer staged ‘step-up’ drainage/debridement when feasible; delay intervention until collections wall off in stable patients, but not in uncontrolled deterioration |
| Postoperative anastomotic leak | Continued contamination, collection, tissue ischaemia; high MDR risk | Imaging and early surgical review; drain/reoperate/divert as appropriate; culture operative samples and reassess residual collections |
| Necrotising soft-tissue infection | Rapid fascial spread, toxin-mediated shock, pain disproportionate to signs | Immediate wide surgical debridement, repeat operations, toxin-suppressing antibiotics when appropriate; no imaging delay if clinical suspicion high |

**Mesenteric ischaemia requires special attention:**

- Non-occlusive mesenteric ischaemia may arise in severe shock with high vasopressor exposure; the primary driver is low effective splanchnic perfusion rather than a major arterial blockage.
- A normal lactate early in disease does not exclude it.
- Worsening abdominal distension, blood per rectum, a persistently high lactate, unexplained metabolic acidosis or escalating pressors despite improving other parameters demands review.
- Management includes correction of low-flow physiology, removing avoidable vasoconstrictive exposures, urgent surgical/vascular assessment and resection when bowel is dead.
- Reperfusion may cause sudden acidosis, potassium release, haemodynamic deterioration and further inflammatory injury.

- **Major abdominal trauma: different initial priorities, similar need for timely source control.** Penetrating or blunt abdominal injury can cause haemorrhagic shock, hollow-viscus contamination, devascularised bowel or a combination.
- Initial management follows trauma resuscitation principles: identify life-threatening haemorrhage, secure airway/oxygenation while protecting the cervical spine as appropriate, obtain early blood products and activate massive haemorrhage protocol when indicated, prevent hypothermia and hypocalcaemia, and pursue urgent surgical or interventional radiological haemostasis.
- A **positive FAST** in a haemodynamically unstable patient suggests free intraperitoneal fluid but cannot tell blood from other fluid or exclude retroperitoneal bleeding.
- A stable patient benefits from contrast CT to define solid-organ injury, active extravasation, mesenteric disruption or free gas.
- Resuscitative endovascular balloon occlusion of the aorta (REBOA), where available, is a highly selective bridge and can worsen distal organ ischaemia; it is not a substitute for surgical haemorrhage control.

- Damage-control surgery prioritises control of haemorrhage and gross contamination with temporary closure, then ICU correction of hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy and hypoperfusion before planned reconstruction.
- Hollow-viscus injuries may be missed on early imaging; deterioration, peritonism, unexplained fever or rising inflammatory/organ-dysfunction signs require repeat assessment and possibly laparoscopy/laparotomy.
- An open abdomen requires careful monitoring for fluid/protein losses, heat loss, fistula, visceral oedema and delayed abdominal closure.
- Broad antibiotics are indicated when enteric contamination or established infection is present but should not be prolonged merely because traumatic drains or packs remain if adequate control is achieved.
- Distinguish **early sterile post-traumatic SIRS** from later secondary sepsis; both can cause shock, but antibiotics are not automatically indicated for every inflammatory response after trauma.

- **Abdominal compartment syndrome** is distinct from ordinary post-operative distension.
- Sustained intra-abdominal pressure **>20 mmHg with new organ dysfunction** defines abdominal compartment syndrome (with or without abdominal perfusion pressure <60 mmHg).
- Measure bladder pressure using standardised technique if concerned; raised pressure reduces venous return and cardiac output, increases airway pressures and impairs renal/splanchnic perfusion.
- Temporise with nasogastric/rectal decompression, adequate sedation, drainage of fluid and judicious volume management; refractory cases need decompressive laparotomy.
- An open abdomen requires specialised management of fluid/protein losses, temperature, fistula prevention and timely fascial closure.

## 3.5 Preparing an unstable patient for drainage or laparotomy

- The practical decision is rarely ‘resuscitate fully then operate’.
- Full normalisation is often impossible before source control; waiting for lactate to fall or all vasopressors to stop may allow infection to progress.
- Instead establish an immediate shared plan: obtain two reliable IV lines, blood samples/crossmatch if operative bleeding is possible, evaluate airway/aspiration, start balanced resuscitation with early noradrenaline, give antimicrobials, and decide what physiological minimum is needed for safe induction or interventional transfer.
- A patient with peritonitis is effectively unfasted regardless of the last meal because paralytic ileus delays gastric emptying.

- At induction the combination of venous capacitance, absolute volume deficit and removal of sympathetic tone creates profound hypotension.
- Prepare a vasopressor infusion beforehand and ensure a rapid-delivery route is functioning; titrate induction agents incrementally, use a definitive airway and minimise apnoeic hypoxaemia.
- Gastric decompression may help but does not remove aspiration risk.
- An arterial line is desirable in shock, but do not delay an emergency procedure to place optional monitoring.
- Invasive lines and regional analgesia carry additional considerations when coagulopathic or bacteraemic; thoracic epidurals are generally inappropriate in poorly controlled shock because sympathectomy can exacerbate circulatory collapse.

- During the procedure, expect major losses into the peritoneum or through the bowel, altered evaporative heat loss, and swings in arterial pressure as collections are drained or the abdomen decompressed.
- Use point-of-care gases and ionised calcium as needed, maintain temperature and glucose, and reassess urine output and cardiac performance.
- Large volumes of chloride-rich fluid worsen acidosis, while excessive crystalloid contributes to bowel oedema and failure of anastomoses or abdominal closure.
- If source control is incomplete, communicate specifically what remains and how it will be addressed; ‘washed out’ is not an adequate operative handover if devitalised bowel or a leak persists.

### 3.5.1 The emergency laparotomy as a time-critical perioperative pathway

- The 2025 Australasian Anaesthesia Blue Book chapter “The emergency laparotomy patient” makes an important distinction: successful emergency laparotomy is a multidisciplinary system of care, not merely an uncomplicated induction followed by surgery.
- The high mortality reflects selection of physiologically unstable patients with frailty, comorbidity, untreated abdominal pathology and a narrow source-control window.
- Assess functional status and frailty (particularly in older adults), operative urgency, organ failures, and ceiling-of-care preferences in parallel with resuscitation.
- Emergency laparotomy risk tools such as SORT and the UK National Emergency Laparotomy Audit (NELA) model supplement, but cannot replace, clinical judgement; scores calibrated in another population must not be treated as precise local mortality predictions.

- The proposed sequence is early recognition and antibiotics, urgent consultant surgical and anaesthetic involvement, arterial access and blood sampling if readily achievable, lactate/acid–base and glucose assessment, bedside echo when it changes fluid/vasopressor strategy, aspiration planning, temperature and bleeding preparation, and immediate access to a monitored postoperative destination.
- The emergency-laparotomy ERAS literature uses indicative source-control targets of around three hours in septic shock and six hours in sepsis; these are pathway goals rather than reasons to postpone a more urgent operation or to ignore clinical instability.
- The 2026 SSC recommendation is to identify promptly when an anatomical source requires intervention and implement source control as soon as medically and logistically practical.

- There is often no meaningful separation between resuscitation and operating: the anaesthetist may continue early noradrenaline and reassessed aliquots of balanced crystalloid while the surgeon releases the obstruction or drains infected fluid.
- Invasive monitoring, lower induction doses, a full-stomach airway strategy, protective tidal volumes approximately 6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight, avoidance of unnecessary high intrathoracic pressures, and early postoperative surveillance for organ injury should form a single plan.
- Epidural analgesia requires careful assessment of shock, thrombocytopenia, systemic infection and perioperative anticoagulation; it is not automatically preferable to systemic multimodal analgesia or abdominal wall techniques in a haemodynamically unstable patient.

## 3.6 After source control: when do antibiotics stop?

- A successful procedure changes the treatment objective.
- The patient may remain tachycardic and inflamed for days without ongoing infection, because the host response and tissue healing lag behind bacterial clearance.
- **Short-course antibiotics** are appropriate after adequate source control in many complicated intra-abdominal infections.
- In the STOP-IT trial, a fixed approximately **four-day** course after satisfactory source control was non-inferior to a longer symptom-guided course for a composite outcome of infection/death; applicability to the most severely immunosuppressed or uncontrolled septic shock requires judgment.
- The 2026 SSC conditionally favours shorter over longer courses when source control is adequate, without prescribing four days for every anatomical infection.

- Persistent fever, leukocytosis, lactate elevation or organ failure should lead first to reassessment of source control and competing diagnoses—not automatic indefinite broadening of antibiotics.
- New CT imaging may be needed for an undrained collection, secondary perforation, infected hardware, biliary/urinary obstruction, Candida infection or resistant organism.
- A clear planned stop/review date, source-control adequacy and daily de-escalation decisions protect patients from C. difficile, renal toxicity and selection of resistant organisms.

items.title: 4. Antimicrobial treatment: pharmacology, spectrum, prescribing and toxicity
items.body:
## 4.1 Think from the organism and the site, not from the drug cupboard

- Selecting an antimicrobial is a probability and exposure problem.
- The likely pathogen is determined by anatomy, community or healthcare acquisition, recent antibiotics, immune state, devices and previous microbiology.
- The drug must then be active against that organism **and** reach the site in sufficient unbound concentration for long enough.
- Sepsis alters the distribution and elimination of drugs, so an otherwise ‘usual’ regimen may underdose during early capillary leak or overdose once acute kidney injury develops.
- A prescribing decision always includes dose, route, infusion duration, timing, renal function, allergies, interactions, monitoring, review date and source control.

- Organisms are usefully grouped into aerobic Gram-positive (staphylococci including MRSA, streptococci, enterococci), aerobic Gram-negative (Enterobacterales, Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter), anaerobes (Bacteroides, Clostridium spp), atypical intracellular pathogens (Legionella, Mycoplasma, Chlamydia) and yeasts/moulds.
- No single broad-spectrum antibiotic reliably covers all groups.
- Bacterial ‘resistance’ can result from β-lactamases (e.g. ESBL, AmpC, carbapenemases), altered binding proteins (MRSA PBP2a), target mutations, efflux pumps and permeability changes.

**A rational empiric sequence:**

- Identify source and likely organisms → estimate severity and risk of resistant pathogens → obtain appropriate cultures without delaying treatment → choose a regimen with the necessary likely coverage → give a full early loading dose → assess penetration and renal function → order prolonged infusion/TDM where appropriate → review at 24–48 hours and when culture/susceptibility results arrive → narrow, convert to oral or stop when justified.
- Seek local infectious-diseases/microbiology input for MDR risk, endocarditis, meningitis, prosthetic infection, severe immunosuppression or complex allergy.

## 4.2 Why pharmacodynamic targets differ across drug classes

**Time-dependent drugs (β-lactams):**

- Bactericidal activity depends mainly on the portion of the dosing interval that free concentration exceeds the organism’s MIC (**fT>MIC**).
- In severe infection some clinicians target 100% fT>MIC or even higher unbound concentrations, although optimal clinical targets remain uncertain.
- Prolonging a piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem infusion over 3–4 hours can improve target attainment at a given daily dose; initial loading must still be prompt.
- The 2026 SSC recommends prolonged β-lactam maintenance infusion after a loading dose for sepsis/shock.
- BLING III (2024) found improved clinical cure with continuous infusion and a mortality difference that did not reach significance in its prespecified unadjusted primary analysis; do not misreport it as proving a survival benefit.

**Concentration-dependent drugs (aminoglycosides):**

- Efficacy correlates with peak concentration relative to MIC (Cmax/MIC), commonly a target around 8–10 for serious Gram-negative infection.
- A high initial dose (e.g. gentamicin approximately 5–7 mg/kg IV in appropriate adults, institution-specific) may be followed by extended intervals; adjust using levels, renal function and clinical indication.
- Aminoglycosides are poorly active against anaerobes and should not be assumed to cover pneumonia well.
- Their nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity increase with prolonged exposure and other nephrotoxins; they are commonly used as short-course adjuncts, not indefinite ‘double cover’.

**Exposure-dependent drugs:**

- Vancomycin activity is linked to AUC/MIC; where relevant, target **AUC24/MIC 400–600** for serious MRSA infection assuming MIC 1 mg/L, balancing efficacy and kidney injury.
- Trough-only 15–20 mg/L targeting increases nephrotoxicity and is no longer the preferred primary strategy where AUC monitoring is available.
- Fluoroquinolones depend on AUC/MIC and peak/MIC; dosing is constrained by QT effects, dysglycaemia, tendinopathy, CNS toxicity and resistance.
- Linezolid has time/exposure-dependent activity, particularly useful in some resistant Gram-positive pulmonary infections but subject to platelet suppression and serotonin toxicity concerns.

- Volume of distribution (**Vd**) increases with capillary leak, aggressive resuscitation and extracorporeal circuits, particularly for hydrophilic drugs (β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides).
- Early septic shock therefore often requires **a full loading dose even when AKI is present**, because loading is driven principally by Vd; subsequent maintenance is adjusted to measured or estimated clearance.
- Augmented renal clearance can develop in younger hyperdynamic patients and lead to underexposure despite ‘normal’ creatinine.
- Continuous renal replacement therapy clears many antimicrobials depending on membrane, effluent dose and protein binding; use specific local dosing guidance and TDM rather than routinely halving everything.

## 4.3 Mechanism and spectrum: know the deliberate gaps

| **Antimicrobial family and mechanism** | **Typical clinically useful activity** | **Important absences, cautions and examples** |
|---|---|---|
| Penicillins/aminopenicillins: bind PBPs, inhibit wall cross-linking | Streptococci; amoxicillin also enterococci and Listeria when susceptible | Plain amoxicillin does **not** reliably cover β-lactamase-producing Gram-negatives or Pseudomonas |
| Flucloxacillin/cefazolin: antistaphylococcal wall drugs | MSSA, streptococci; cefazolin some community Gram-negative rods | Not MRSA, Enterococcus or Pseudomonas; cefazolin lacks meaningful anaerobic coverage |
| Amoxicillin–clavulanate | Many community Gram-positives, Enterobacterales and anaerobes | Not reliable ESBL/AmpC, Pseudomonas or MRSA; local resistance varies |
| Ceftriaxone (third-generation cephalosporin) | Streptococci, pneumococcus, meningococcus, many Enterobacterales | **No reliable Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, Listeria, MRSA or anaerobic Bacteroides coverage**; add metronidazole for many abdominal indications |
| Cefepime (fourth-generation cephalosporin) | Broad Gram-negative including susceptible Pseudomonas; MSSA and streptococci | Not Enterococcus, MRSA or anaerobes; **encephalopathy, myoclonus, seizures** especially with renal accumulation |
| Piperacillin–tazobactam | Broad Gram-negative incl susceptible Pseudomonas; many anaerobes, streptococci and E. faecalis | Not MRSA; **not dependable for serious invasive ESBL disease** even if a test reports susceptibility; some AmpC/carbapenemase resistance |
| Meropenem (carbapenem) | ESBL Enterobacterales, many anaerobes, susceptible Pseudomonas | **Not MRSA, VRE or atypical respiratory pathogens**; seizure potential and major valproate interaction |
| Vancomycin: cell-wall glycopeptide | MRSA and other susceptible Gram-positives including enterococci (not VRE) | **No Gram-negative or atypical activity**; AUC guided monitoring, kidney injury, infusion reaction; IV is needed for systemic infection, oral for luminal C. difficile |
| Linezolid: 50S protein synthesis inhibitor | MRSA and VRE; good lung tissue exposure | **No Gram-negative cover**; thrombocytopenia, neuropathy, lactic acidosis, serotonin syndrome risk |
| Clindamycin: 50S inhibitor | Susceptible Gram-positives, some anaerobes; suppresses certain streptococcal/clostridial toxin production | High C. difficile risk; resistance common in some Bacteroides/MRSA strains; not broad Gram-negative therapy |
| Metronidazole: DNA damage in anaerobes | Most obligate anaerobes and protozoa | **No aerobic bacterial cover**; neuropathy with prolonged use; consider interactions |
| Aminoglycosides: 30S inhibitors | Rapid bactericidal Gram-negative activity including some Pseudomonas | Poor anaerobic coverage; nephro-/ototoxicity; TDM and short courses preferred |
| Macrolides: 50S inhibitors | Atypical respiratory bacteria; some streptococci | Not reliable invasive Gram-negative therapy; QT and drug interactions (particularly clarithromycin) |
| Fluoroquinolones: DNA gyrase/topoisomerase inhibition | Variable Gram-negative and atypical activity; ciprofloxacin has Pseudomonas activity | Tendon, CNS, QT (agent-dependent), C. difficile, dysglycaemia, resistance; avoid uncritical routine use |
| Trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole: folate pathway inhibition | Some MRSA, Stenotrophomonas, Pneumocystis, Nocardia and urinary pathogens | Hyperkalaemia, cytopenias, rash/SJS, renal effects and drug interactions; not a default septic shock monotherapy |
| Echinocandins: inhibit fungal β-glucan synthesis | Most clinically important Candida including many azole-resistant isolates | Not an antibacterial; poor urinary and CNS penetration; limited activity against some uncommon yeasts |

**High-yield comparisons:**

- Ceftriaxone plus metronidazole may suit many community-acquired abdominal infections but does not cover Pseudomonas or enterococci; whether either needs empiric cover depends on source, acuity and host.
- Piperacillin–tazobactam adds Pseudomonas and many anaerobes but no MRSA cover and may be unsuitable for serious ESBL bacteraemia.
- Meropenem broadens reliable ESBL activity but still does not treat MRSA or VRE.
- Adding vancomycin solely because a patient is hypotensive is poor stewardship unless MRSA or relevant resistant Gram-positive risk exists.
- Likewise, double anaerobic cover (e.g. piperacillin–tazobactam **plus** metronidazole) is usually unnecessary.

### Adult dose examples: understand why the first dose and subsequent dose differ

- The following **illustrative severe-infection doses assume a typical adult with broadly preserved renal function**; they are not prescriptions for an individual patient.
- Local NZ/Australian hospital antibiotic guidelines, weight, infection site, renal replacement, augmented clearance and specialist advice take precedence.
- The loading-dose concept is particularly important in shock: capillary leak expands distribution, while AKI primarily changes subsequent clearance.

| **Agent** | **Illustrative initial/maintenance regimen** | **What to reassess immediately** |
|---|---|---|
| Ceftriaxone | **2 g IV every 24 h** for many serious infections (selected CNS indications use more frequent dosing per protocol) | Enterobacterales susceptibility, biliary disease, concomitant anaerobic or Listeria coverage |
| Piperacillin–tazobactam | **4.5 g IV every 6–8 h**, often via prolonged 3–4 h maintenance infusions after prompt loading | Renal function, Pseudomonas susceptibility and ESBL/AmpC concerns |
| Meropenem | **1 g IV every 8 h** for many severe infections; higher doses such as **2 g every 8 h** for selected CNS/less susceptible pathogens | Prolonged infusion, renal dose, seizure risk and valproate interaction |
| Cefepime | **2 g IV every 8–12 h** in serious susceptible infection | **Rapid renal dose adjustment** to prevent encephalopathy/myoclonus; no anaerobe or MRSA coverage |
| Vancomycin | Severe infection commonly warrants a **20–25 mg/kg IV loading dose** by actual body weight (max and infusion rate per policy), then individualised maintenance | AUC24/MIC goal **400–600**, kidney function, infusion reaction; only cover MRSA when indicated |
| Gentamicin | Selected serious Gram-negative infections: often **5–7 mg/kg IV initial dose** using an institution-specific dosing weight and protocol | Early drug levels, renal/ototoxicity and whether one dose suffices |
| Metronidazole | **500 mg IV/oral every 8–12 h** according to infection/policy | Need for anaerobic therapy; avoid duplicate cover and review prolonged-course neuropathy |
| Clindamycin | In severe toxin-mediated infection, for example **900 mg IV every 8 h** as an adjunct where indicated | Susceptibility/resistance and C. difficile risk; never substitute for source control |

- The same drug may require a different dose for meningitis, endocarditis, bacterial CNS abscess, obesity or continuous kidney replacement therapy.
- All beta-lactam **prolonged/continuous infusion regimens require a loading dose** if immediate effective concentrations are needed.
- Write the next review and adjustment time on the drug chart, because dynamic organ dysfunction makes yesterday’s ‘normal renal dose’ unreliable.

**2026 resistance guidance:**

- The IDSA 2026 antimicrobial-resistant Gram-negative guidance supersedes its 2024 version.
- For invasive ESBL-producing Enterobacterales disease **outside the urinary tract**, a susceptible carbapenem remains preferred, especially with sepsis, bacteraemia or high inoculum.
- Piperacillin–tazobactam is **not suggested** for ESBL infections outside the urinary tract even if the laboratory reports in-vitro susceptibility.
- For selected complicated urinary infection without critical illness or bacteraemia, it may be an alternative in carefully selected circumstances, but this is not permission to use it as definitive therapy for septic ESBL bloodstream infection.
- **AmpC-producing organisms** (for example Enterobacter cloacae complex, Klebsiella aerogenes and Citrobacter freundii) may acquire resistance during third-generation cephalosporin treatment; cefepime may be appropriate when susceptible, but severe infection or ESBL co-production changes the choice.
- Carbapenemase-producing organisms require mechanism-specific agents and expert microbiology input rather than simply doubling meropenem.
- These distinctions are examined because a “broad-spectrum” drug can be microbiologically broad yet clinically unreliable for a resistance mechanism.

## 4.4 Practical empirical therapy: why the syndrome matters

- The following examples are **patterns of coverage**, not a replacement for local NZ/Australian guidelines, susceptibilities or renal adjustment.
- In community-acquired intra-abdominal sepsis, cover Enterobacterales and anaerobes, for example ceftriaxone plus metronidazole if local susceptibility supports it; patients with severe hospital-acquired disease, recent broad antibiotics or proven resistant organisms may need piperacillin–tazobactam or meropenem with specialist input.
- In severe community-acquired pneumonia, cover pneumococcus and relevant atypicals, e.g. a suitable β-lactam plus macrolide, with Legionella consideration; anti-Pseudomonal treatment should follow validated risk rather than universal use.
- In obstructive urosepsis, Gram-negative activity and **urgent decompression** are decisive.
- In suspected bacterial meningitis, rapidly administer a CNS-penetrant regimen appropriate to age/immunocompromise and local guidelines; ceftriaxone alone does not cover Listeria.
- In necrotising fasciitis, combine prompt debridement with broad initial coverage and toxin-suppressing therapy when streptococcal or clostridial toxin disease is suspected.

**Antifungals require an independent risk assessment:**

- Echinocandin therapy (e.g. micafungin or anidulafungin) may be appropriate for high-risk septic shock with plausible invasive candidiasis, particularly post-abdominal surgery, recurrent leaks, total parenteral nutrition, prolonged antibiotics, Candida colonisation or severe immunosuppression.
- Antifungal therapy is not mandatory for all septic shock.
- Fluconazole is useful for susceptible species in stable patients and step-down treatment, but species and susceptibility matter; Candida glabrata may have reduced susceptibility and Candida krusei is intrinsically resistant.
- Amphotericin B may cover invasive mould/rare fungal infection but has important nephrotoxicity and electrolyte consequences; voriconazole/isavuconazole and mould-active prophylaxis require specialist oversight.
- Invasive candidiasis generally demands bloodstream clearance, assessment for disseminated infection and removal of an infected line when feasible.

## 4.5 Antibiotic adverse effects and anaesthetic interactions

- **IgE-mediated immediate hypersensitivity** can produce life-threatening anaphylaxis, but nausea, a remote childhood maculopapular rash or nonspecific intolerance is not equivalent to anaphylaxis.
- A structured history of the exact drug, time to reaction, phenotype, treatment and subsequent β-lactam tolerance prevents unnecessary broad-spectrum substitution.
- Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is influenced more by side-chain similarity than the shared β-lactam ring; many patients labelled penicillin allergic can safely receive cefazolin after appropriate assessment.
- Severe delayed immune reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS, certain organ injuries) require avoidance and specialist advice rather than routine graded challenge.

**Kidney and neurological injury:**

- Aminoglycosides, vancomycin (especially high exposures), amphotericin B and some combinations increase AKI risk.
- Cefepime accumulation can cause fluctuating consciousness, dysphasia, myoclonus or non-convulsive seizures; dose-adjust and consider the diagnosis in ICU delirium.
- Imipenem has greater seizure propensity than some other carbapenems, particularly with CNS disease or renal dysfunction. β-lactams can cause encephalopathy at extreme concentrations, especially in renal failure.
- Metronidazole and linezolid can cause peripheral neuropathy with prolonged treatment.

**Distinctive interactions:**

- Carbapenems rapidly decrease sodium valproate concentrations, sometimes provoking breakthrough seizures; dose increases of valproate are often ineffective while the carbapenem is continued, so use an alternative antimicrobial or antiepileptic plan with expert advice.
- Linezolid inhibits monoamine oxidase reversibly and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, methylene blue or other serotonergic drugs; balance urgency and monitor carefully.
- Macrolides and azole antifungals inhibit CYP enzymes and prolong QT, interacting with antiarrhythmics, some sedatives, statins and immunosuppressants (e.g. tacrolimus).
- Trimethoprim can cause hyperkalaemia, particularly with ACE inhibitors, ARBs or spironolactone.
- Rifampicin strongly induces CYP metabolism, reducing the effect of many drugs including some anticoagulants.
- Fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides can potentiate neuromuscular blockade and merit caution in myasthenia gravis.
- Daptomycin treats certain bloodstream Gram-positive infections but cannot treat pneumonia because pulmonary surfactant inactivates it.

**Gastrointestinal and haematological harm:**

- Broad-spectrum therapy disrupts microbiota and predisposes to C. difficile diarrhoea, particularly with clindamycin, cephalosporins and fluoroquinolones.
- Linezolid can cause thrombocytopenia after sustained treatment; chloramphenicol can cause marrow suppression; trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole and β-lactams can cause immune cytopenias.
- Piperacillin–tazobactam, cephalosporins and other agents occasionally cause interstitial nephritis or cholestatic injury.
- Monitor liver tests and full blood count during prolonged therapy.
- C. difficile management requires stopping the precipitating agent when possible, diagnostic testing of appropriate symptomatic stool, oral fidaxomicin/vancomycin according to current local protocols, and fulminant-disease management including surgical advice when needed.

## 4.6 Stewardship is part of intensive care quality

- Every ICU antimicrobial prescription should document the **indication, likely source, empirical organism targets, cultures sent, dose/infusion plan, anticipated duration and review point**.
- At 24–48 hours ask whether infection is still likely, whether all active agents are needed, whether drug levels require adjustment and whether source control is complete.
- De-escalation may mean discontinuing vancomycin when MRSA is unlikely, changing meropenem to a narrower susceptible agent, converting IV to oral therapy when absorption and severity allow, or stopping antibiotics entirely when the alternative diagnosis is clear.
- Do not prolong treatment merely because the CRP is falling slowly.

- Aminoglycoside levels and kidney function should be reviewed from the first day.
- Vancomycin exposure should be guided by AUC-based systems where available.
- TDM can be considered for critically ill patients with changing clearance or CRRT, and specialist β-lactam TDM can be useful when available; the 2026 SSC supports selected case-by-case use.
- Unexpected treatment failure should prompt reassessment of source control, wrong diagnosis, resistance, underexposure and non-infectious mimics in that order—not merely progressively broader antibiotics.

items.title: 5. Preventing infection in theatre, intensive care and vulnerable patients
