| [ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 (2025)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.20402) | Personalised CRT/echo/fluid-responsiveness algorithm improved a hierarchical composite, mainly shorter organ-support duration; not proof of mortality reduction in isolation |
| [CLASSIC (2022)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2202707) | Post-initial ICU fluid restriction did not reduce 90-day mortality versus standard care |
| [CLOVERS (2023)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2212663) | Early fluid-restrictive/pressor-forward strategy showed no significant 90-day survival advantage over liberal fluids |
| [ARISE FLUIDS (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2516225) | Australia/NZ-led: early pressor/restricted fluid did not increase days alive and out of hospital at 90 days, though pulmonary oedema was less frequent; supports individualisation |
| [ADRENAL (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1705835) | Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day accelerated shock resolution without statistically significant overall 90-day mortality benefit |
| [APROCCHSS (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1705716) | Hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone reduced 90-day mortality in a different septic shock population; discuss contrasting inclusion/severity/regimens |
| [BLING III (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2024.9779) | Continuous β-lactam infusion improved clinical cure; primary unadjusted mortality difference not statistically significant, supporting careful evidence interpretation |
| [MERINO (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2018.12163) | Piperacillin–tazobactam not supported as definitive therapy for ceftriaxone-resistant E. coli/Klebsiella bacteraemia relative to meropenem |
| [STOP-IT (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1411162) | After adequate source control, fixed ≈4-day therapy comparable to longer symptom-driven courses in complicated intra-abdominal infection; requires appropriate patient selection |

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Primary guidelines, curriculum and exam reports

- **1.** **ANZCA.** Anaesthesia Training Program Curriculum, version 1.14, December 2025. User-supplied document; the primary source for outcome terminology and codes.
- **2.** **SCCM/European Society of Intensive Care Medicine.** [Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock (2026)](https://www.sccm.org/clinical-resources/guidelines/guidelines/surviving-sepsis-campaign-international-guidelines-for-management-of-sepsis-and-septic-shock-2026). Central evidence source for antibiotic and source-control timing, fluids, vasopressors, steroids and organ support.
- **3.** **ANZCA.** [PG28 Infection Prevention and Control (2025)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/41b75be4-4c78-4318-8ac4-3d0dd2ca8f8f/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG28-Infection-prevention-and-control-2025.pdf?language=en). Equipment reprocessing, injection safety, airway devices, infection precautions and theatre practice.
- **4.** **ANZAAG/ANZCA.** [Perioperative Anaphylaxis Management Guideline (2022)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/resources/professional-documents/endorsed-guidelines/anaphylaxis-guideline-2022.pdf). Australian/New Zealand adult and paediatric crisis algorithms, adrenaline, fluids and post-crisis response; consult the [ANZCA algorithm/card collection](https://www.anzca.edu.au/safety-and-advocacy/standards-of-practice/perioperative-anaphylaxis-management-guidelines) in practice.
- **5.** **ANZCA.** [PG69 Prevention, Investigation and Follow-up of Perioperative Hypersensitivity Reactions and Anaphylaxis (2025)](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/0f526e72-c35f-46d7-a816-746e63f92079/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/PG69-Perioperative-hypersensitivity-reactions-2025.pdf?language=en). Specialist referral, testing, documentation, future anaesthetic planning.
- **6.** **IDSA.** [Guidance on Treatment of Antimicrobial-Resistant Gram-Negative Infections (2026 update)](https://www.idsociety.org/practice-guideline/amr-guidance/). Resistance mechanism and ESBL/AmpC/CRE/DTR-Pseudomonas treatment interpretation; supersedes the 2024 version.
- **7.** **ASHP/IDSA/SIS/SHEA.** [Clinical Practice Guidelines for Antimicrobial Prophylaxis in Surgery](https://academic.oup.com/ajhp/article/70/3/195/5112717). Procedure-dependent prophylaxis, administration timing and cefazolin redosing; reconcile with current local surgical guidance.
- **8.** **ANZCA Final Examination Chairs’ Reports (provided):** 2023.2, 2024.2, 2025.1, 2025.2 and 2026.1; read question-specific examiner standards alongside curriculum, not as evidence for obsolete recommendations.

## BJA Education and complementary clinical reading

- **1.** **Dewachter P, Savic L.** [Perioperative anaphylaxis: pathophysiology, clinical presentation and management](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807982/). BJA Education 2019;19:313–320. Useful for mediator physiology, absent cutaneous signs, testing and differential; use ANZAAG for local doses.
- **2.** Manigrasso J, Desai N, Naoum E. Maternal sepsis: background, diagnosis and management. BJA Education 2024;24:389–398. DOI 10.1016/j.bjae.2024.06.004. Maternal sepsis assessment and treatment; cite alongside obstetric guidelines.
- **3.** **BJA Education.** [Metabolic acidosis in anaesthesia and critical care](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10874758/). Relevant to lactate interpretation, acid–base differential and selected bicarbonate decisions.
- **4.** **Sepsis-3 task force (Singer et al).** [Third International Consensus Definitions for Sepsis and Septic Shock](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2492881). JAMA 2016. Definitions, SOFA and septic shock phenotype; SIRS terminology retained in curriculum for historical comparison.
- **5.** **NAP6 investigators.** [Anaesthesia, surgery and life-threatening allergic reactions: sixth National Audit Project](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29935567/). Epidemiology, suspected triggers and serious perioperative outcomes; local incidence may vary.

## ANZCA Blue Book chapters audited (relevant editions)

- Chang K, Haseeb A, Khoyratty S. The emergency laparotomy patient. Australasian Anaesthesia 2025, pp 131–148. Source control, NELA/SORT, frailty, perioperative emergency-laparotomy care.  [https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1386](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1386)
- Martyr L, Cook S, Senthuran S. Keep calm and know sepsis. Australasian Anaesthesia 2019. Useful for sepsis physiology and history; apply current 2026 SSC recommendations instead of historical algorithms.  [https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/23f2add6-d29f-495a-a094-81157ded47b3/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book-2019.pdf?language=en](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/23f2add6-d29f-495a-a094-81157ded47b3/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book-2019.pdf?language=en)
- Nguyen TM, Szental J, Bramley D. A narrative review of the perioperative management of DMARDs. Australasian Anaesthesia 2023, pp 23–36. Balance infection and flare risks with medication holds.  [https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1194](https://hdl.handle.net/11055/1194)
- Platt PR, Sadleir P, Clarke R. Anaphylactic shock under anaesthesia: a reappraisal of the pathophysiology and management. Australasian Anaesthesia 2015. Historic pathophysiology; current ANZAAG takes priority.  [https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/5d46b97a-87c1-4055-8ebf-cac65388433a/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book-2015.pdf?language=en](https://www.anzca.edu.au/getContentAsset/5d46b97a-87c1-4055-8ebf-cac65388433a/80feb437-d24d-46b8-a858-4a2a28b9b970/Blue-Book-2015.pdf?language=en)

## 2024–2026 CNS infection and topical evidence updates

- World Health Organization. WHO guidelines on meningitis diagnosis, treatment and care (2025).  [https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240108042](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240108042)
- NICE. NG240: Bacterial meningitis and meningococcal disease recognition, investigation and management (2024).  [https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/Recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/Recommendations)
- UK Joint Societies. Management of suspected infectious and autoimmune encephalitis in adults (published 11 October 2026). Journal of Infection; DOI 10.1016/j.jinf.2026.106873.  [https://www.journalofinfection.com/article/S0163-4453%2826%2900199-4/fulltext](https://www.journalofinfection.com/article/S0163-4453%2826%2900199-4/fulltext)
- ANZAAG. Perioperative anaphylaxis testing recommendations (four to six weeks; early negative tests require caution).  [https://media.anzaag.com/2022/09/26104018/testing-guidelines.pdf](https://media.anzaag.com/2022/09/26104018/testing-guidelines.pdf)
- Australian Government. Immunisations for health care workers (updated 18 June 2025).  [https://www.health.gov.au/topics/immunisation/immunisation-information-for-health-professionals/immunisations-for-health-care-workers](https://www.health.gov.au/topics/immunisation/immunisation-information-for-health-professionals/immunisations-for-health-care-workers)
- Manigrasso J, Desai N, Naoum E. Maternal sepsis: background, diagnosis and management. BJA Education 2024;24:389–398.  [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.06.004](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2024.06.004)
- Pisano A, Venditto M, Palmieri C, Landoni G. Novel therapies and interventions in sepsis and septic shock. BJA Education 2025;25:206–217.  [https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.01.003](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bjae.2025.01.003)

## Evidence audit and boundaries

**Examiner report application check.** The supplied **2026.1** report tested management under the 2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign, physiological optimisation for emergency surgery in severe sepsis, and decision-making for transfer of a deteriorating septic patient. The **2025.2** report listed steroid treatment in septic shock and paediatric anaphylaxis. The **2025.1** report identified major omissions in severe maternal pneumonia answers when candidates described fetal management but not maternal ventilation, circulation and antibiotics. The **2024.2** report examined grade 2 anaphylaxis during emergency surgery and obstructive urosepsis; the **2023.2** report examined septic shock recommendations and perioperative anaphylaxis. These scenarios informed the practical clinical reasoning woven into Chapters 2, 3 and 6; historical examiner questions are not evidence that an older guideline remains correct.

Evidence-audit boundaries. The supplied workbook has now been checked row by row, and all 20 rows have identifiable teaching sections (15 complete-assigned outcomes and five allocated components). Publicly accessible Blue Book editions (2015, 2019, 2023 and 2025) were checked for relevant chapters. The 2019 sepsis and 2015 anaphylaxis chapters inform mechanisms and historical perspectives but are not used to override the 2026 SSC, 2025 PG69, or current ANZAAG crisis guidance. Proprietary textbook and subscription-only full-text access was not independently verified; evidence certainty remains variable for local antimicrobial doses, neuraxial placement during infection, rescue anaphylaxis therapies and individualised surgery timing. Clinicians must cross-check current local NZ prescribing, emergency pathways and infection-prevention policies. The mapping audit is complete for the provided workbook sheet, not for all ANZCA learning outcomes assigned to other sets.

items.title: How do you recognise anaphylaxis under anaesthesia?
items.q: How do you recognise anaphylaxis under anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Hypotension, tachycardia or arrhythmia.
- Bronchospasm with high airway pressure.
- Flushing, urticaria or angioedema (may be hidden).
- Onset within minutes of an IV drug.

> **Closing point:** Collapse is often the first sign.

items.title: What is the first-line drug for anaphylaxis and how is it given?
items.q: What is the first-line drug for anaphylaxis and how is it given?
items.a:
- Adrenaline.
- Monitored adult IV: grade 2 10–20 micrograms, grade 3 50–100 micrograms, titrated/repeated to response.
- IM 0.5 mg if there is no IV access.
- Infusion for refractory shock; 1 mg IV in arrest.

> **Closing point:** Adrenaline early and titrated.

## Audit clarification and extension

These are monitored adult perioperative IV doses: grade 2 uses 10–20 micrograms, grade 3 50–100 micrograms, titrated to response. Use the current ANZAAG card; do not give an arrest-dose bolus to a patient with a pulse.

items.title: What are your immediate actions for suspected intraoperative anaphylaxis?
items.q: What are your immediate actions for suspected intraoperative anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- Call for help and stop the trigger.
- 100% oxygen and secure the airway.
- Adrenaline and rapid fluids.
- Take tryptase and record times.

> **Closing point:** Treat first, test as you go.

items.title: What do you do if anaphylaxis is refractory to adrenaline?
items.q: What do you do if anaphylaxis is refractory to adrenaline?
items.a:
- Adrenaline infusion.
- Vasopressin or noradrenaline.
- Glucagon if on a beta-blocker.
- Exceptional expert rescue may include ECMO; methylene blue has limited evidence and important risks, so is not routine escalation. First check adrenaline delivery, volume, continuing trigger and alternative shock causes.

> **Closing point:** Reassess delivery and physiology while escalating expert support, fluids and vasopressors appropriately.

items.title: What is the differential diagnosis for sudden collapse after induction?
items.q: What is the differential diagnosis for sudden collapse after induction?
items.a:
- Anaphylaxis and drug overdose.
- Hypovolaemia and tension pneumothorax.
- High neuraxial block and aspiration.
- Embolism and cardiac causes.

> **Closing point:** Treat common causes early.

items.title: What is the role of steroids and antihistamines in anaphylaxis?
items.q: What is the role of steroids and antihistamines in anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- Not first line.
- Adjuncts after adrenaline.
- Do not delay adrenaline.
- Steroids do not prevent biphasic reactions reliably.

> **Closing point:** Adrenaline saves lives.

items.title: What is a biphasic reaction and how does it affect disposition?
items.q: What is a biphasic reaction and how does it affect disposition?
items.a:
- Recurrence hours after resolution.
- Risk higher after severe reactions and delayed adrenaline.
- Observe at least 6 hours.
- Longer or overnight for severe reactions.

> **Closing point:** Monitored observation.

items.title: When do you proceed with surgery after intraoperative anaphylaxis?
items.q: When do you proceed with surgery after intraoperative anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- Abandon if the reaction was severe.
- Proceed only if urgent or life-saving.
- Remove the suspected trigger.
- Use invasive monitoring and ICU afterwards.

> **Closing point:** Severity and urgency decide.

## Audit clarification and extension

Severity, urgency, response and surgical stage guide this decision with the surgeon; not every reaction mandates abandonment, and severe ongoing instability strongly favours postponement when feasible.

items.title: What are the most common causes of perioperative anaphylaxis?
items.q: What are the most common causes of perioperative anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- Neuromuscular blocking drugs.
- Antibiotics, especially cefazolin.
- Chlorhexidine, dyes, sugammadex and latex.
- Gelatin and blood products.

> **Closing point:** NMBDs and antibiotics lead.

items.title: How is mast cell tryptase sampled after anaphylaxis?
items.q: How is mast cell tryptase sampled after anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- Sample immediately when feasible without delaying resuscitation.
- Repeat at 1 hour and 4 hours after onset.
- Baseline after 24 hours, or later follow-up.
- Record exact times.

> **Closing point:** Four local card time points, including time zero.

items.title: How do you interpret tryptase?
items.q: How do you interpret tryptase?
items.a:
- Positive above 1.2 times baseline plus 2 micrograms/L.
- A normal value does not exclude anaphylaxis.
- High baseline needs assessment for mast-cell disease, hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia and other causes.
- Half-life about 2 hours.

> **Closing point:** Compare with baseline.

items.title: When and how are patients tested for allergy after a reaction?
items.q: When and how are patients tested for allergy after a reaction?
items.a:
- At 4 to 6 weeks.
- Skin prick and intradermal tests.
- Specific IgE where available.
- Drug challenge for safe alternatives.

> **Closing point:** Provide every exposure; the specialist selects relevant tests and alternatives.

items.title: What communication follows an anaphylactic reaction?
items.q: What communication follows an anaphylactic reaction?
items.a:
- Open disclosure to the patient.
- Interim letter to GP and surgeon.
- Final letter after allergy testing.
- Alert in the record and a medical alert bracelet.

> **Closing point:** Written information protects future care.

items.title: How do you plan an anaesthetic for a patient with a history of perioperative reaction?
items.q: How do you plan an anaesthetic for a patient with a history of perioperative reaction?
items.a:
- Get records and history; assume risk if unknown.
- Discuss with the surgeon and patient.
- Low-trigger drug plan and latex-free.
- Prepare for anaphylaxis and arrange HDU.

> **Closing point:** Information, plan, preparation.

## Audit clarification and extension

Avoid likely previous triggers/cross-reactants, including chlorhexidine and latex; consider NMBA-free techniques and specialist advice. Rocuronium plus available sugammadex is not a safe default.

items.title: Why is neuromuscular blocker allergy often unexpected?
items.q: Why is neuromuscular blocker allergy often unexpected?
items.a:
- Cross-sensitisation from quaternary ammonium compounds.
- Found in cosmetics and household products.
- May react on first exposure.
- Cross-reactivity between agents is common.

> **Closing point:** No prior exposure is needed.

items.title: What are the features of latex allergy?
items.q: What are the features of latex allergy?
items.a:
- Type I anaphylaxis, type IV dermatitis.
- Risk groups: spina bifida, healthcare workers, repeated surgery.
- Cross-reaction with banana, avocado and kiwi.
- Latex-free theatre, first on the list.

> **Closing point:** Remove exposure.

## Audit clarification and extension

First-case scheduling is most relevant with environmental powdered-latex contamination; verify a latex-safe pathway throughout admission and recovery.

items.title: Why is chlorhexidine allergy easily missed?
items.q: Why is chlorhexidine allergy easily missed?
items.a:
- Hidden in lines, catheters, gels and dressings.
- Onset can be delayed 20 to 40 minutes.
- Often misattributed to antibiotics.
- Consider it in all unexplained reactions.

> **Closing point:** Check exposure to chlorhexidine.

items.title: How is sepsis defined?
items.q: How is sepsis defined?
items.a:
- Life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response.
- Acute SOFA rise of 2 or more with suspected infection; treatment is clinical and must not await a complete score.
- Septic shock: vasopressors for MAP 65 and lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate volume assessment/resuscitation.
- qSOFA is a prognostic warning and must not be the sole sepsis screen.

> **Closing point:** Sepsis-3 definitions.

items.title: What are the pathophysiological features of sepsis?
items.q: What are the pathophysiological features of sepsis?
items.a:
- Cytokine response via Toll-like receptors.
- Endothelial dysfunction and capillary leak.
- Vasodilatation from nitric oxide.
- Coagulopathy and mitochondrial dysfunction.

> **Closing point:** Dysregulated inflammation.

items.title: What mechanisms cause organ dysfunction in sepsis?
items.q: What mechanisms cause organ dysfunction in sepsis?
items.a:
- Microcirculatory failure and shunting.
- Cytopathic hypoxia.
- Endothelial injury and microthrombi.
- Septic cardiomyopathy.

> **Closing point:** Perfusion and cellular failure.

items.title: What is the sepsis first-hour bundle?
items.q: What is the sepsis first-hour bundle?
items.a:
- Lactate and blood cultures.
- Antibiotics within 1 hour.
- Initial crystalloid for hypoperfusion/shock with reassessment; 30 mL/kg within 3 h is conditional, not a requirement for every infection.
- Vasopressors for MAP below 65.

> **Closing point:** Time-critical care.

items.title: What are your initial resuscitation goals in septic shock?
items.q: What are your initial resuscitation goals in septic shock?
items.a:
- MAP at least 65.
- Falling lactate and good perfusion.
- Urine output at least 0.5 mL/kg/h.
- Source control and antibiotics.

> **Closing point:** Perfusion, not numbers alone.

items.title: Which fluid do you choose in septic shock?
items.q: Which fluid do you choose in septic shock?
items.a:
- Balanced crystalloid preferred.
- Albumin when large volumes are needed.
- Avoid starches (6S, CHEST).
- Avoid gelatins.

> **Closing point:** Balanced crystalloid first.

items.title: When do you start vasopressors in septic shock?
items.q: When do you start vasopressors in septic shock?
items.a:
- Early, if hypotensive after initial fluid.
- Noradrenaline first line.
- Peripheral access acceptable initially.
- Add vasopressin, then adrenaline.

> **Closing point:** Do not chase hypotension with fluid.

items.title: How do you assess fluid responsiveness?
items.q: How do you assess fluid responsiveness?
items.a:
- Passive leg raise.
- Pulse-pressure/stroke-volume variation only when rhythm and ventilation conditions make them valid.
- PLR needs measured stroke-volume response; IVC size alone is unreliable.
- Avoid fixed CVP targets.

> **Closing point:** Dynamic over static.

items.title: When is hydrocortisone used in septic shock?
items.q: When is hydrocortisone used in septic shock?
items.a:
- Escalating vasopressor requirement.
- 200 mg/day.
- No compulsory 0.25-microgram/kg/min threshold or four-hour wait; individualise for ongoing shock.
- May shorten shock duration.

> **Closing point:** Refractory shock.

items.title: What is the role of source control?
items.q: What is the role of source control?
items.a:
- Drain abscesses.
- Relieve obstruction.
- Debride necrotic tissue.
- Remove infected devices.

> **Closing point:** Antibiotics alone are not enough.

items.title: How do you manage meningococcal septicaemia?
items.q: How do you manage meningococcal septicaemia?
items.a:
- Immediate ceftriaxone or cefotaxime.
- Fluid boluses and early inotrope.
- Early intubation.
- Isolation, notification and contact prophylaxis.

> **Closing point:** Treat on suspicion.

## Audit clarification and extension

For the 14-year-old: titrated 10–20 mL/kg boluses with reassessment, early vasoactive support if needed, immediate meningitis-dose ceftriaxone and PICU retrieval. Avoid etomidate and LP in shock/coma/coagulopathy.

items.title: Why avoid lumbar puncture in meningococcal shock?
items.q: Why avoid lumbar puncture in meningococcal shock?
items.a:
- Risk of herniation or bleeding.
- Delays antibiotics.
- Coagulopathy is likely.
- Blood PCR gives the diagnosis.

> **Closing point:** Do not delay antibiotics.

items.title: What does universal precautions mean?
items.q: What does universal precautions mean?
items.a:
- Treat every patient as potentially infectious.
- Aimed at blood-borne pathogens.
- Applies to blood and specified body fluids.
- Now incorporated into standard precautions.

> **Closing point:** Applies to all patients.

items.title: How do you apply universal precautions in daily anaesthesia?
items.q: How do you apply universal precautions in daily anaesthesia?
items.a:
- Hand hygiene.
- Gloves, masks and eye protection.
- Safe sharps handling.
- Single-use equipment and disinfection of reusable items.

> **Closing point:** Habits that protect staff and patients.

items.title: How do universal, standard and additional precautions differ?
items.q: How do universal, standard and additional precautions differ?
items.a:
- Universal: blood-borne pathogens.
- Standard: blood/body fluids, secretions/excretions except sweat, skin/mucosa and respiratory hygiene.
- Additional: airborne, droplet or contact for known infection.
- TB and CJD need additional precautions.

> **Closing point:** Know the three tiers.

items.title: Define decontamination, disinfection and sterilisation.
items.q: Define decontamination, disinfection and sterilisation.
items.a:
- Decontamination: make an item safe by removing/inactivating contamination; cleaning removes soil first.
- Disinfection: kills non-sporing organisms.
- Sterilisation: kills all including spores.
- Clean first.

> **Closing point:** Spores separate disinfection from sterilisation.

items.title: What measures protect the patient airway from cross-infection?
items.q: What measures protect the patient airway from cross-infection?
items.a:
- Hand hygiene and disposable equipment.
- Breathing system filters.
- Laryngoscope blades disinfected and handles decontaminated.
- Absorber and ventilator maintenance.

> **Closing point:** Filters and clean airway devices.

items.title: How do you reprocess laryngoscope blades?
items.q: How do you reprocess laryngoscope blades?
items.a:
- Single-use where possible.
- Clean then high-level disinfect or sterilise.
- Handles are cleaned and disinfected.
- Track reprocessing.

> **Closing point:** Semi-critical items.

items.title: What is the Spaulding classification?
items.q: What is the Spaulding classification?
items.a:
- Critical: sterile tissue.
- Semi-critical: mucous membrane.
- Non-critical: intact skin.
- Each needs a matching level of processing.

> **Closing point:** Match risk to processing.

items.title: What is the role of a breathing system filter?
items.q: What is the role of a breathing system filter?
items.a:
- Protects the patient from circuit contamination.
- Protects the circuit and machine.
- Placed at the patient end.
- Replace between patients.

> **Closing point:** Two-way protection.

items.title: What are the infection control precautions for tuberculosis?
items.q: What are the infection control precautions for tuberculosis?
items.a:
- Postpone elective surgery.
- N95 respirator for staff.
- Filter on the circuit.
- Isolated recovery and air changes.

> **Closing point:** Airborne precautions.

items.title: What are the precautions for a patient with suspected CJD?
items.q: What are the precautions for a patient with suspected CJD?
items.a:
- Single-use equipment.
- Quarantine instruments in contact with high-infectivity tissue.
- Standard precautions for blood and CSF.
- Notify infection control.

> **Closing point:** Prions resist routine sterilisation.

items.title: How do you manage a needlestick injury?
items.q: How do you manage a needlestick injury?
items.a:
- Wash promptly; allow spontaneous bleeding, without squeezing or sucking.
- Report and document.
- Test source and recipient.
- Post-exposure prophylaxis and follow-up.

> **Closing point:** Act within hours.

items.title: Which vaccinations are recommended for healthcare workers?
items.q: Which vaccinations are recommended for healthcare workers?
items.a:
- Hepatitis B with titre check.
- Influenza and COVID-19.
- MMR and varicella.
- Pertussis booster.

> **Closing point:** Hepatitis B first.

items.title: How do you minimise central line infection?
items.q: How do you minimise central line infection?
items.a:
- Consider whether the line is needed.
- Hand hygiene and full barrier precautions.
- Chlorhexidine-alcohol skin preparation.
- Daily review and early removal.

> **Closing point:** Bundle of care.

items.title: Which central line site has the highest infection risk?
items.q: Which central line site has the highest infection risk?
items.a:
- Femoral has infection/thrombosis concerns; risk is context-dependent.
- Internal jugular is intermediate.
- Subclavian is lowest but has higher mechanical risk.
- Use ultrasound guidance.

> **Closing point:** Balance infection, thrombosis and mechanical risks for this patient.

items.title: Compare povidone-iodine and chlorhexidine skin preparation.
items.q: Compare povidone-iodine and chlorhexidine skin preparation.
items.a:
- Chlorhexidine-alcohol: bactericidal, persistent, less affected by organic matter; still remove visible contamination.
- Povidone-iodine: slower, inactivated by blood.
- Both can cause anaphylaxis.
- Allow to dry before neuraxial puncture.

> **Closing point:** Chlorhexidine-alcohol is preferred.

items.title: What guidelines reduce epidural infection?
items.q: What guidelines reduce epidural infection?
items.a:
- Select patients and justify use.
- Aseptic insertion and filter use.
- Limit catheter duration.
- Monitor and educate patients.

> **Closing point:** Prevent and detect early.

items.title: How do you manage a suspected epidural abscess?
items.q: How do you manage a suspected epidural abscess?
items.a:
- Urgent MRI.
- Blood cultures and antibiotics including MRSA cover.
- Neurosurgical referral.
- Remove the catheter.

> **Closing point:** Decompress early.

items.title: How do you prevent infection in the trauma setting?
items.q: How do you prevent infection in the trauma setting?
items.a:
- Early antibiotics for open fractures.
- Tetanus prophylaxis.
- Wound debridement.
- Aseptic technique for lines.

> **Closing point:** Time to antibiotics matters.

items.title: When should antibiotic prophylaxis be given?
items.q: When should antibiotic prophylaxis be given?
items.a:
- Within 60 minutes before incision.
- Before tourniquet inflation.
- Single dose usually suffices.
- Redose for long surgery or heavy bleeding.

> **Closing point:** Timing is critical.

items.title: Which surgery needs antibiotic prophylaxis?
items.q: Which surgery needs antibiotic prophylaxis?
items.a:
- Clean-contaminated and contaminated surgery.
- Clean surgery with prosthesis.
- Cardiac and vascular implants.
- Not routine for most clean surgery.

> **Closing point:** Risk of infection and consequences.

items.title: How are antimicrobials classified by mechanism?
items.q: How are antimicrobials classified by mechanism?
items.a:
- Cell wall: beta-lactams and glycopeptides.
- Protein synthesis: aminoglycosides, macrolides, tetracyclines.
- Nucleic acid: quinolones and rifampicin.
- Membrane: polymyxins and daptomycin.

> **Closing point:** Four main targets.

items.title: What are important adverse effects of antibiotics in ICU?
items.q: What are important adverse effects of antibiotics in ICU?
items.a:
- Nephrotoxicity from aminoglycosides, vancomycin, colistin.
- Neurotoxicity from beta-lactams in renal failure.
- QT prolongation from macrolides and quinolones.
- C. difficile and resistance.

> **Closing point:** Dose for organ function.

items.title: How do you prescribe antibiotics rationally?
items.q: How do you prescribe antibiotics rationally?
items.a:
- Take cultures first.
- Choose by source and local resistance.
- Use loading doses and adjust for organ dysfunction.
- De-escalate and limit duration.

> **Closing point:** Right drug, dose and duration.

items.title: What is the cross-reactivity risk between penicillin and cephalosporins?
items.q: What is the cross-reactivity risk between penicillin and cephalosporins?
items.a:
- No single class-wide percentage: risk depends on the exact drug and R1 side chain.
- Related to side-chain similarity.
- Most reported penicillin allergy is not true.
- Cefazolin has unique side chains.

> **Closing point:** Low risk in most patients.

items.title: What is red man syndrome?
items.q: What is red man syndrome?
items.a:
- Vancomycin histamine release.
- Related to infusion rate.
- Flushing and hypotension.
- Slow the infusion and give antihistamine.

> **Closing point:** Usually a rate-related non-IgE infusion reaction; severe collapse still needs assessment/treatment for anaphylaxis.

items.title: What are the features of bacterial meningitis?
items.q: What are the features of bacterial meningitis?
items.a:
- Fever, headache and neck stiffness.
- Reduced consciousness and seizures.
- Petechial rash in meningococcal disease.
- Raised ICP signs.

> **Closing point:** Treat quickly.

items.title: How do you treat bacterial meningitis?
items.q: How do you treat bacterial meningitis?
items.a:
- Ceftriaxone, with vancomycin and ampicillin where indicated.
- Dexamethasone with the first dose when bacterial meningitis is strongly suspected, then pathogen/CSF-based review.
- CT before lumbar puncture if indicated.
- Manage raised ICP.

> **Closing point:** Antibiotics before investigations.

## Audit clarification and extension

LP first only if safe and without treatment delay; shock or coagulopathy still contraindicates LP despite a normal CT. Reassess dexamethasone when CSF/pathogen results return.

items.title: How do you treat suspected encephalitis?
items.q: How do you treat suspected encephalitis?
items.a:
- IV aciclovir early.
- MRI, EEG and CSF PCR.
- Control seizures.
- Consider autoimmune causes.

> **Closing point:** Treat as HSV until excluded.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic issues in a transplant recipient?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic issues in a transplant recipient?
items.a:
- Immunosuppression and infection risk.
- Organ-specific dysfunction; only a transplanted heart is denervated.
- Drug interactions with ciclosporin or tacrolimus.
- Aseptic technique and renal protection.

> **Closing point:** Protect graft function, continue an agreed immunosuppressant plan, and prevent infection.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic issues in necrotising fasciitis?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic issues in necrotising fasciitis?
items.a:
- Urgent debridement is the priority.
- Resuscitation and vasopressors.
- Antibiotics with clindamycin.
- Prepare for blood loss and repeat surgery.

> **Closing point:** Do not delay source control.

items.title: What are the anaesthetic implications of HIV infection?
items.q: What are the anaesthetic implications of HIV infection?
items.a:
- Review CD4/viral load for elective risk assessment; do not delay urgent surgery for results.
- Drug interactions with antiretrovirals.
- Opportunistic infection and organ involvement.
- Universal precautions.

> **Closing point:** Treat as for any infection risk.

items.title: What were SIRS and severe sepsis, and how do they differ from current sepsis?
items.q: What were SIRS and severe sepsis, and how do they differ from current sepsis?
items.a:
- SIRS was ≥2 of temperature >38 or <36°C, pulse >90/min, respiratory rate >20/min or PaCO2 <32 mmHg, WBC >12 or <4 ×10⁹/L or >10% immature forms.
- Legacy sepsis was infection plus SIRS; severe sepsis added organ dysfunction.
- Current sepsis is life-threatening organ dysfunction due to dysregulated response to infection, operationally acute SOFA rise ≥2.
- SIRS is not specific; qSOFA cannot exclude sepsis and a complete score must not delay treatment.

items.title: What determines antibiotic timing when sepsis is only possible?
items.q: What determines antibiotic timing when sepsis is only possible?
items.a:
- Shock or probable/definite sepsis: effective treatment urgently, ideally within one hour.
- Possible sepsis without shock: rapid assessment for infection and alternatives; treat within three hours if concern persists.
- Obtain cultures first if this causes no meaningful delay.
- Reassess and stop antibiotics if an alternative diagnosis becomes likely; do not use a low procalcitonin alone to withhold urgent treatment.

items.title: How do fluid need, responsiveness and tolerance differ?
items.q: How do fluid need, responsiveness and tolerance differ?
items.a:
- Need means a perfusion deficit that volume may improve.
- Responsiveness means stroke volume rises with a preload challenge; measure output during passive leg raise.
- Tolerance means volume can be given without harmful pulmonary/venous congestion.
- A responsive but adequately perfused patient does not automatically need a bolus.

items.title: When would you remove fluid after septic shock?
items.q: When would you remove fluid after septic shock?
items.a:
- Once acute shock is controlled, assess clinically important overload and organ congestion.
- Stop unnecessary maintenance and account for drug/flush/feed inputs.
- Use an individual diuretic target; kidney replacement is for suitable refractory overload or other indications.
- Monitor perfusion, pressure, renal function and electrolytes; pause for intolerance.
- Do not claim routine aggressive removal has proven survival benefit.

items.title: What did ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 show?
items.q: What did ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 show?
items.a:
- A personalised capillary-refill-guided haemodynamic strategy improved a hierarchical composite outcome.
- The composite prioritised death, duration of vital support and hospital stay.
- The advantage was largely driven by vital-support duration, not established isolated mortality reduction.
- Capillary refill complements clinical assessment, lactate and haemodynamics; it does not replace diagnosis or source control.

items.title: Why might a septic patient need a loading dose despite AKI?
items.q: Why might a septic patient need a loading dose despite AKI?
items.a:
- Capillary leak and fluid expansion increase distribution of hydrophilic drugs.
- The loading dose principally addresses distribution; maintenance addresses clearance.
- A full appropriate loading dose may therefore be needed with renal-adjusted subsequent dosing.
- Reassess rapidly changing renal function and use drug monitoring/pharmacy advice.

items.title: How do you dose beta-lactams during critical illness?
items.q: How do you dose beta-lactams during critical illness?
items.a:
- Efficacy depends mainly on free time above MIC.
- Give a loading dose before prolonged/continuous maintenance infusion.
- Check renal clearance, augmented clearance, RRT, site penetration and stability/compatibility.
- BLING III primary mortality endpoint was neutral; pooled randomised evidence favoured prolonged infusion and SSC 2026 recommends it.

items.title: What changes antimicrobial dosing during kidney replacement?
items.q: What changes antimicrobial dosing during kidney replacement?
items.a:
- Identify intermittent versus continuous modality, effluent rate and residual renal function.
- Drug protein binding, volume of distribution and membrane/circuit factors influence removal.
- Avoid automatically applying a non-dialysis renal-failure maintenance dose.
- Use pharmacist/ID advice and TDM when available; reconsider after circuit interruption or recovery.

items.title: What are important antifungal mechanisms and toxicities?
items.q: What are important antifungal mechanisms and toxicities?
items.a:
- Azoles inhibit ergosterol synthesis; consider CYP interactions, hepatotoxicity and QT effects.
- Echinocandins inhibit fungal cell-wall beta-glucan synthesis; monitor liver function and interactions.
- Amphotericin binds ergosterol; renal injury, potassium/magnesium loss and infusion reactions matter.
- Choice depends on organism, site, immune state and resistance rather than a universal empirical agent.

items.title: What should you remember about aciclovir?
items.q: What should you remember about aciclovir?
items.a:
- It inhibits viral DNA polymerase after activation and is urgent treatment for suspected HSV encephalitis.
- Typical adult HSV encephalitis dosing is 10 mg/kg IV eight-hourly, adjusted for renal function and the agreed obesity weight scalar.
- Monitor renal function, hydration and possible crystal nephropathy/neurotoxicity.
- Do not stop because of one early negative CSF HSV PCR if clinical suspicion remains.

items.title: Who can receive seven days for bloodstream infection after BALANCE?
items.q: Who can receive seven days for bloodstream infection after BALANCE?
items.a:
- Select clinically appropriate patients with effective therapy and adequate source control.
- Seven days was noninferior to fourteen for 90-day mortality in the trial population.
- Do not extrapolate to S. aureus, severe immunosuppression, endocarditis or other prolonged-treatment foci excluded from the trial.
- Persistent bacteraemia or deterioration requires investigation, not an automatic day-seven stop.

items.title: What is the role of SDD in ICU?
items.q: What is the role of SDD in ICU?
items.a:
- SDD combines oral/gastric antimicrobials with a short systemic component to reduce pathogenic colonisation.
- Full international SuDDICU did not demonstrate a mortality reduction.
- Some microbiological outcomes improved, but ecological noninferiority for resistant organisms was not established.
- SSC 2026 gives a conditional low-resistance-unit recommendation; use a unit stewardship policy, not universal ad hoc prescribing.

items.title: How do you investigate encephalitis?
items.q: How do you investigate encephalitis?
items.a:
- Assess infectious, autoimmune and metabolic/seizure mimics while stabilising the patient.
- MRI is more sensitive than early CT; EEG identifies non-convulsive seizures.
- Safe LP includes cells, glucose/protein, bacterial studies and targeted HSV/VZV PCR; tailor other tests to host/exposure.
- A normal early CSF/MRI or negative early PCR does not exclude HSV; repeat testing may be required.
- Start aciclovir without waiting for LP or imaging.

items.title: When should you consider autoimmune encephalitis?
items.q: When should you consider autoimmune encephalitis?
items.a:
- Psychiatric change, movement disorder, autonomic instability or refractory seizures can suggest it.
- HSV and other infections remain urgent alternatives; autoimmunity can also follow HSV.
- Seek neurology advice for serum/CSF antibodies, MRI/EEG and tumour screening.
- Coordinate immunotherapy after assessing infection risk rather than giving blanket steroids to all encephalitis.

items.title: What are the priorities in abdominal sepsis?
items.q: What are the priorities in abdominal sepsis?
items.a:
- Recognise shock and call surgery, anaesthesia and ICU early.
- Cultures and prompt therapeutic antibiotics with enteric Gram-negative/anaerobic cover adjusted to risk.
- Assessed crystalloid and early noradrenaline while arranging drainage, debridement or resection.
- Do not wait for normal lactate before source control; aim for urgent intervention, faster in shock.
- Plan aspiration-safe induction, cardiovascular support and postoperative ICU.

items.title: What makes induction hazardous in septic peritonitis?
items.q: What makes induction hazardous in septic peritonitis?
items.a:
- Full stomach and ileus create aspiration risk.
- Vasoplegia, hypovolaemia and myocardial dysfunction create profound hypotension risk.
- Preoxygenate, plan rapid-sequence airway/rescue and titrate induction with vasopressor ready or running.
- Use experienced help, appropriate monitoring and assessed volume; a single fixed induction dose is unsafe.

items.title: What are the three Fs of HLH?
items.q: What are the three Fs of HLH?
items.a:
- Fever, falling blood counts and raised ferritin.
- Look for liver dysfunction, low fibrinogen, high triglycerides, organomegaly and organ failure.
- Ferritin alone is not diagnostic in adults; infection and HLH can coexist.
- Seek urgent haematology/rheumatology/ICU advice and investigate the trigger.

items.title: How do you diagnose and treat suspected HLH in ICU?
items.q: How do you diagnose and treat suspected HLH in ICU?
items.a:
- Use serial blood counts, ferritin, triglycerides, fibrinogen and organ-function tests with an HScore/criteria framework.
- Marrow haemophagocytosis is neither essential nor specific; do not await every test in deterioration.
- Continue infection treatment and organ support.
- Specialists tailor immunomodulation, often corticosteroids and selected anakinra, plus treatment of malignancy/infection/autoimmune triggers.

items.title: How do you manage a septic immunocompromised patient?
items.q: How do you manage a septic immunocompromised patient?
items.a:
- Treat shock promptly and control ordinary surgical infection as well as considering opportunistic organisms.
- Identify the immune defect, transplant/treatment timeline, prophylaxis and previous resistant isolates.
- Shock excludes a low-risk outpatient neutropenic-fever pathway; avoid rectal instrumentation in profound neutropenia.
- Coordinate antimicrobial spectrum and immunosuppressant changes with the treating team, with drug-level/interaction review.

items.title: Should methotrexate and biologics be stopped for every operation?
items.q: Should methotrexate and biologics be stopped for every operation?
items.a:
- No: balance infection risk against flare and procedure urgency.
- Conventional DMARDs including methotrexate are often continued; reconsider with AKI, toxicity or significant infection.
- Biologic/JAK plans differ by disease, drug and procedure; agree interruption and restart with the specialist.
- Avoid nitrous oxide with methotrexate and check interacting medicines.

items.title: How does bloodborne hepatitis alter anaesthetic planning?
items.q: How does bloodborne hepatitis alter anaesthetic planning?
items.a:
- Assess hepatitis activity, cirrhosis/decompensation, renal function and relevant treatment.
- Review platelets/coagulation, ascites, encephalopathy and bleeding/thrombosis risks.
- Tailor drug handling and surgery timing to organ dysfunction, not just the viral label.
- Use standard precautions; HBV/HCV alone does not need airborne isolation or a separate machine.

items.title: What changes in elective versus urgent surgery for a patient with HIV?
items.q: What changes in elective versus urgent surgery for a patient with HIV?
items.a:
- Urgent surgery must not wait for CD4/viral-load results.
- For elective surgery review control, ART adherence, opportunistic disease and organ comorbidity; seek optimisation advice if uncontrolled.
- Continue ART and indicated prophylaxis where possible.
- Check ritonavir/cobicistat interactions with sedatives/analgesics and maintain standard precautions/confidentiality.

items.title: How do you distinguish catheter infection from a positive line culture?
items.q: How do you distinguish catheter infection from a positive line culture?
items.a:
- Assess clinical sepsis, local/tunnel infection, alternative sources and contamination.
- Obtain paired peripheral/line cultures with reliable timing when feasible before antibiotics.
- A differential time to positivity of about two hours can support a catheter source; it is not required before urgent source control.
- Severe infection, S. aureus, Candida, persistent bacteraemia or complications favour removal and specialist treatment.

items.title: What is different about infection prevention in trauma?
items.q: What is different about infection prevention in trauma?
items.a:
- Use blood/splash PPE and safe sharps coordination despite time pressure.
- Maintain aseptic drug/access handling; document emergency breaches and review replacement of devices.
- Give injury-specific early antibiotics, tetanus prophylaxis and debridement/source control as indicated.
- Handover contamination, device conditions and doses; activate immediate occupational exposure care if needed.

items.title: What does current PG28 say about neuraxial antisepsis?
items.q: What does current PG28 say about neuraxial antisepsis?
items.a:
- Use the local approved preparation; PG28 2025 allows 0.5–2% chlorhexidine in alcohol for neuraxial skin preparation.
- Prevent pooling, allow complete drying, and keep antiseptic away from drugs, needles and the neuraxial space.
- Use an effective alternative for chlorhexidine allergy; povidone-iodine is not harmless if introduced neuraxially.
- Catheter insertion needs full aseptic barriers; do not impose a fixed drying time or universal three-day epidural expiry.

items.title: Can filtered breathing circuits be reused indefinitely?
items.q: Can filtered breathing circuits be reused indefinitely?
items.a:
- No: PG28 permits use up to seven days in an appropriate filtered system under policy/manufacturer requirements.
- Inspect before every case and change earlier if contaminated, damaged or clinically indicated.
- Use an appropriate bacterial/viral filter; an HME alone is not necessarily a validated microbial filter.
- Place sampling on the machine side of the patient filter and follow requirements for returned sample gas.

items.title: How do you reprocess an ultrasound probe?
items.q: How do you reprocess an ultrasound probe?
items.a:
- Classify by actual contact and procedure, following manufacturer and AS5369 requirements.
- Noncritical intact-skin contact differs from mucosal/endocavitary use needing high-level disinfection.
- For invasive procedures use the appropriate sterile cover and sterile gel.
- A cover does not replace cleaning/disinfection; avoid contaminating sterile equipment while manipulating the machine.

items.title: Can cefazolin be used after penicillin anaphylaxis?
items.q: Can cefazolin be used after penicillin anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- Often yes: cefazolin has a distinct side-chain profile and a penicillin label alone is not a contraindication under PG69.
- Clarify the exact culprit, phenotype, timing and subsequent tolerated agents.
- Prior cefazolin anaphylaxis or a severe delayed beta-lactam reaction needs an alternative specialist plan.
- This does not mean every cephalosporin is safe or that oral cephalexin follows identical advice.

items.title: What are the adult IV adrenaline doses in perioperative anaphylaxis?
items.q: What are the adult IV adrenaline doses in perioperative anaphylaxis?
items.a:
- In a monitored anaesthetised adult, grade 2 commonly starts with 10–20 micrograms IV, grade 3 with 50–100 micrograms IV, titrated.
- Use the current cognitive aid and infusion for persistent instability; check concentration and delivery.
- Give assessed crystalloid for capillary leak and venodilation.
- Use arrest dosing for arrest, not routinely with a pulse; the perioperative guideline supports compressions with SBP <50 mmHg despite treatment.

items.title: What can make apparent adrenaline-resistant anaphylaxis worse?
items.q: What can make apparent adrenaline-resistant anaphylaxis worse?
items.a:
- Failed IV/pump delivery, inadequate volume or continuing trigger exposure.
- An alternative cause such as haemorrhage, airway/circuit obstruction, embolism or tension pneumothorax.
- Myocardial dysfunction or dynamic LV outflow obstruction; echo helps avoid blind escalation.
- Sugammadex is not reliable rescue and steroids/antihistamines do not replace adrenaline.

items.title: What post-sepsis problems need follow-up?
items.q: What post-sepsis problems need follow-up?
items.a:
- Physical weakness, impaired mobility, swallowing problems and persistent organ dysfunction.
- Cognitive impairment, anxiety, depression, PTSD symptoms and family/carer strain.
- Medication reconciliation, antibiotic stop dates, pending results and recurrent-infection safety-netting.
- Arrange rehabilitation and coordinated follow-up rather than treating ICU discharge as complete recovery.

items.title: What does PADDI tell you about a single dexamethasone dose?
items.q: What does PADDI tell you about a single dexamethasone dose?
items.a:
- In the studied nonurgent noncardiac surgical population, 8 mg IV dexamethasone was noninferior to placebo for SSI.
- The result does not prove safety of repeated high-dose steroids or every severely immunocompromised setting.
- Consider transient hyperglycaemia and monitor susceptible patients.
- Use the drug for an appropriate indication such as PONV prevention with the rest of the SSI bundle.

items.title: How do noradrenaline, adrenaline and vasopressin differ?
items.q: How do noradrenaline, adrenaline and vasopressin differ?
items.a:
- Noradrenaline: mainly alpha with some beta-1 activity; first-line septic-shock vasopressor.
- Adrenaline adds inotropy but can cause arrhythmia and aerobic hyperlactataemia.
- Vasopressin acts at V1 receptors and can spare catecholamine exposure, with ischaemic risk.
- Reassess volume, cardiac output, source and reliable pressure measurement rather than escalating pressure treatment blindly.

items.title: What is the role and risk of IVIG in septic patients?
items.q: What is the role and risk of IVIG in septic patients?
items.a:
- Pooled immunoglobulin has antibody-replacement and immunomodulatory roles.
- It is not routine treatment for undifferentiated septic shock; selected toxin-mediated/immune disease needs specialist advice.
- Confirm indication, approved product/dose and rate; limited supply supports careful prescribing.
- Monitor infusion reactions, haemolysis, thrombosis, AKI and aseptic meningitis.

items.title: How does POCUS help in apparent septic shock?
items.q: How does POCUS help in apparent septic shock?
items.a:
- Identify mixed physiology: LV/RV dysfunction, underfilling, pericardial disease or another shock cause.
- Integrate lung congestion and possible infection/source findings; normal views do not exclude all pathology.
- Measured flow response to passive leg raise is more informative than IVC size alone.
- Repeat after interventions, document limitations and seek formal imaging when needed; do not delay antibiotics/source control.

items.title: 1. Describe the recognition and immediate management of anaphylaxis occurring short
items.q: Describe the recognition and immediate management of anaphylaxis occurring shortly after induction of general anaesthesia.
items.a:
## Recognition

Anaphylaxis under anaesthesia is easy to miss because the patient is asleep and covered. Suspect it with any unexplained combination of hypotension (the commonest and often the only sign), tachycardia or bradycardia, bronchospasm or rising airway pressure with a fall in ETCO2, and skin signs (flushing, urticaria, angioedema, which may be absent). Onset is usually within minutes of intravenous exposure, so the drugs given in the last 5 to 10 minutes are the main suspects: neuromuscular blockers, antibiotics, chlorhexidine, latex, patent blue, gelatin, sugammadex, opioids. The differential includes bleeding, high spinal, tension pneumothorax, pulmonary embolism, tamponade, malignant hyperthermia, and drug error; serial tryptase later supports mast-cell activation but does not alone confirm the diagnosis or the culprit.

## Immediate management (ANZAAG-ANZCA)

- **1.** **Call for help and declare it.** Stop the suspected trigger (and surgery if possible), remove chlorhexidine and latex, give 100% oxygen, and stop volatile and other anaesthetic drugs as haemodynamics require.
- **2.** **Adrenaline** is the only first-line drug. In monitored anaesthetised adults give severity-appropriate IV aliquots: usually 10–20 micrograms for grade 2, 50–100 micrograms for grade 3, repeated every 1 to 2 minutes as needed; if no IV access, 0.5 mg IM into the anterolateral thigh. Start an infusion (0.05 to 0.1 micrograms/kg/min) when repeated boluses are needed. In cardiac arrest, give 1 mg and follow ALS with high-quality CPR.
- **3.** **Fluid:** rapid crystalloid, 20 mL/kg boluses (up to several litres), because of vasodilatation and capillary leak.
- **4.** **Airway and breathing:** intubate if not already (angioedema); bronchospasm responds to adrenaline, with salbutamol as an adjunct.
- **5.** **Refractory shock:** verify adrenaline delivery, adequate volume and removal of ongoing triggers, reassess alternatives/echo, then use expert-guided noradrenaline or vasopressin. Consider glucagon for beta-blocked patients under the cognitive aid/local protocol. Methylene blue is exceptional rescue with risks, not routine escalation; extracorporeal support is a selected specialist rescue option.
- **6.** Steroids and antihistamines have no role in the acute phase; do not delay adrenaline for them.
- **7.** **Tryptase:** **ANZAAG–ANZCA post-crisis card (2022): serum tryptase immediately once feasible without delaying resuscitation, at 1 hour, at 4 hours, and a baseline after 24 hours.** Record onset and sample times; a later outpatient baseline may be needed. A peak exceeding 1.2 × baseline + 2 micrograms/L supports mast-cell activation but neither proves IgE mediation nor identifies the culprit; a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.
- **8.** **Surgery:** decide with the surgeon whether to proceed (severity, urgency and response guide proceed/postpone decisions), then risk-based monitored care; consider 24 h ICU/HDU after moderate–severe reactions, documentation, disclosure and referral to an allergy service.

## Evidence (Blue Book 2015)

Platt and colleagues describe IgE-mediated reactions through FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils, with histamine the main early cardiovascular mediator. The collapse is mostly a fall in systemic vascular resistance with failure of venous return: veins dilate, blood pools, and up to about 35% of blood volume can leak into the interstitium, which is why echo shows a hyperdynamic but empty heart. In Fisher's series of 227 cases, 205 had cardiovascular depression, and bronchospasm was uncommon without asthma. They argue that large-volume resuscitation through large-bore access, raising the legs, and adrenaline are the mainstays; alpha agonists (metaraminol) and vasopressin are options in refractory shock, with TOE if available. The historical chapter discussed a sugammadex hypothesis, including laboratory skin-model data that do not establish clinical efficacy. Current practice does not rely on sugammadex as rescue or assume that availability makes rocuronium safe. Avoid the suspected NMBA and cross-reactants pending specialist testing, usually after 4–6 weeks; re-exposure follows an individual specialist plan, not merely passage of four weeks.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Severity matters: in monitored anaesthetised adults, the ANZAAG card uses 10–20 micrograms IV for grade 2 and 50–100 micrograms IV for grade 3; titrate/repeat to response and start infusion early if repeated boluses are required. These IV aliquots assume experienced staff and close monitoring; 0.5 mg IM is the adult alternative when IV delivery is unavailable/inappropriate. In an anaesthetised patient with profound hypotension (SBP <50 mmHg), start chest compressions rather than waiting for an impalpable pulse. Use the current card and avoid adrenaline dilution errors. In refractory cases first check adequate adrenaline delivery, volume, ongoing trigger and alternative diagnoses; echo can reveal pump failure or dynamic LVOT obstruction. Sugammadex is not established rescue treatment. Source: ANZAAG–ANZCA 2022 adult card and management guideline; PG69 2025.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognises features under anaesthesia
- Considers the differential
- Stops trigger, calls for help, 100% oxygen
- Adrenaline route and dose
- Fluid resuscitation
- Adjuncts for refractory cases
- Tryptase sampling
- Next steps (surgery, disposition, referral)

items.title: 2. Discuss the common causes of perioperative anaphylaxis and how the risk of a rec
items.q: Discuss the common causes of perioperative anaphylaxis and how the risk of a recurrent reaction can be reduced.
items.a:
## Common causes of perioperative anaphylaxis

- **Neuromuscular blocking drugs** (a leading cause; proportions vary by country, case definition and period): rocuronium and suxamethonium; sensitisation is thought to follow cross-reactive quaternary ammonium compounds in cosmetics, disinfectants and some medicines, so a first exposure can react.
- **Antibiotics** (another leading cause; avoid universal percentages): beta-lactams (cefazolin, penicillins), teicoplanin, vancomycin (rate-related infusion reactions are usually non-IgE, but true anaphylaxis also occurs).
- **Chlorhexidine,** latex (declining in prevalence), patent blue and isosulfan blue, gelatin colloids (Gelofusine), sugammadex, opioids (non-IgE histamine release), propofol (rare, not an egg contraindication), NSAIDs, contrast media and blood products.
- Non-IgE mechanisms (MRGPRX2 pathways, direct mast cell degranulation by opioids and some relaxants), and complement activation by lipid emulsions.

## Risk factors

Previous anaphylaxis to an anaesthetic drug, repeated exposure, atopy (an unclear predictor), mastocytosis, female sex (relaxants), beta-blockers and ACE inhibitors (more severe reactions), health-care workers, and spina bifida (latex).

## Reducing the risk of a recurrence

- **1.** **Identify the culprit** with allergy testing 4 to 6 weeks after the event (skin tests and specific IgE, see the testing item), and provide a written report, allergy alert/bracelet and letter to the GP.
- **2.** **Avoid** the culprit and, if indicated, cross-reactive drugs (all aminosteroid relaxants for a confirmed rocuronium reaction unless tested); use alternative agents confirmed negative on testing.
- **3.** **Prepare** for future anaesthesia: informed consent, atraumatic and standardised preparation, avoiding unnecessary drugs, slow administration, and readiness to treat (adrenaline, monitoring).
- **4.** **Notify** the national anaphylaxis registry (ANZAAG) and the drug regulator, and update hospital allergy records; label the patient's electronic record.
- **5.** Do not use pre-medication with steroids or antihistamines as a substitute for avoiding the trigger; they do not prevent anaphylaxis and may mask early signs.

## Evidence (Blue Book 2015)

The chapter identifies neuromuscular blockers as the commonest triggers, with the bivalent substituted ammonium structure as the allergenic site; sensitisation may follow exposure to pholcodine, morphine, suxamethonium and possibly hairdressing chemicals, and cross-reactivity between relaxants is unpredictable. It reports succinylated gelatin as a trigger on cardiopulmonary bypass and notes that antibiotics are sometimes the true cause when sugammadex was given for presumed rocuronium anaphylaxis. The authors suggest cisatracurium is the relaxant least likely to cross-react, based on their own clinic data.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

A negative skin test lowers but does not abolish risk. NMBA structural class alone cannot establish a safe alternative. Pholcodine sensitisation is relevant history; it was withdrawn in Australia/NZ in 2023 because of the NMBA-anaphylaxis association. Atopy or egg allergy alone does not justify blanket avoidance of all induction drugs. Reporting should follow institutional/WebAIRS and TGA/CARM systems; do not promise a universal ANZAAG registry referral pathway. Current prevention/testing authority: PG69 2025, including hidden chlorhexidine exposures and antibiotic allergy labels.

## Self-marking checklist

- Lists major triggers in order of frequency
- NMBDs and antibiotics as the leading causes
- Other triggers (chlorhexidine, dyes, sugammadex, latex)
- Testing and identification of the culprit
- Communication and alert
- Avoidance and alternatives
- Premedication not effective
- Reporting

items.title: 3. Outline the initial management of a patient in septic shock presenting to the em
items.q: Outline the initial management of a patient in septic shock presenting to the emergency department.
items.a:
## Initial management in the first hour

- **1.** **Recognise and call for help.** Sepsis is infection with life-threatening organ dysfunction (an increase of 2 or more SOFA points); septic shock is sepsis needing vasopressors to keep MAP at 65 mmHg or more with a lactate above 2 mmol/L after fluid.
- **2.** **Oxygen and monitoring;** establish IV access (two large cannulae, or intraosseous) and an arterial line when possible.
- **3.** **Cultures first if no delay:** blood cultures (two sets), plus urine, sputum, wound or CSF according to the source, then **broad-spectrum antibiotics within one hour** (the sooner the better in shock), chosen for the likely source, local resistance, allergy and immune status; add antifungal or antiviral therapy for high-risk patients.
- **4.** **Fluid:** 30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid in the first 3 hours for hypoperfusion (a weak recommendation), guided by dynamic assessment, lactate clearance, capillary refill and echo. Avoid hydroxyethyl starch; consider albumin when large volumes are needed.
- **5.** **Vasopressors:** noradrenaline first-line through a peripheral line if necessary, to MAP 65; add vasopressin (0.03 units/min) if the dose rises, then adrenaline; dobutamine for persistent hypoperfusion with a low-output state.
- **6.** **Hydrocortisone** 200 mg/day for persistent vasopressor-dependent septic shock, with individual timing rather than a compulsory four-hour wait.
- **7.** **Source control:** identify and drain or remove the focus as soon as practical, ideally within 6 hours when an anatomical source-control procedure is needed (abscess, perforation, infected device, necrotising infection).
- **8.** **Lactate** measurement and repeat within 2 to 4 hours; urine output; avoid hypoglycaemia and marked hyperglycaemia; initiate insulin for persistent glucose ≥10 mmol/L under the local ICU protocol; VTE prophylaxis; stress ulcer prophylaxis if risk factors; nutrition; early mobilisation.
- **9.** Reassess frequently, de-escalate antibiotics with cultures, and set goals of care.

## Evidence (Blue Book 2019)

Martyr and colleagues note that early goal-directed therapy (Rivers, 2001) was not reproduced by ProCESS, ProMISe and ARISE. Antibiotics should be given as early as possible: the Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends within one hour, an observational study reported a 12% mortality increase per hour of delay in septic shock, but a systematic review of 16,178 patients found no benefit from antibiotics within 3 hours of triage or 1 hour of recognised shock, so exact time thresholds are not established by randomised trials. Current SSC 2026 nevertheless recommends urgent antibiotics for shock/probable sepsis; historical uncertainty is not a reason to delay treatment. Source control within 6 hours of organ failure was associated with 28-day mortality of 26.7% against 40.7% later (a German cohort of 1011). Starch fluids increase renal impairment (Myburgh); albumin did not impair renal function in SAFE and may help in severe sepsis. Noradrenaline is best supported first-line (dopamine causes more arrhythmia; adrenaline more tachycardia and lactate); VASST and VANISH found no mortality difference with vasopressin; dobutamine has most inotrope safety data and levosimendan did not help (LeoPARDS). TRISS found a haemoglobin threshold of 70 g/L non-inferior to 90. Steroids: ADRENAL found faster shock resolution but no mortality difference, while APROCCHSS (with fludrocortisone) reduced 90-day mortality.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Do not use qSOFA alone to rule out sepsis or wait for every SOFA component before treating deterioration. Initial fluids are conditional and reassessed, with early concurrent noradrenaline in unstable shock. Lactate may reflect adrenergic metabolism or impaired clearance as well as hypoperfusion: do not keep giving fluid until it normalises. Assess source control and ICU admission early, with repeated ABC, capillary refill, mentation, urine output, lactate and cardiac/lung ultrasound. ICU support includes appropriate ventilation, renal support for indications, insulin when persistently hyperglycaemic rather than tight normoglycaemia, nutrition and rehabilitation. Sources: SSC 2026; BJA Education 2026 “Fluids in sepsis”; current antimicrobial decision review. See the separate update model for newer trial findings.

## Focused ultrasound during resuscitation

Use a focused, repeatable examination to answer a clinical question while antibiotics, haemodynamic support and source-control planning continue. Assess LV/RV function, pericardial fluid/tamponade physiology and marked underfilling; consider mixed septic/cardiogenic/obstructive shock rather than assuming every hypotensive infected patient has pure vasoplegia. A hyperdynamic LV can reflect low afterload and does not prove adequate circulation. Lung ultrasound may identify consolidation, pleural fluid or an increasing interstitial pattern; B-lines are not specific for hydrostatic overload. Abdominal/urinary views may identify an obstructed infected system or a drainable focus but do not exclude intra-abdominal pathology when normal.

For additional volume, a passive-leg-raise change in measured LVOT velocity–time integral can support responsiveness when acquisition is reliable. Integrate the result with perfusion need and fluid tolerance. IVC size/variation alone is confounded by ventilation, RV disease and abdominal pressure. Repeat after interventions; document images, interpretation, action and uncertainty. Poor windows/operator limitations require formal echocardiography or other imaging when management depends on precision. A focused study is not a comprehensive structural examination, and improved diagnostic confidence does not itself prove a survival benefit.

**Additional self-mark (/4):** identifies mixed shock; integrates cardiac/lung/source findings; interprets dynamic flow and congestion cautiously; acts within competence without treatment delay.

## Self-marking checklist

- Definition of sepsis and septic shock
- Lactate and cultures
- Antibiotics within 1 hour
- Source control
- Fluids with dynamic reassessment
- Noradrenaline and MAP target
- Adjuncts (vasopressin, hydrocortisone)
- Supportive care and de-escalation

items.title: 4. Outline the pathophysiology of sepsis and septic shock and the mechanisms of org
items.q: Outline the pathophysiology of sepsis and septic shock and the mechanisms of organ dysfunction.
items.a:
## Initiation: the host response

Sepsis is a dysregulated host response to infection. Pathogen-associated molecular patterns (lipopolysaccharide, peptidoglycan, flagellin) and damage-associated patterns from injured tissue bind pattern-recognition receptors (Toll-like receptors, NOD-like receptors) on macrophages, endothelium and neutrophils. This activates NF-kappa B, producing the early cytokines **TNF-alpha, IL-1 and IL-6**, then chemokines, nitric oxide, prostaglandins and complement activation. Simultaneously, anti-inflammatory mediators (IL-10) are released, causing a mixed state that evolves into **immunoparalysis** (monocyte HLA-DR down-regulation, lymphocyte apoptosis, regulatory T cells), explaining late infections and mortality.

## Mechanisms of organ dysfunction

- **Endothelium and microcirculation:** loss of the glycocalyx, increased permeability (capillary leak, oedema), loss of vascular tone, heterogeneity of flow with shunting, so oxygen delivery and extraction fall even when global flow is high.
- **Vasoplegia:** inducible nitric oxide synthase, K-ATP channel opening, relative vasopressin deficiency and catecholamine hyporesponsiveness cause refractory hypotension.
- **Coagulation:** tissue factor expression, impaired natural anticoagulants (antithrombin, protein C, TFPI), fibrinolytic shutdown by PAI-1, and platelet activation lead to DIC and microvascular thrombosis.
- **Mitochondrial dysfunction:** cytopathic hypoxia reduces ATP production despite adequate oxygen, with oxidative stress.
- **Cardiac:** septic cardiomyopathy with reversible depression of both ventricles.
- **Specific organs:** ARDS, AKI (tubular injury, microvascular changes), liver dysfunction, gut barrier failure, encephalopathy, critical illness neuromyopathy and adrenal insufficiency.
- **Metabolic:** hyperlactataemia (partly from adrenergic glycolysis, not only hypoperfusion), insulin resistance, hypoglycaemia in severe disease.

## Clinical meaning

The organ failures produce the SOFA score and the picture of shock with lactic acidosis. Treatments target the cause (antibiotics, source control), the circulation (fluid, vasopressors) and organ support; immunomodulation has been unsuccessful in trials (anti-TNF, anti-endotoxin, activated protein C).

## Evidence

Blue Book 2019 (Martyr et al.) notes that immunomodulatory trials have largely failed (several immune-modulating strategies have been investigated; a small IL-7 trial was one example), that heparin appears safe without clear mortality benefit (HETRASE), that antithrombin improved DIC resolution but not SOFA or mortality, and that thrombomodulin did not improve mortality in a 741-patient trial. The mechanisms were checked against the current sepsis education review.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

SIRS also arises from sterile inflammation such as pancreatitis, burns, trauma and ischaemia–reperfusion. Hyperinflammatory and immunosuppressed responses overlap rather than occurring in a fixed two-stage sequence. Reduced oxygen extraction, microvascular shunting, endothelial leak and organ-specific mechanisms can coexist despite preserved global cardiac output. “Cytopathic hypoxia” is a proposed contributory mechanism, not proof that every organ fails through irreversible mitochondrial poisoning. Sources: BJA Education 2026 sepsis-fluid pathophysiology; Sepsis-3; the historical Blue Book sepsis chapter.

## Self-marking checklist

- Sepsis-3 definitions
- Pathogen recognition and cytokine response
- Endothelial dysfunction and vasodilation
- Coagulation abnormalities
- Microcirculation and mitochondria
- Septic cardiomyopathy
- Organ dysfunction by system
- Outcome

items.title: 5. Outline the recommended vaccinations and measures to protect healthcare workers,
items.q: Outline the recommended vaccinations and measures to protect healthcare workers, including the management of a needlestick injury.
items.a:
## Vaccination and health protection for staff

- **Hepatitis B** (three-dose course, check anti-HBs levels at least 1 to 2 months afterwards; a level at least 10 mIU/mL is protective, and non-responders need further doses or specialist input).
- **Annual influenza** vaccination, **COVID-19**, **MMR** (measles, mumps, rubella), **varicella**, **dTpa** (pertussis), and TB risk assessment according to local policy (BCG is not routine in NZ for staff).
- Hepatitis A and meningococcal vaccination for selected exposures.

## Standard precautions

Hand hygiene (the five moments), appropriate personal protective equipment (gloves, mask, eye protection and gown for splashes), safe sharps handling (no recapping, immediate disposal in a sharps container, needleless systems and safety devices), cleaning of blood spills, safe handling of laryngoscope blades, and respiratory etiquette. Exclude sick staff. Maintain immunisation records and occupational health surveillance.

## Needlestick or blood and body fluid exposure

- **1.** **First aid immediately:** wash with soap and running water, allow spontaneous bleeding but do not squeeze, scrub or suck the wound; irrigate mucous membranes and eyes with water or saline.
- **2.** **Report** to the supervisor and occupational health, and complete an incident form.
- **3.** **Risk assessment:** type of injury (deep, hollow-bore needle, visible blood), source patient (HIV, hepatitis B and C status), and exposed person's vaccination status.
- **4.** **Source patient testing** with consent (HBsAg, anti-HCV, HIV) and baseline staff testing.
- **5.** **Post-exposure prophylaxis:** HIV (a 4-week antiretroviral course started within 2 hours, ideally, and not later than 72 hours; the risk from a percutaneous exposure is about 0.3%); hepatitis B (vaccine booster and HBIG if non-immune; risk up to 30% from an e-antigen positive source); hepatitis C (no PEP, but monitor and treat early; risk around 0.2% in contemporary CDC occupational cohorts, with variation by exposure/source viraemia).
- **6.** **Follow-up** with pathogen- and test-specific follow-up (for example early HCV RNA at 3–6 weeks and later serology; HIV follow-up according to current PEP guidance), rather than the same six-month schedule for every virus, counselling, and safe practices in the interim.
- **7.** Review the circumstances and prevent recurrence.

## Evidence

Transmission risks derive from occupational cohort studies; HIV PEP efficacy is from case-control data; national guidance (the Australian National Guidelines for PEP, NZ Ministry of Health) sets timing.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

HIV PEP is urgent: seek occupational-health/ID advice immediately, start as soon as possible without waiting for delayed source results, generally within 72 h, and complete the prescribed 28-day regimen if indicated. Undetectable source HIV RNA and exposure details influence specialist assessment; do not apply historic risk percentages without that context. HBV prophylaxis depends on documented vaccine response, source HBsAg and prior vaccine courses; it is not automatically both booster and HBIG in everyone. There is no proven HCV PEP. Use consent/confidentiality, counselling and systems review. Sources: Australian National PEP Guidelines 2025; CDC occupational HCV guidance; PG28 2025; current staff immunisation schedule.

## Self-marking checklist

- Hepatitis B vaccine and titre
- Other recommended vaccines
- Standard precautions and PPE
- First aid after exposure
- Reporting and source testing
- HIV PEP timing
- Hepatitis B and C management
- Follow-up and review

items.title: 6. Discuss the infection control considerations for anaesthetising a patient with (
items.q: Discuss the infection control considerations for anaesthetising a patient with (a) infectious pulmonary tuberculosis or (b) suspected Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.
items.a:
## Principle: match the precaution to the route of transmission

Standard precautions apply to every patient; transmission-based precautions are added for known or suspected infections. The anaesthetist's task is to protect the patient, theatre staff and the next patient without delaying essential care.

## Tuberculosis (airborne)

- **Elective surgery:** postpone until non-infectious where possible. For emergencies, use an **N95/P2 respirator** for all staff in the room, a negative-pressure theatre if available (otherwise arrange an approved airborne-infection plan with engineering/infection control; being last on a list is not a substitute for safe airflow), and limit staff numbers.
- **Anaesthesia:** avoid general anaesthesia and airway instrumentation if a regional technique is suitable. If intubation is needed, place a **high-efficiency bacterial/viral filter** between the tracheal tube and the breathing circuit, and another on the expiratory limb.
