Use a closed suction system, and extubate in theatre if possible; recover the patient in the theatre or an isolation room, not an open recovery area. Transport with a surgical mask on the patient.
- **Equipment:** change circuits and filters; standard disinfection of laryngoscopes, since TB is not spread by the anaesthetic machine itself. Clean the theatre and allow the air to clear for the time the air-change rate requires (calculated from measured air changes and the required clearance; do not assume a fixed 30–60 minutes).

## Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (prions)

Prions resist usual sterilisation and are not spread by droplets. Risk comes from high-infectivity tissue (brain, spinal cord, eye, dura, tonsil in variant CJD). Select **single-use** equipment or quarantine/reprocess exposed reusable instruments when required by the actual tissue/procedure-specific prion-risk pathway. Routine airway equipment is not automatically equivalent to instruments exposed to high-infectivity neural tissue. Seek infection-control advice; when prion-specific processing is indicated, usual sterilisation is inadequate. Standard personal protective equipment is sufficient; there is no need to avoid the airway. Record instruments used for look-back.

## MRSA and other contact-transmitted organisms

- Screen high-risk patients (preoperative swabs); decolonise with mupirocin and chlorhexidine (noting allergy).
- Contact precautions: gown and gloves, hand hygiene, dedicated equipment (stethoscope, monitoring), cleaning of high-touch surfaces after the case.
- Tailor surgical prophylaxis to MRSA carriage, procedure and local policy; add an appropriate glycopeptide when indicated without omitting needed MSSA/other procedural coverage. MRSA carriage alone is not an indication for an indiscriminate prolonged course.
- Use contact precautions and effective between-case cleaning; MRSA carriage alone does not require a universal last-on-list rule.

## Evidence

The guidance comes from infection control policy, case reports and expert consensus, because randomised trials do not exist.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Differentiate classical CJD from variant CJD tissue risk; do not quarantine every routine item merely because prion disease is suspected. Consult the national tissue/procedure-specific pathway and maintain instrument traceability; instruments exposed to relevant high-risk tissue need a validated prion pathway. For TB, do not disable a positive-pressure theatre ventilation system ad hoc; agree room, recovery, respirator and air-clearance arrangements with infection control. Add perioperative TB-drug issues: rifampicin induction of drug metabolism, isoniazid/rifampicin hepatotoxicity, neuropathy and airborne infectivity assessment. Sources: PG28 2025; national TB/prion guidance.

## Self-marking checklist

- Postpones elective surgery in infectious TB
- Respiratory protection for staff
- Environment and air changes
- Appropriate filters, circuit policy and airborne precautions
- Isolated recovery
- Prion resistance to sterilisation
- Single-use equipment and quarantine
- Notification and communication

items.title: 7. Describe the standards for cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising reusable anaes
items.q: Describe the standards for cleaning, disinfecting and sterilising reusable anaesthetic equipment between patients.
items.a:
## Risk: the anaesthetic circuit is a potential route for cross-infection

Contamination of equipment can transmit organisms between patients (hepatitis B and C, bacteria, viruses). The main concerns are laryngoscopes and blades, airway devices, the breathing system and filters, the anaesthetic machine surfaces, unsafe reuse of syringes, vials and multi-dose containers, and the intravenous line.

## Principles of reprocessing (Spaulding classification)

- **Critical** items entering sterile tissue or the vascular system (needles, cannulae, spinal needles, epidural catheters): single use, sterile.
- **Semi-critical** items contacting mucous membranes (laryngoscope blades, LMAs, tracheal tubes, bronchoscopes): single-use preferred, or reusable devices need cleaning then **high-level disinfection or sterilisation**. Laryngoscope handles are non-critical but are often contaminated, so clean and disinfect them between patients.
- **Non-critical** items touching intact skin (ECG leads, BP cuffs, pulse oximeter probes, stethoscopes): cleaning with detergent, or low-level disinfection.

## Practical points

- **1.** **Between every patient:** hand hygiene, replace the face mask, tracheal tube, airway device and **filter** (an HME filter with a viral and bacterial filter at the patient end protects the circuit and machine; circuits may be reused only within a validated local/manufacturer protocol with an effective filter; change if soiled, contaminated, damaged or filtration has failed), and wipe all contact surfaces (machine knobs, screen, drug trolley).
- **2.** **Drugs and syringes:** one syringe and needle per patient and per drug preparation; never reuse a used syringe for another patient or to re-enter a vial/ampoule, and use aseptic access for intended single-patient administration; prepare drugs aseptically just before use (follow the actual product/manufacturer time limits for propofol and infusions rather than a universal 6-hour rule); discard unused opened ampoules; multi-dose vials are discarded within local time limits.
- **3.** **Ultrasound probes:** probe covers, sterile gel for sterile procedures, and cleaning.
- **4.** **Bronchoscopes, fibreoptics and video-laryngoscope blades:** single-use or fully reprocessed, with documented tracking.
- **5.** **Infected patients:** use single-use equipment and the transmission-based precautions in the previous item.
- **6.** **Cleaning of the anaesthetic machine** after each list (the CO2 absorbent follows manufacturer guidance) and monitor audits.

## Evidence

Outbreaks of hepatitis and bacteria have been traced to reused syringes and multi-dose vials; guidance comes from ANZCA PG28 (2025) (infection control in anaesthesia) and national standards, not from trials.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Use current PG28 (2025) and AS 5369:2023, rather than relying on superseded PS28/AS4187 terminology. Clean reusable laryngoscope handles then at least low-level disinfect after every use; blades need high-level disinfection or sterilisation. Device labelling/manufacturer instructions govern whether an item is reusable. HME alone is not necessarily a bacterial/viral filter. Filtered circuits still need inspection, change if contaminated/damaged and a defined validated change policy; filtration is not indefinite permission to reuse. Reprocess reusable masks as semi-critical devices and protect all clean airway equipment from handling/environmental contamination. A sterile probe cover does not replace the required cleaning/disinfection level.

## Self-marking checklist

- Spaulding classification
- Cleaning before disinfection or sterilisation
- Laryngoscope handling
- Bronchoscope reprocessing
- Breathing systems and filters
- Single-use equipment
- Traceability and audit
- Staff training

items.title: 8. Discuss the principles of antibiotic prophylaxis for the prevention of surgical
items.q: Discuss the principles of antibiotic prophylaxis for the prevention of surgical site infection, including the anaesthetist's role.
items.a:
## Surgical site infection (SSI) risk and when prophylaxis is indicated

SSI risk depends on the wound class (clean, clean-contaminated, contaminated, dirty), patient factors (diabetes, obesity, smoking, immunosuppression, malnutrition, ASA grade) and the operation. Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated for clean-contaminated and contaminated surgery, and for clean surgery involving an implant (joint replacement, cardiac surgery, vascular grafts) or where an infection would be catastrophic.

## Principles of prophylaxis

- **1.** **Choose an agent against the likely organisms:** cefazolin 2 g IV (3 g at 120 kg or above according to the local adult regimen) for most procedures; add metronidazole for colorectal and abdominal surgery (anaerobes); vancomycin or teicoplanin for MRSA carriers or beta-lactam allergy (with gram-negative cover if needed); gentamicin for urology, and local protocols.
- **2.** **Timing:** give within **60 minutes before incision** (120 minutes for vancomycin), and before tourniquet inflation. Giving it after incision or more than 60 minutes earlier increases the SSI rate.
- **3.** **Redosing** for operations longer than two half-lives (cefazolin: after 4 hours) or blood loss over 1500 mL.
- **4.** **Duration:** a single pre-operative dose, usually stopped at wound closure for routine prophylaxis; procedure-specific protocols govern exceptions, and drains do not justify continuing antibiotics; avoid prolonged courses.
- **5.** **Beta-lactam allergy:** clarify the history; most labels are inaccurate, and cefazolin has a unique side chain, so it is acceptable in many penicillin-allergic patients (not after anaphylaxis to cefazolin).

## Other measures within the anaesthetist's control

Normothermia (above 36 degrees), **supplemental oxygen** (the evidence is mixed; the WHO suggests 80% FiO2 but this is contested), perioperative glucose control (below 10 mmol/L), adequate fluid, skin preparation with an alcohol-based solution, hair clipping, surgical safety checklist, hand hygiene, and aseptic technique for lines and regional blocks.

## Evidence

Timing was shown in cohort studies to affect SSI rates (Classen, 1992), and the surgical care improvement programme recommended the 60-minute window; the benefit of prolonged courses is not supported.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Do not add vancomycin solely for an unverified penicillin label: cefazolin is suitable for many patients including prior immediate penicillin reactions, while prior cefazolin anaphylaxis or severe delayed beta-lactam reactions require a different plan. Vancomycin alone lacks usual Gram-negative cover and is less effective than cefazolin for MSSA; selected MRSA carriers may require it in addition to the standard regimen. Dirty/infected surgery needs therapeutic antibiotics plus source control. Document actual dose/time and allocate redosing ownership. Sources: PG28/PG69 2025; 2017.1 Q12 and 2019.2 Q10 examiner reports; current local prophylaxis policy.

## Self-marking checklist

- Indications for prophylaxis
- Choice of agent
- Timing before incision
- Dose and re-dosing
- Short duration
- Anaesthetist's other SSI measures
- Allergy considerations
- Resistance and C. difficile

items.title: 9. Discuss the strategies to prevent healthcare-associated infections in the intens
items.q: Discuss the strategies to prevent healthcare-associated infections in the intensive care unit.
items.a:
## The problem

Healthcare-associated infection (HAI) in intensive care is common and costly: ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP), central line-associated bloodstream infection (CLABSI), catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI), surgical site infection, and Clostridioides difficile. Risks come from invasive devices, immunosuppression, broad-spectrum antibiotics and cross-infection between patients. Resistant organisms (MRSA, VRE, ESBL and carbapenemase-producing Enterobacterales, Acinetobacter, Pseudomonas) increase mortality and cost.

## Prevention through bundles

- **Hand hygiene** (the five moments), and cleaning of surfaces and equipment.
- **CLABSI bundle:** hand hygiene, maximal barrier precautions at insertion, **chlorhexidine skin preparation** (2% in alcohol), preferred insertion site (subclavian over femoral, with ultrasound), daily review of line need and prompt removal, and aseptic care of the hub. Chlorhexidine-impregnated dressings reduce infection.
- **VAP bundle:** head of bed elevated 30 to 45 degrees, daily sedation interruption and spontaneous breathing trials to limit ventilator time, oral hygiene (chlorhexidine is not clearly beneficial and may harm), subglottic secretion drainage for expected prolonged ventilation, cuff pressure 20 to 30 cmH2O, and avoiding unnecessary circuit changes. Selective decontamination of the digestive tract has been studied in many trials, with mixed results (the large SuDDICU trial found no clear mortality benefit).
- **CAUTI:** insert only if indicated, aseptic technique, closed drainage, and early removal.
- **Antimicrobial stewardship:** culture before treatment, narrow the spectrum when results are known (de-escalation), and limit duration.
- **Isolation and screening** for resistant organisms, with contact precautions.
- **Environment and staffing:** single rooms, adequate nurse-to-patient ratios, and surveillance with feedback.

## Management of a suspected HAI

Identify the source (lines, chest, urine, wound, abdomen, C. difficile), take cultures, remove or replace the device, start empirical treatment according to local resistance patterns, and review at 48 to 72 hours.

## Evidence

The Keystone ICU project (Pronovost, 2006) reported a large fall in CLABSI after a checklist bundle; stewardship reduces resistance, while the effect of oral chlorhexidine and selective decontamination on mortality remains contested.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Include impaired innate/adaptive immunity, loss of skin/mucosal barriers, severity of illness, altered microbiome, biofilm, device duration, transfers and crowding as reasons ICU patients are susceptible. Add C. difficile prevention through stewardship, isolation, soap-and-water hand hygiene after exposure and sporicidal environmental cleaning; do not routinely screen/treat asymptomatic colonisation. ICU prophylaxis requires a reasoned decision, not antibiotics for every device. SDD is a unit-level strategy whose benefit/resistance balance depends on setting; individual antibiotic prophylaxis at intubation is not interchangeable with SDD. Sources: PG28 2025; BJA Education VAP 2025; SuDDICU primary evidence; see dedicated prophylaxis model.

## Self-marking checklist

- Reasons for susceptibility
- Hand hygiene and isolation
- CLABSI bundle
- VAP bundle
- CAUTI prevention
- Antimicrobial stewardship
- Environment and surveillance
- Nutrition and glycaemic control

items.title: 10. A 45-year-old has a penicillin allergy label and needs cefazolin prophylaxis for
items.q: A 45-year-old has a penicillin allergy label and needs cefazolin prophylaxis for a hernia repair. How would you approach antibiotic choice?
items.a:
## Clarify what the label means

Up to 90% of patients labelled penicillin-allergic are not allergic on testing, and the label leads to more vancomycin, clindamycin and fluoroquinolone use, with more surgical site infection, C. difficile and resistant organisms. Ask: which drug, when, what happened, how long after the dose, treatment required, and later beta-lactam exposure. An IgE-mediated reaction occurs within about an hour (urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension); a remote, vague, gastrointestinal or non-urticarial rash history is low risk. Severe delayed reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome, toxic epidermal necrolysis, DRESS, haemolytic anaemia, interstitial nephritis) are absolute contraindications to the drug class.

## Cross-reactivity

Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is determined by the **R1 side chain**, not the beta-lactam ring. It is low (about 1 to 2%, not the 10% once quoted). **Cefazolin has a unique side chain** that is not shared with other beta-lactams, so it can usually be given to patients with penicillin allergy, including most with IgE-mediated histories, except where the reaction was to cefazolin itself. Cefalexin, cefaclor and amoxicillin/ampicillin share side chains, so avoid cephalosporins sharing these after a reaction to the matching penicillin. Carbapenem cross-reactivity is below 1%, and aztreonam cross-reacts only with ceftazidime.

## Practical plan

- **1.** **Low-risk history** (remote, benign, non-urticarial): give cefazolin as normal, with usual monitoring.
- **2.** **Previous immediate or anaphylactic reaction to penicillin:** cefazolin is acceptable in most guidance, with monitoring and resuscitation capability, since the side chain is unique; if there is diagnostic uncertainty, obtain specialist advice and choose a procedure-appropriate regimen rather than defaulting to a less effective alternative solely from clinician discomfort.
- **3.** **Severe delayed reaction (SJS/TEN/DRESS):** avoid all beta-lactams, and seek specialist input.
- **4.** **Refer** for formal delabelling (direct oral challenge for low-risk patients, skin testing for higher risk) and update the record.

## Evidence

Studies show that cefazolin is tolerated by the large majority of penicillin-allergic patients, and that vancomycin and clindamycin prophylaxis is associated with higher SSI rates than beta-lactams; PEN-FAST is a validated tool for predicting a true allergy.

**Scoring (/ 6, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

PG69 2025 Appendix 3 specifically supports cefazolin after immediate hypersensitivity, including anaphylaxis, to other beta-lactams because it has a distinct side chain. This does not apply to prior cefazolin reaction or SCAR (SJS/TEN/DRESS), where specialist advice is required. A “test dose” is not a dependable safety test for severe allergy. PEN-FAST/direct oral challenge is used within a validated allergy pathway, not improvised immediately before urgent surgery. Document the exact drug, reaction phenotype, timing and tolerated alternatives, and remove an inaccurate label only through an appropriate assessment.

## Self-marking checklist

- Clarify the history
- Cefazolin side chain
- Risk stratification
- When to avoid beta-lactams
- Alternatives
- Delabelling

items.title: 11. Compare the current definitions of sepsis and septic shock and discuss the role
items.q: Compare the current definitions of sepsis and septic shock and discuss the role of scoring systems and biomarkers in diagnosis and antibiotic decisions.
items.a:
## Definitions (Sepsis-3, 2016)

**Sepsis** is life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, operationalised as an acute rise of 2 or more points in the SOFA score. **Septic shock** is sepsis with vasopressor need to maintain a MAP of 65 mmHg or more and a lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation, associated with high mortality in the original derivation cohorts; the actual rate varies by population and care. The earlier definitions (SIRS plus infection) were replaced because SIRS is sensitive but non-specific: many hospitalised patients meet SIRS criteria without dysregulated host responses.

## Scores

- **SOFA** (respiration, coagulation, liver, cardiovascular, CNS, renal) is used in ICU and for trials.
- **qSOFA** (respiratory rate 22 or more, altered mentation, systolic BP 100 or less) is a bedside prompt for outside ICU; it is specific but insensitive, and should not be a screening tool alone (the Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommends against its use as a single screen). NEWS2 and similar early-warning scores are more sensitive.
- SSC 2026 supports systematic screening in at-risk patients and favours suitable early-warning tools/SIRS over qSOFA as the sole screen.

## Biomarkers

- **Lactate:** prognostic and a target for resuscitation; it can be raised by adrenaline, liver failure and metformin; repeat to confirm clearance.
- **Procalcitonin:** rises within 3 to 6 hours of bacterial infection; useful to **support stopping antibiotics** (the ProRATA and SAPS trials showed reduced antibiotic duration and, in some, reduced mortality) but poor for diagnosis. C-reactive protein is less specific.
- Blood cultures can remain negative in septic shock; yield depends on prior antibiotics, sampling, organism and source, so a negative result does not exclude infection.

## Stewardship

Treat quickly, culture first, choose the narrowest effective agent once the organism is known (de-escalation), use the shortest effective duration (individualised by pathogen, source control, immune status and response; avoid a universal 7-day rule or 5-day rule for severe pneumonia), consider IV to oral conversion, and review daily. Overtreatment drives resistance, C. difficile and toxicity.

## Evidence (Blue Book 2019)

The chapter traces the move from the 1991 SIRS criteria (neither sensitive nor specific) to Sepsis-3: life-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response, a SOFA rise of 2 or more, qSOFA outside ICU (two of systolic pressure 100 or less, altered mentation, respiratory rate 22 or more), and septic shock as vasopressor need to keep MAP above 65 with lactate above 2 despite fluid. It notes that lactate is neither specific nor sensitive for diagnosis, and that procalcitonin had a pooled sensitivity of 77% and specificity of 79% in one meta-analysis, with the PASS trial suggesting no benefit (and possible harm) from procalcitonin-guided antibiotic escalation. One electronic screening algorithm detected fewer septic patients than a nurse-administered score.

**Scoring (/ 6, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

For this outcome also know the legacy definition: SIRS is at least two of temperature >38 or <36 °C, HR >90/min, RR >20/min or PaCO2 <32 mmHg, WCC >12 or <4 ×10^9/L or >10% immature cells; old “severe sepsis” meant infection-associated SIRS plus organ dysfunction. These are historical terms, not the current requirement for diagnosis. qSOFA is a prognostic warning, not a sensitive exclusion screen. Blood culture yield depends on prior antibiotics, source and sampling; no single fixed 30–40% applies to every septic-shock cohort. Source: Sepsis-3, Blue Book 2019 definitions; SSC 2026 screening recommendations.

## Self-marking checklist

- Sepsis-3 definitions
- qSOFA and SOFA
- SIRS limitations
- Lactate
- Procalcitonin
- Stewardship

items.title: 12. Classify antimicrobial agents according to their mode of action and outline the
items.q: Classify antimicrobial agents according to their mode of action and outline the adverse effects relevant to the critically ill.
items.a:
## Classification by mechanism of action

- **Cell wall synthesis inhibitors:** beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems, monobactams) and glycopeptides (vancomycin, teicoplanin). Bactericidal.
- **Protein synthesis inhibitors (30S):** aminoglycosides (bactericidal), tetracyclines (bacteriostatic).
- **Protein synthesis inhibitors (50S):** macrolides, clindamycin, linezolid, chloramphenicol (generally bacteriostatic).
- **Nucleic acid synthesis inhibitors:** fluoroquinolones (DNA gyrase), metronidazole (DNA damage in anaerobes), rifampicin (RNA polymerase).
- **Folate pathway inhibitors:** trimethoprim and sulfonamides (co-trimoxazole).
- **Cell membrane:** daptomycin, polymyxins (colistin).

## Pharmacodynamic patterns

- **Time-dependent exposure** (beta-lactams): efficacy depends on the time free drug concentration is above the MIC, so prolonged or continuous infusion is advantageous in critical illness.
- **Concentration-dependent killing** is classically illustrated by aminoglycosides (peak/MIC and AUC/MIC, with a post-antibiotic effect); appropriate extended-interval gentamicin dosing is patient/protocol dependent. Fluoroquinolone efficacy is better related to AUC/MIC than a simple peak-only classification.
- **AUC/MIC** dependent: vancomycin (AUC-guided dosing is replacing trough levels), azithromycin.

## Spectrum and common clinical uses

Cefazolin covers staphylococci and streptococci (surgical prophylaxis); piperacillin-tazobactam gives broad gram-negative, anaerobic and pseudomonal cover; ceftriaxone is used for meningitis and community-acquired infection; meropenem for resistant gram-negatives and ESBL; vancomycin for MRSA; metronidazole for anaerobes; gentamicin for synergy and urinary or abdominal sepsis; clindamycin for toxin suppression in toxic shock and necrotising infection; linezolid for MRSA and VRE.

## Resistance and critical-illness pharmacokinetics

Mechanisms include beta-lactamase production (ESBL, AmpC, carbapenemase), altered target (MRSA PBP2a), efflux pumps and reduced permeability. In sepsis the volume of distribution rises, and renal clearance can be augmented (so under-dosing) or reduced (accumulation, with neurotoxicity from beta-lactams and carbapenems), so therapeutic drug monitoring and renal replacement dose adjustment are useful.

## Important adverse effects

- **Beta-lactams:** hypersensitivity, neurotoxicity (seizures, encephalopathy) with accumulation in renal failure, C. difficile.
- **Aminoglycosides:** nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity, neuromuscular blockade potentiation.
- **Vancomycin:** nephrotoxicity (especially with piperacillin-tazobactam), infusion reaction, ototoxicity.
- **Fluoroquinolones:** QT prolongation, tendon rupture, seizures, dysglycaemia.
- **Macrolides:** QT prolongation and interactions (CYP3A4).
- **Linezolid:** serotonin syndrome with serotonergic drugs, myelosuppression.
- **Clindamycin:** C. difficile colitis.
- **Metronidazole:** neuropathy and disulfiram-like effects.

## Evidence

BLING III (continuous versus intermittent infusion) was neutral for its primary mortality endpoint (P=.08), while clinical cure favoured continuous infusion. A contemporary randomised-trial meta-analysis favoured prolonged infusion; SSC 2026 recommends prolonged beta-lactam maintenance infusion after an appropriate loading dose. Do not attribute the pooled mortality result to BLING III alone.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

The curriculum includes antimicrobials beyond antibacterials: azoles inhibit fungal ergosterol synthesis, echinocandins inhibit fungal cell-wall beta-glucan, amphotericin binds ergosterol; aciclovir inhibits viral DNA polymerase after activation, and neuraminidase inhibitors treat influenza. Toxicity examples: azole CYP interactions/QT effects/hepatotoxicity; amphotericin renal injury, K/Mg loss and infusion reactions; aciclovir crystal nephropathy/neurotoxicity (hydration and renal adjustment). Daptomycin is inactivated by surfactant and is not a pneumonia drug. Vancomycin exposure is assessed using AUC/MIC where available. The creatinine signal with vancomycin/piperacillin-tazobactam is not proof that every rise represents structural injury. Sources: BJA Education antimicrobial decision review; BLING III 2024 and 2024 prolonged-infusion meta-analysis.

## Additional spectrum distinctions

Spectrum is organism- and resistance-dependent, not simply “broad” or “narrow”. Cefazolin covers susceptible MSSA/streptococci but not MRSA, Enterococcus or Pseudomonas. Ceftriaxone does not reliably cover those three either; it is useful for susceptible community organisms and CNS infection at meningitis doses. Piperacillin–tazobactam has anaerobic and antipseudomonal activity but is not reliable definitive treatment for every ESBL bloodstream infection. Meropenem covers many ESBL producers and anaerobes but not MRSA or all carbapenemase producers. Vancomycin treats susceptible Gram-positive organisms only; oral administration is for intestinal C. difficile disease, not systemic bacteraemia. Linezolid covers susceptible MRSA/VRE, while daptomycin cannot be used for pneumonia because surfactant inactivates it. Metronidazole covers anaerobes rather than aerobic Gram-negative sepsis.

Echinocandins are useful for invasive Candida, but not Cryptococcus; fluconazole covers susceptible yeasts and does not cover Aspergillus. Voriconazole has mould activity with important hepatic/CYP interactions. Amphotericin has broad fungal activity but meaningful renal/electrolyte toxicity. Antiviral targets differ: aciclovir is for HSV/VZV, ganciclovir/valganciclovir for susceptible CMV with marrow/renal monitoring, and oseltamivir inhibits influenza neuraminidase. Resistant organisms and sanctuary-site infection require susceptibility/site-specific specialist selection. These examples expand the broad-classification outcome without implying memorisation of every local treatment regimen.

**Additional self-check (/4):** explain one antibacterial spectrum gap; one antifungal distinction; one antiviral distinction; and one clinically relevant toxicity/interaction.

## Self-marking checklist

- Cell wall agents
- Protein synthesis inhibitors
- Nucleic acid agents
- Membrane-active agents
- Beta-lactam adverse effects
- Aminoglycoside and vancomycin toxicity
- Rational prescribing approach
- De-escalation and stewardship

items.title: 13. Outline the investigation and management of a patient admitted to the intensive
items.q: Outline the investigation and management of a patient admitted to the intensive care unit with suspected bacterial meningitis.
items.a:
## Recognition and initial assessment

Bacterial meningitis presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness and sometimes seizures or a petechial rash (meningococcus). The classical triad is present in a minority. Common organisms: Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, Listeria monocytogenes (older adults—WHO 2025 uses >60 years—pregnancy or immunocompromise; follow local thresholds), Haemophilus influenzae (unvaccinated), and after neurosurgery or trauma, staphylococci and gram-negatives.

## Management: time-critical

- **1.** **Resuscitate (ABC)** and recognise sepsis; manage the airway if the GCS is 8 or less or seizures persist.
- **2.** **Blood cultures,** then **empirical antibiotics immediately,** without waiting for CT or lumbar puncture: ceftriaxone 2 g IV 12-hourly (or cefotaxime) plus vancomycin if penicillin-resistant pneumococci are possible; add **amoxicillin/ampicillin** for Listeria risk; consider aciclovir for possible encephalitis.
- **3.** **Dexamethasone** 0.15 mg/kg (about 10 mg) 6-hourly for 4 days, started before or with the first antibiotic dose, for suspected pneumococcal meningitis; it reduces death and neurological sequelae in adults (de Gans, 2002) and is continued only if the diagnosis is confirmed.
- **4.** **Lumbar puncture** if safe: defer LP and assess for cranial imaging if there is severely reduced consciousness (e.g. GCS <10), focal signs/cranial-nerve deficits, papilloedema, adult new-onset seizures or severe immunocompromise; local guidance applies. Check coagulation, and do not delay antibiotics. CSF shows raised neutrophils, high protein and low glucose; send Gram stain, culture and PCR.
- **5.** **Intracranial pressure:** head up 30 degrees, avoid hypotension and hypoxia, treat seizures, normothermia, osmotherapy as needed; avoid hyponatraemia. Fluid resuscitation is appropriate in septic shock, in contrast to children in resource-poor settings.
- **6.** **Public health:** notify; **prophylaxis for close contacts** in meningococcal disease (ciprofloxacin or rifampicin).
- **7.** **Complications:** hearing loss, seizures, cerebral oedema, venous thrombosis, hydrocephalus, DIC, and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

## Evidence

The dexamethasone trial by de Gans and van de Beek (2002) showed benefit in pneumococcal disease; observational studies link delayed antibiotics to worse outcomes.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

A normal CT does not prove LP safe. Shock, respiratory instability, significant coagulopathy or concerning neurological findings still require deferral. If safe and immediately available, LP before antibiotics improves yield; if any meaningful delay is likely, cultures and antibiotics take priority. Paired serum glucose supports CSF interpretation; send cell count, protein, glucose, Gram stain/culture and bacterial/viral PCR as indicated. Dexamethasone is started with the first antibiotic when bacterial meningitis is strongly suspected in a non-epidemic setting, then reviewed against CSF/pathogen findings; it is not automatically continued for every organism. Ensure hearing assessment, neurorehabilitation and public-health follow-up. Sources: WHO meningitis 2025 and NICE NG240; original de Gans trial.

## Self-marking checklist

- Cultures and immediate antibiotics
- Antibiotic regimen including Listeria cover
- Dexamethasone
- Lumbar puncture indications and contraindications
- Management of raised ICP
- Supportive care
- Encephalitis and aciclovir
- Public health measures

items.title: 14. Which adjunctive therapies have been investigated in septic shock beyond fluids,
items.q: Which adjunctive therapies have been investigated in septic shock beyond fluids, vasopressors and antibiotics, and what is the evidence for each?
items.a:
## Corticosteroids

Hydrocortisone 200 mg/day (50 mg 6-hourly, or infusion) is suggested for septic shock with ongoing vasopressor requirement. **CORTICUS** (2008) showed no mortality benefit but faster shock reversal; **ADRENAL** (2018, 3800 patients) found no difference in 90-day mortality but faster resolution of shock and fewer days on ventilation; **APROCCHSS** (hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone) showed reduced 90-day mortality. Adverse effects include hyperglycaemia, hypernatraemia and neuromuscular weakness. The 0.25-microgram/kg/min for 4-hour threshold is an older practical example, not a compulsory current gate; consider low-dose IV hydrocortisone for ongoing vasopressor-dependent septic shock after resuscitation.

## Vasopressin and other vasopressors

**VASST** (2008) compared vasopressin 0.03 units/min with noradrenaline; there was no overall mortality difference, with a possible benefit in less severe shock. It is used as a catecholamine-sparing second agent. Angiotensin II (ATHOS-3) raised MAP in refractory shock, but no mortality benefit has been shown. Methylene blue is used for vasoplegia in selected cases.

## Others

- **Vitamin C, thiamine and hydrocortisone ("HAT"):** early enthusiasm was not supported by VITAMINS, CITRIS-ALI or LOVIT (which suggested harm with high-dose vitamin C), so it is not recommended.
- **Beta-blockade (esmolol, landiolol):** small trials generated interest, but STRESS-L stopped early with possible harm; do not use short-acting beta-blockers routinely as treatment for septic shock.
- **Renal replacement therapy** for established indications such as refractory overload, hyperkalaemia or severe acid–base disturbance; high-volume haemofiltration and cytokine adsorption (CytoSorb, polymyxin B haemoperfusion, e.g. EUPHRATES) have not improved survival.
- **Intravenous immunoglobulin:** not routine sepsis treatment; consider only selected toxin-mediated infections with specialist advice and recognition of limited evidence.
- **Activated protein C (drotrecogin alfa):** PROWESS-SHOCK showed no benefit and the drug was withdrawn; **anti-TNF, anti-endotoxin and TLR4 antagonists** failed.
- **Bicarbonate:** a selective option for severe metabolic acidaemia with AKI; BICARICU-2 (2025) did not lower 90-day mortality, although kidney-replacement use was reduced.

## Evidence summary (Blue Book 2019)

Steroids are the best-supported adjunct: Annane's 2002 trial found a 28-day survival benefit (no difference at one year), CORTICUS and ADRENAL found no mortality difference but faster shock reversal (ADRENAL adverse events 1.1% versus 0.3%), and APROCCHSS (hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone) found lower 90-day mortality with more hyperglycaemia. VASST and VANISH showed no mortality difference with vasopressin; LeoPARDS (519 patients) found no benefit from levosimendan; antithrombin and thrombomodulin did not improve survival; immunomodulation has largely failed. These areas were updated using the current sources identified above.

**Scoring (/ 6, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Evaluate the endpoint and population, not just a positive physiological effect. Angiotensin II and methylene blue can improve pressure/catecholamine requirements without established broad survival benefit; methylene blue risks serotonin toxicity (MAO inhibition) and can interfere with oximetry. Hydroxocobalamin is rescue/experimental for vasoplegia and can interfere with laboratory and dialysis optical systems. Immunoglobulin is not routine sepsis therapy; toxin-mediated infection requires a separate specialist decision. VA-ECMO may be considered in selected severe reversible septic cardiomyopathy, not as established treatment for isolated vasoplegia. Warming afebrile patients, omega-3 formulations and immune-phenotype therapies remain research questions. Sources: BJA Education novel sepsis interventions 2025 (targeted reading); SSC 2026; STRESS-L and BICARICU-2 primary reports.

## Vasopressor mechanisms and practical limitations

Noradrenaline acts mainly through alpha receptors with some beta-1 activity, supporting arteriolar and venous tone; adverse effects include arrhythmia, excessive vasoconstriction and extravasation injury. Adrenaline adds beta-mediated inotropy but can cause tachyarrhythmia and aerobic lactate production. Vasopressin acts through non-adrenergic V1 receptors and may spare catecholamine exposure, with ischaemic risk. Angiotensin II targets AT1 receptors; a pressure response is not equivalent to proven survival benefit. Treat ongoing infection, hypovolaemia and pump failure alongside tone, and do not pursue MAP at the expense of falling cardiac output. Check arterial waveform quality and whether a peripheral pressure underestimates central pressure in severe vasoplegia.

**Self-check (/4):** explains adrenergic versus non-adrenergic actions; relevant adverse effects; mixed-shock reassessment; pressure-versus-flow limitation. **Source:** BJA Education, Management of vasoplegic shock (2025), DOI:10.1016/j.bjae.2024.10.004, targeted mechanism/assessment/vasopressor sections; current septic-shock choices checked against SSC 2026. Post-CPB management is shared cardiac material, not wholly allocated here.

## Intravenous immunoglobulin: relevant infection/immune overlap

IVIG provides pooled antibodies and immunomodulatory effects. Replacement in selected antibody deficiency differs from high-dose immunomodulation. It is not routine treatment for undifferentiated septic shock or every necrotising infection; toxin-mediated disease and HLH require a separate specialist decision. Other recognised ICU uses include selected neurological/haematological immune diseases, whose full management belongs to their own sets.

Before use confirm the specific indication, product, national/local approval pathway, dose/weight basis and infusion rate. Monitor for infusion reactions, haemolysis, thrombosis, AKI, aseptic meningitis and rare severe pulmonary/allergic reactions; consider baseline renal function, hydration and thrombosis risk. Limited supply/cost reinforces indication-based prescribing. A new fever or renal injury after IVIG can be an adverse effect as well as infection.

**Self-check (/3):** distinguishes replacement/immunomodulation; rejects blanket sepsis use; identifies important toxicity/monitoring. **Source:** BJA Education, The use of intravenous immunoglobulin in intensive care (2024), DOI:10.1016/j.bjae.2023.10.004, targeted indications/controversies/adverse-effects sections; SSC 2026. Historical UK commissioning detail is not presented as current NZ eligibility.

## Self-marking checklist

- Hydrocortisone
- Vasopressin
- Fludrocortisone
- Vitamin C
- Blood purification
- Failed therapies

items.title: 15. A patient develops a fever of 39
items.q: A patient develops a fever of 39.5 degrees within an hour of induction for elective surgery. Outline your differential diagnosis and management.
items.a:
## Causes to consider in the first hours of anaesthesia

- **1.** **Malignant hyperthermia** (rising ETCO2, tachycardia, masseter rigidity, hyperkalaemia, metabolic acidosis, rhabdomyolysis); temperature rise is a late sign, and this is time-critical (see the specific malignant hyperthermia item).
- **2.** **Iatrogenic overheating:** forced-air warmers, heating blankets, humidified circuits, and warmed fluids in a patient with impaired heat loss.
- **3.** **Infection:** pre-existing sepsis, bacteraemia from instrumentation (urological, biliary, dental, colonic), infected necrotic tissue, and contaminated infusions or lines.
- **4.** **Drug-related:** anticholinergic toxicity, neuroleptic malignant syndrome (dopamine antagonists, withdrawal of levodopa), serotonin syndrome (with pethidine, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue, MAOI), amphetamines or cocaine, and thyroid storm.
- **5.** **Transfusion reactions** (febrile non-haemolytic, haemolytic, TRALI, bacterial contamination).
- **6.** **Endocrine:** thyroid storm and phaeochromocytoma crisis.
- **7.** **Neurological:** hypothalamic injury, central fever after intracranial surgery, and intrathecal contrast or blood.
- **8.** **Others:** anaphylaxis, pulmonary embolism, and tissue injury; later (days) causes include wound infection, pneumonia, line infection, anastomotic leak and venous thromboembolism; atelectasis alone is not a well-supported explanation for postoperative fever.

## Management

Check the whole circuit: **stop warming,** stop volatile agents and suxamethonium if there is a suspicion of malignant hyperthermia, increase ventilation, review the vital signs and ETCO2, check temperature with a core probe, request arterial blood gas (potassium, lactate, pH) and creatine kinase, take cultures, and examine the patient. Cool actively if above 39 to 40 degrees (surface cooling, cold fluids, ice packs), give paracetamol, and send tests for infection and consider antibiotics. If malignant hyperthermia is possible, give **dantrolene** (2.5 mg/kg, repeated) and follow the protocol.

## Evidence

Evidence for the differential diagnosis is based on case series and malignant hyperthermia registry data; the diagnostic yield of routine fever work-up on postoperative day 1 is low.

**Scoring (/ 6, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Do not reflexively label early fever as sepsis or order an indiscriminate septic screen in every stable patient. Confirm a reliable core temperature, review the temporal drug/transfusion/procedure history and examine for a treatable source. Hypermetabolic MH needs the full crisis response and dantrolene (initial 2.5 mg/kg actual weight, current ANZCA per-dose maximum 300 mg) rather than waiting for fever confirmation. Antipyresis is for comfort or another specific indication; it is not proven to improve sepsis outcomes. This is a retained shared differential with the crisis sets, not proof the entire MH/endocrine syllabus belongs in Set 4.

## Self-marking checklist

- Malignant hyperthermia
- Anaphylaxis
- Sepsis and bacteraemia
- Drug and transfusion reactions
- Iatrogenic causes
- Management

items.title: 16. Outline your perioperative management of a patient with a known latex allergy
items.q: Outline your perioperative management of a patient with a known latex allergy.
items.a:
## Latex allergy: recognise and plan

Latex allergy is a type I (IgE) reaction to natural rubber proteins, and the risk groups are health-care workers, patients with spina bifida or multiple surgeries, atopy, and cross-reactive food allergy (banana, avocado, kiwi, chestnut). Type IV contact dermatitis is different and is not anaphylaxis. Confirm the diagnosis with the history and testing (specific IgE, skin prick).

## Perioperative management

- **Schedule** according to the local latex-safe pathway; first-case scheduling is especially relevant where powdered latex gloves may have contaminated the environment, tell theatre staff, put a sign on the door, and prepare a latex-free trolley. Modern theatres are largely latex-free, which has reduced reactions.
- **Equipment:** non-latex gloves (nitrile), tourniquets, drains, catheters, breathing circuits and bags, masks, airways, syringes with non-latex plunger, IV tubing without latex ports, bungs and rubber stoppers (draw drugs without piercing latex stoppers). Check the labels and stock.
- **Premedication** with steroids or antihistamines is not shown to prevent reactions and is not routine.
- Anaesthetic technique is unchanged; use standard monitoring and have adrenaline and resuscitation drugs ready.
- **Recognise and treat anaphylaxis** (see the first item): remove latex, call for help, adrenaline, fluid.
- Post-anaesthesia care in a latex-free area.

## Chlorhexidine allergy

Chlorhexidine is a leading cause of perioperative anaphylaxis (skin preparation, lubricating gel, impregnated central lines, mouthwash, urinary catheters, dressings). Reactions can be delayed (30 to 60 minutes) and can follow mucosal contact. Management: ask about previous reactions, check the allergy label, **avoid chlorhexidine** in all forms, and use povidone-iodine or alternative skin preparation (noting iodine allergy is not a contraindication to iodine skin prep); use plain gels; and check central venous catheters and dressings. Confirm with specific IgE and skin tests.

## Evidence

Reactions to latex have fallen with latex-free policies; chlorhexidine anaphylaxis is increasingly reported in Australia, NZ and the UK (NAP6).

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

A latex-safe environment extends from reception and transport through theatre, recovery and ward; verify product composition rather than assuming every rubber stopper contains natural rubber latex or removing closures in a way that compromises sterility. Pharmacy/manufacturer advice can identify safe presentations. Persistent chlorhexidine alerts must cover impregnated devices, dressings, line connectors, gels and oral care. Source: PG69 2025 hidden-allergen appendix and allergy service guidance.

## Self-marking checklist

- Types of latex allergy and risk groups
- First case on the list and latex-free theatre
- Equipment substitutions
- Premedication not effective
- Anaphylaxis plan
- Recognises late onset
- Testing after a reaction
- Chlorhexidine as another hidden allergen

items.title: 17. During a respiratory pandemic, you are asked to intubate an infected patient
items.q: During a respiratory pandemic, you are asked to intubate an infected patient. How do you protect staff and patients?
items.a:
## What generates risk

Droplet and contact transmission is covered by a surgical mask, eye protection, gown and gloves; **airborne transmission** (or aerosol generation) requires a fit-tested **N95/P2 respirator**. Aerosol-generating procedures (AGPs) include tracheal intubation and extubation, bag-mask ventilation, non-invasive ventilation, high-flow nasal oxygen, bronchoscopy, tracheostomy, open suctioning and CPR. Intubation carries one of the highest risks to anaesthetists, owing to proximity to the airway.

## Personal protective equipment

- **1.** **Donning and doffing** with a trained observer and checklist: hand hygiene, gown, N95/P2 (with seal check), eye protection (goggles or face shield), hair cover, double gloves. Doffing is the highest-risk step; remove outer gloves and gown first, then hands, face shield, and finally the respirator, with hand hygiene between steps.
- **2.** **Powered air-purifying respirators** can be used where fit testing fails.

## Planning and technique

- **Room:** negative-pressure room if available, door closed, minimal staff, and equipment prepared in advance (intubation checklist, kit in a sealed box). Intubate where the patient is when appropriate, with one experienced operator.
- **Technique:** pre-oxygenation with a tight-fitting mask and a filter (use the oxygenation method needed to avoid hypoxaemia, with appropriate PPE/ventilation; do not withhold necessary HFNO/NIV solely because of an older blanket AGP label); **rapid sequence induction** with full neuromuscular blockade to avoid coughing and bag-mask ventilation; **video laryngoscopy** for distance from the airway and first-pass success; a viral filter between the tube and circuit; cuff inflated before ventilation; avoid unnecessary circuit disconnections; if disconnection is essential, pause ventilation and use the local circuit-safety procedure, avoiding unrecognised prolonged tube clamping.
- **Extubation:** a high-risk event; consider smooth emergence, avoid unnecessary coughing, and perform in a controlled area with PPE.
- **Aftercare:** disinfect equipment, dispose of single-use items, and clean the room after the appropriate air-change interval.

## Evidence

The evidence comes from observational data in SARS and COVID-19 outbreaks and simulation studies; the ANZCA/ANZICS/ASA airway guidance was based on expert consensus, and N95 versus surgical mask comparisons are inconclusive.

**Scoring (/ 6, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Respiratory infection risk is a function of pathogen, coughing, proximity, exposure duration and room ventilation, not only the name of a device. Use current disease-specific guidance, respirator fit testing/seal checks and supervised donning/doffing. A surgical mask alone is inadequate for an airborne infection. Preoxygenation and gentle bag-mask ventilation remain appropriate when needed to prevent dangerous desaturation. These updates qualify historic COVID-era advice; source: PG28 2025 and contemporary national airborne-precaution guidance.

## Self-marking checklist

- Aerosol-generating procedures
- PPE
- Room and team
- Airway technique
- Extubation and recovery
- Equipment cleaning

items.title: 18. Discuss the anaesthetic and perioperative management of a patient with necrotisi
items.q: Discuss the anaesthetic and perioperative management of a patient with necrotising fasciitis requiring urgent debridement.
items.a:
## Recognition

Necrotising soft tissue infection (NSTI; necrotising fasciitis, Fournier's gangrene, gas gangrene) is a surgical emergency with mortality of 20 to 30% even with treatment. Suspect it with pain out of proportion to the findings, rapidly spreading erythema, skin discolouration, bullae, crepitus, anaesthesia over the area, and systemic toxicity (shock, fever or hypothermia, confusion). Risk factors are diabetes, injecting drug use, immunosuppression, obesity, recent surgery or trauma, and perineal infection. Type 1 is polymicrobial (including anaerobes), type 2 is group A streptococcus (and sometimes Staphylococcus aureus), type 3 is clostridial or marine organisms (Vibrio). Imaging (CT, ultrasound) can show gas, but it must not delay surgery, and the LRINEC score is not reliable enough to exclude it.

## Management

- **1.** **Early surgical debridement** is the key intervention, and delay is associated with increased mortality. Take the patient promptly to theatre, with repeat exploration at 24 hours and further debridement as required; amputation may be needed.
- **2.** **Antibiotics immediately:** broad-spectrum cover with a carbapenem or piperacillin-tazobactam plus appropriate MRSA coverage. Include a toxin-suppressing protein-synthesis inhibitor (classically clindamycin; linezolid is an alternative in selected protocols) for suspected streptococcal/clostridial disease. Do not automatically prescribe both linezolid and clindamycin; tailor to cultures and local ID guidance.
- **3.** **Resuscitation:** fluid, vasopressors, and invasive monitoring; intubation for airway or ventilation if shocked.
- **4.** **Organ support:** renal replacement, correction of coagulopathy, glycaemic control.
- **5.** **Adjuncts:** intravenous immunoglobulin may be considered for streptococcal toxic shock (a small trial and observational data; the INSTINCT trial of IVIG for NSTI showed no benefit). Hyperbaric oxygen is not proven and should never delay surgery.
- **6.** **Reconstruction and wound care:** negative pressure dressings, nutrition, rehabilitation, and psychological support.

## Anaesthetic considerations

Rapid sequence induction if unwell, vasopressor-ready induction, large-bore access, arterial line, blood available, temperature control, anticipated large fluid and blood requirements, and postoperative ICU care.

## Evidence

Evidence comes from observational studies showing the effect of timing of debridement; trials of IVIG and hyperbaric oxygen are inconclusive.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain.

## Self-marking checklist

- Recognition and urgency of debridement
- Resuscitation and vasopressors
- Antibiotics with toxin suppression
- IVIG for toxic shock
- Cardiostable induction
- Monitoring and blood product preparation
- Second-look surgery
- ICU care

items.title: 19. A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve is scheduled for a dental extraction an
items.q: A patient with a prosthetic aortic valve is scheduled for a dental extraction and a patient with suspected infective endocarditis requires urgent surgery. Discuss prophylaxis and perioperative management.
items.a:
## Who needs prophylaxis

Current guidance (AHA, ESC and the Australian Therapeutic Guidelines) restricts prophylaxis to patients at the **highest risk of an adverse outcome** from endocarditis: prosthetic valves or prosthetic material used for valve repair, previous infective endocarditis, certain congenital heart disease (unrepaired cyanotic disease, repaired defects with prosthetic material in the first 6 months or with residual shunts), and cardiac transplant recipients with valvulopathy. Do not generalise this US/European list to all NZ patients: New Zealand guidance also includes rheumatic valvular heart disease and specified additional risk groups. Use the current local dental/cardiology protocol.

## Which procedures

Dental procedures that manipulate gingival tissue, the periapical region, or perforate oral mucosa. For non-dental procedures, indications differ between jurisdictions and infected-site procedures may need organism-directed cover; ESC 2023 allows consideration in selected high-risk patients. Routine TOE alone does not require IE prophylaxis. Distinguish treatment of established infection from dental prophylaxis. Good oral hygiene matters more than antibiotics.

## Regimen

A single dose 30 to 60 minutes before the procedure: amoxicillin 2 g orally (or ampicillin/cefazolin IV if unable to take orally); with penicillin allergy, clindamycin is no longer favoured, and cefalexin (if no anaphylaxis history), azithromycin or doxycycline are alternatives.

## The patient with active endocarditis

- **Recognise:** fever, new murmur, embolic phenomena, heart failure, positive blood cultures (usually three sets before antibiotics when feasible; never delay urgent treatment of shock to achieve this), and vegetations on echocardiography (modified Duke criteria).
- **Indications for surgery:** heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection (abscess, persistent bacteraemia, resistant or fungal organisms), and large vegetations with embolic risk (over 10 mm). Timing is balanced against neurological complications (embolic stroke, haemorrhage), as the EASE trial supported early surgery for left-sided disease with large vegetations.
- **Anaesthetic considerations:** haemodynamic goals of the valve lesion (aortic regurgitation: avoid bradycardia; stenosis: preserve preload and sinus rhythm), heart block from aortic root abscess (pacing pads), anticoagulation and intracranial haemorrhage risk, injecting drug use (difficult access, withdrawal), antibiotic continuity, and consideration of transoesophageal echo.

## Evidence

The restriction of prophylaxis follows a lack of trial evidence and the low absolute risk; guidelines changed in 2007 and have been maintained.

**Scoring (/ 6, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

This mixed item is retained as a shared infection/cardiac topic, not allocated comprehensive valve-surgery coverage. For the prosthetic-valve dental extraction, prophylaxis is indicated; choose a current local regimen, commonly amoxicillin 2 g orally 30–60 min beforehand in adults without relevant allergy. Anaphylaxis to penicillin affects oral cephalexin decisions differently from the cefazolin-specific perioperative evidence. Avoid routinely prescribing clindamycin when current local alternatives are available because of C. difficile risk. Sources: NZ Heart Foundation IE prevention guidance (still listed on its website); ESC 2023; current AHA prophylaxis card. See 2009.2 Q9 model for the historical/current distinction.

## Self-marking checklist

- Indications for prophylaxis
- Procedures
- Regimen
- Recognise endocarditis
- Surgical indications
- Anaesthetic considerations

items.title: 20. A neutropenic patient on chemotherapy develops fever and hypotension
items.q: A neutropenic patient on chemotherapy develops fever and hypotension. Outline your approach, and discuss the perioperative considerations for patients with HIV and solid organ transplants.
items.a:
## Febrile neutropenia: a medical emergency

Neutropenia is a neutrophil count below 0.5 x 10^9/L (or expected to fall); fever is a temperature of 38 degrees or higher. Signs may be blunted. Treat as sepsis: resuscitate, cultures (blood from every lumen of a central line), and **empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics within the first hour**, anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam monotherapy (piperacillin-tazobactam or cefepime, or meropenem if unstable), adding vancomycin for line infection, skin infection, pneumonia or haemodynamic instability, aminoglycoside for shock or resistant organisms. Persistent fever after several days in prolonged high-risk neutropenia prompts fungal investigation (including CT when appropriate) and a specialist empirical/pre-emptive strategy. MASCC/outpatient pathways apply only to selected stable patients, not this hypotensive patient. G-CSF is not routine.

## HIV

Effective antiretroviral therapy has made HIV a chronic illness. Check CD4 count and viral load, continue antiretrovirals perioperatively (avoid interruption; note interactions with cytochrome P450 inhibitors such as ritonavir/cobicistat, which increase levels of fentanyl, midazolam, and local anaesthetics), consider cardiovascular, hepatic, renal and neurological complications, and opportunistic infections (Pneumocystis, TB) when CD4 counts are below 200. Standard precautions are sufficient; post-exposure prophylaxis is available.

## Transplant recipients

- **Immunosuppression** (tacrolimus, ciclosporin, mycophenolate, steroids): continue perioperatively; levels and drug interactions matter (tacrolimus nephrotoxicity, azole interactions); continue usual steroid and assess adrenal-suppression risk and surgical stress; supplement when indicated rather than automatically in every long-term recipient.
- **Infection risk** is highest 1 to 6 months post-transplant (opportunistic: CMV, Pneumocystis, fungi); prophylaxis is used.
- Denervated allograft physiology (heart: no response to atropine, dependent on preload and direct-acting agents), renal function, and strict asepsis for lines.

## Evidence

Recommendations come from IDSA/ESMO febrile neutropenia guidance and transplant society consensus; there are no randomised perioperative trials.

**Scoring (/ 6, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Shock excludes a low-risk febrile-neutropenia outpatient pathway regardless of MASCC score. Do not perform rectal temperature/DRE or unnecessary traumatic mucosal procedures in profound neutropenia. Empiric antifungals depend on duration, neutropenia and fungal risk rather than every immunocompromised septic patient. Consider resistant bacteria, CMV, PJP and fungi according to the immune defect and transplant timeline, without missing ordinary surgical infection. Coordinate immunosuppressant route/levels with the transplant team; do not stop all agents automatically. Treat HIV with standard precautions, protect confidentiality, and continue an effective ART regimen after checking interactions. Source: BJA Education antimicrobial review (general principles); transplant/HIV perioperative guidance; Blue Book 2023 DMARD review (medication risk principles).

## Self-marking checklist

- Febrile neutropenia
- Empirical therapy
- HIV
- Transplant recipients
- Infection control
- Anaesthetic implications

items.title: 21. Discuss the investigation of a patient referred after a suspected anaphylactic r
items.q: Discuss the investigation of a patient referred after a suspected anaphylactic reaction under anaesthesia, including interpretation of mast cell tryptase and skin testing.
items.a:
## Early investigation: mast cell tryptase

**ANZAAG–ANZCA post-crisis card (2022): serum tryptase immediately once feasible without delaying resuscitation, at 1 hour, at 4 hours, and a baseline after 24 hours.** Record onset and sample times; a later outpatient baseline may be needed. A peak exceeding 1.2 × baseline + 2 micrograms/L supports mast-cell activation but neither proves IgE mediation nor identifies the culprit; a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis. Persistent baseline elevation has several causes, including hereditary alpha-tryptasaemia, mast-cell disorders and renal impairment; it warrants specialist interpretation rather than automatically diagnosing mastocytosis.

## Allergy testing (4 to 6 weeks later, at an allergy centre)

- **Skin prick and intradermal tests** with the drugs given during anaesthesia, at standardised non-irritant concentrations (a negative skin test with an NMBA or antibiotic has a good negative predictive value but not perfect). Positive histamine and negative saline controls are required, and antihistamines must be stopped beforehand.
- **Specific IgE** to latex, chlorhexidine, morphine/suxamethonium (limited availability) and beta-lactams.
- **Basophil activation test** where available (useful for NMBAs, sugammadex and drugs with non-IgE mechanisms).
- **Drug provocation (challenge)** under supervision for antibiotics and local anaesthetics, where a validated specialist protocol and a favourable risk–benefit assessment exist; NMBA provocation is not routine after negative skin tests.
- **Cross-reactivity testing** among neuromuscular blockers (many cross-react), and tests for latex, chlorhexidine, patent blue and gelatin.

## What to do with the results

Identify the likely/confirmed culprit and alternatives considered acceptable after testing, explaining residual risk; give a written report and an allergy label; inform the patient, GP and hospital; update the electronic record; and plan future anaesthetics with the safe drugs. If no culprit is found, an individual risk-reduction plan minimises suspected exposures and unnecessary drugs, with readiness to treat; unexplained negative testing does not guarantee safety.

## Evidence (Blue Book 2015)

The chapter uses tryptase to grade severity but gives no timing or cut-offs; the local sampling schedule is the ANZAAG card schedule above; interpretation uses paired baseline/peak values. It states that skin testing should be done about four weeks after the event, and that rapid drug desensitisation protects only while the drug continues to be given. The differential includes Takotsubo (reverse Takotsubo) cardiomyopathy, possibly from adrenaline used for treatment, and allergic myocardial infarction (Kounis syndrome).

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Skin testing is usually performed after 4–6 weeks, using non-irritant concentrations, relevant controls and review of interfering medicines. Earlier testing for urgent surgery is possible with specialist interpretation; early negative results may need repeat assessment. The exposure list must include hidden agents, surgical dyes, disinfectants and catheter components. Specialist challenge is mainly relevant to selected antibiotics/local anaesthetics; do not automatically challenge an NMBA. Document both prohibited agents/cross-reactants and acceptable alternatives, along with residual uncertainty. Sources: PG69 2025; ANZAAG investigation guideline; current local post-crisis card.

## Self-marking checklist

- Tryptase timing and interpretation
- Limits of a normal tryptase
- Timing of allergy testing
- Skin prick and intradermal tests
- Specific IgE and basophil activation test
- Drug challenge for alternatives
- Pitfalls (antihistamines, early testing)
- Reporting and communication

items.title: 22. Discuss the perioperative management of abdominal sepsis requiring emergency lap
items.q: Discuss the perioperative management of abdominal sepsis requiring emergency laparotomy.
items.a:
## Recognise and organise

Perforation, anastomotic leak, ischaemic bowel, abscess and biliary obstruction require a source-control decision as well as resuscitation. Call senior surgery, anaesthesia and ICU early; obtain a focused history, examination and imaging when this will guide treatment without unsafe delay. Assess shock, organ dysfunction, aspiration risk, frailty, comorbidity, anticoagulation and treatment goals. Explain operative risk and likely postoperative critical care. Use a validated risk tool such as NELA alongside clinical judgement; its numerical prediction does not incorporate every aspect of frailty or patient preference.

## Resuscitate while preparing source control

Provide oxygen for need, monitoring, two reliable IV lines, blood gas/lactate, FBC, electrolytes/renal/liver function, coagulation and crossmatch. Take blood cultures before antibiotics if this causes no meaningful delay. Give prompt IV treatment covering likely enteric Gram-negative organisms and anaerobes, adjusted to local resistance, recent healthcare exposure and previous cultures. Consider enterococcal, MRSA or fungal coverage selectively. Surgical prophylaxis alone is inadequate treatment of established peritonitis.

Give small assessed crystalloid boluses for hypoperfusion, use dynamic response where practicable, and start noradrenaline early when hypotension persists. Do not wait for a central line or force a large fluid volume into an unresponsive/congested patient. Trend perfusion, consciousness, urine output and lactate without requiring lactate to normalise before surgery. Correct important electrolyte/glucose abnormalities and reverse anticoagulation where indicated in parallel.

Drain, debride, resect or relieve obstruction as soon as practical. The 2025 Blue Book emergency-laparotomy pathway describes faster surgery in shock (within three hours) and within six hours for sepsis; SSC 2026 suggests source control ideally within six hours. These are escalation goals, not permission to wait in rapidly deteriorating shock. Resuscitation and source control proceed together.

## Anaesthesia and recovery

Prepare for a full stomach, difficult physiological airway and peri-induction cardiovascular collapse. Consider gastric decompression; use an individually planned rapid-sequence technique with preoxygenation, titrated induction, vasopressor ready/running, experienced help and explicit airway rescue. Place an arterial line when useful without delaying life-saving surgery. Give lung-protective ventilation, active warming, glucose monitoring, appropriate analgesia and fluid/vasopressor titration to perfusion. Epidural suitability is limited by shock, bacteraemia, coagulopathy and urgency; choose alternatives when risk is unacceptable.

Plan ICU/HDU admission, ongoing ventilation if needed, antibiotic review and cultures from the source. Reassess source-control adequacy if shock persists. Provide thromboprophylaxis when safe, nutrition, delirium prevention, mobilisation and kidney/fluid monitoring. Handover includes cultures, antimicrobial doses/redosing, remaining source-control concerns, blood loss, haemodynamics and escalation limits.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Recognises source, shock, risk and senior multidisciplinary needs.
- **2 marks** — Cultures and prompt appropriate therapeutic antibiotics.
- **2 marks** — Assessed fluid/vasopressor resuscitation in parallel with urgent source control.
- **2 marks** — Safe physiological-airway and intraoperative plan.
- **2 marks** — Critical-care handover, source review and postoperative recovery.

items.title: 23. Describe the investigation and management of suspected encephalitis in an adult
items.q: Describe the investigation and management of suspected encephalitis in an adult.
items.a:
Encephalitis is inflammatory brain dysfunction, often presenting with altered behaviour/consciousness, fever, seizures or focal signs. Consider HSV/VZV, other viruses according to travel/exposure, bacterial or opportunistic infection, autoimmune encephalitis and mimics such as metabolic/toxic encephalopathy, stroke and non-convulsive status. Sepsis-associated encephalopathy is a diagnosis requiring assessment for these alternatives, not a reason to omit CNS investigation.

Stabilise airway/oxygenation and perfusion, check glucose and treat seizures promptly; involve neurology, infectious diseases and ICU. Protect the airway for loss of reflexes or refractory seizures. Avoid hypoxia, hypotension and major sodium/glucose disturbance. Examine for focal deficit, meningism, rash, raised intracranial pressure and an infectious exposure or immune deficit.

Send blood cultures, FBC, electrolytes, renal/liver function and targeted infectious tests. Obtain MRI brain when feasible (more sensitive than early CT); CT is useful when MRI is not immediately available or a mass/urgent complication is suspected. EEG helps identify non-convulsive seizures. Perform LP promptly if safe, with opening pressure, cells, glucose paired with serum, protein, bacterial studies and pathogen-specific HSV/VZV PCR. Request other tests according to geography, host and syndrome; retain CSF for additional studies. A normal early MRI or CSF count does not exclude HSV, and a negative early HSV PCR may require repeat LP/PCR while treatment continues. Multiplex panels do not replace all appropriate pathogen-specific tests. Defer LP with instability, significant coagulopathy or concerning intracranial signs; do not delay treatment for imaging or LP.

Start IV aciclovir immediately when encephalitis is suspected, ideally within six hours of presentation; a typical adult HSV regimen is 10 mg/kg every eight hours, with renal adjustment and a locally agreed weight scalar in obesity. Ensure appropriate hydration and monitor creatinine, fluid balance and neurotoxicity. Give bacterial-meningitis antibiotics too when that diagnosis remains plausible. Confirmed HSV usually needs 14–21 days, commonly longer in immunocompromised patients, with specialist review of clinical response and end-of-treatment/repeat PCR decisions. Do not stop solely because one early PCR is negative.

Consider autoimmune encephalitis when the course, movement disorder, psychiatric symptoms, autonomic dysfunction or refractory seizures suggest it; obtain specialist-directed serum/CSF antibody tests and tumour evaluation. Infection and autoimmunity can overlap, including autoimmune disease after HSV. Immunotherapy requires a coordinated decision, not uncritical steroids in every undifferentiated infection. Provide rehabilitation, cognitive/psychiatric follow-up, seizure counselling and family support.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Recognises syndrome and infectious/autoimmune/metabolic differential.
- **2 marks** — Immediate stabilisation and seizure management.
- **2 marks** — MRI/EEG and safe LP with targeted tests.
- **2 marks** — Prompt renal-adjusted aciclovir and appropriate duration/repeat testing.
- **2 marks** — Specialist autoimmune assessment and rehabilitation.

items.title: 24. Discuss fluid stewardship during resuscitation and recovery from septic shock
items.q: Discuss fluid stewardship during resuscitation and recovery from septic shock.
items.a:
Fluid is a treatment with an indication, dose, response and stopping rule. Distinguish rescue resuscitation from optimisation, stabilisation and later evacuation of accumulated fluid. Endothelial/glycocalyx injury increases interstitial fluid accumulation, while venous congestion can impair organ function even when arterial pressure seems acceptable. Revised Starling physiology emphasises lymphatic return rather than reliable sustained venous reabsorption of oedema.

Before a bolus ask three questions: is there a perfusion problem that fluid might improve; is the patient likely to increase stroke volume; and can the patient tolerate additional volume? A positive responsiveness test alone is not an indication in an adequately perfused patient. Assess capillary refill, mental state, urine output, pressure and lactate in context, with bedside echo for ventricular function and alternative shock causes. Passive leg raise requires real-time stroke-volume/cardiac-output measurement. Pulse-pressure/stroke-volume variation needs suitable rhythm/ventilation conditions; IVC size alone is unreliable. Give a measured bolus, reassess benefit and stop when ineffective or harmful.

Balanced crystalloid is generally preferred in sepsis, with saline favoured for some neurological indications. Avoid starch. Noradrenaline can restore vascular tone while limiting indiscriminate fluid administration; hypotension does not automatically mean hypovolaemia. The conditional initial 30 mL/kg recommendation requires reassessment and does not justify repeated unassessed boluses. Restrictive versus liberal strategies in CLASSIC and CLOVERS were neutral for mortality after initial fluids; they do not establish that no patient needs rescue volume.

During stabilisation count all inputs, including drug carriers, flushes, feeds and blood products. Concentrate infusions where safe, stop unnecessary maintenance and assess daily weight, balance, oedema, lung ultrasound/oxygenation and venous congestion alongside perfusion. Lactate may remain elevated from adrenergic stimulation or impaired clearance; attempting to normalise it with unlimited fluid can cause harm.

Once shock is controlled, consider active removal for clinically important overload using diuretics, or kidney replacement for appropriate refractory fluid/electrolyte/acid-base indications. Set an individual net target and monitor pressure, perfusion, renal function and electrolytes; pause if removal causes intolerance. Evidence does not prove routine aggressive de-resuscitation improves survival. ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 supports a personalised capillary-refill-guided haemodynamic strategy for a hierarchical composite outcome, largely through less vital-support time; it is not proof of an isolated mortality reduction or a mandate to abandon other assessment.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Indication, responsiveness and tolerance distinguished.
- **2 marks** — Dynamic testing correctly interpreted.
- **2 marks** — Assessed balanced crystalloid and early vasopressors.
- **2 marks** — Accounts for fluid creep and organ congestion.
- **2 marks** — Individualised removal and accurate trial limitations.

items.title: 25. How do you optimise antimicrobial dosing in a critically ill patient
items.q: How do you optimise antimicrobial dosing in a critically ill patient?
items.a:
Choose a drug active against the likely organism at the actual infection site, using local resistance, source, prior cultures, recent antibiotics and host immune status. Obtain appropriate cultures first when feasible without delaying urgent treatment. Source control remains essential: higher concentrations cannot sterilise an undrained abscess reliably. Review allergy phenotype rather than accepting every beta-lactam label as absolute.

Critical illness changes pharmacokinetics. Capillary leak and fluid loading expand the distribution of hydrophilic drugs, often requiring a full loading dose even with AKI. Subsequent maintenance depends on clearance: augmented renal clearance can underdose a young hyperdynamic patient, whereas evolving AKI causes accumulation. Creatinine may lag and estimated GFR may be misleading. Obesity, hypoalbuminaemia, hepatic dysfunction, extracorporeal circuits and renal-replacement modality/effluent rate add uncertainty.
