Seek pharmacist/ID advice and reassess as physiology or support changes; do not keep an initial renal dose unchanged for days.

Match administration to pharmacodynamics. Beta-lactams depend mainly on free time above MIC: give an appropriate loading dose before extended or continuous maintenance infusion, check stability/compatibility and reliable delivery. Aminoglycosides depend on high exposure/peak with toxicity risk, so individualise the interval and monitor concentrations. Vancomycin generally uses AUC-guided monitoring when available; fluoroquinolones also relate efficacy to AUC/MIC. Tissue penetration matters in CNS, bone, prostate and lung infections; daptomycin is unsuitable for pneumonia.

Use therapeutic drug monitoring where available and meaningful, especially aminoglycosides and vancomycin, and selected beta-lactams in unstable clearance or extracorporeal support. Monitor response, cultures, renal/liver function, QT interval where relevant, marrow suppression and neurological toxicity. Examples include beta-lactam encephalopathy in accumulation, aminoglycoside nephro/ototoxicity, vancomycin toxicity/infusion reactions and azole CYP interactions with immunosuppressants.

At 24–48 hours and daily thereafter review diagnosis, source, susceptibility and clinical response; narrow, change route or stop when appropriate and document a review/stop date. BLING III did not meet its primary mortality endpoint (P=.08), although cure favoured continuous infusion. A contemporary randomised-trial meta-analysis favoured prolonged infusion; SSC 2026 recommends prolonged beta-lactam maintenance after loading. Explain both findings rather than calling BLING III itself a positive survival trial.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Source/spectrum/resistance and cultures.
- **2 marks** — Loading versus maintenance with changing distribution/clearance.
- **2 marks** — Correct pharmacodynamic targets and infusion delivery.
- **2 marks** — TDM, organ support, interactions and toxicity.
- **2 marks** — Daily stewardship and balanced interpretation of BLING III.

items.title: 26. When is a shorter antibiotic course appropriate for bloodstream infection
items.q: When is a shorter antibiotic course appropriate for bloodstream infection? Discuss BALANCE.
items.a:
Duration follows the organism, focus, source-control adequacy, host and response. Confirm true bacteraemia rather than a contaminant; locate and control the source, review susceptibilities and assess for persistent infection or endovascular disease. A fixed seven-day course for every positive blood culture is unsafe.

BALANCE randomised hospitalised patients with bloodstream infection, including ICU patients, to seven or fourteen days. Seven days was noninferior for 90-day mortality within the prespecified four-percentage-point margin. This was a pragmatic duration trial rather than a trial of delayed antibiotics, inadequate source control, or routine oral treatment. Its result supports shorter treatment in clinically appropriate patients and strengthens daily stewardship review.

Important exclusions included Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia, severe immunosuppression, likely contaminants and foci requiring prolonged therapy. Do not extrapolate the result uncritically to endocarditis, osteomyelitis, undrained abscess, complicated S. aureus disease or profoundly immunocompromised hosts. A persistent fever or positive repeat cultures requires reassessment, not an automatic stop on day seven.

In practice establish the treatment start point and organism-specific plan, ensure an active drug at an adequate dose, reassess clinical stability and source control, and check whether an exclusion or complication applies. Obtain repeat blood cultures when indicated by the organism or clinical scenario, especially S. aureus, suspected endovascular infection or persistent instability; routine repeats are not required for every uncomplicated Gram-negative infection. Discuss oral switch separately, considering susceptibility, absorption, bioavailability and focus.

Document the proposed duration, review date, rationale and red flags for extension or further investigation. Benefits of an appropriate shorter course include fewer adverse effects, interactions, line days, C. difficile and antimicrobial selection pressure. Avoid implying that every theoretical benefit was proven as a mortality advantage in BALANCE. Arrange follow-up if relapse would be consequential, and do not confuse source-controlled abdominal-infection duration evidence with an arbitrary universal bacteraemia rule.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Individualises by organism, focus, host and source control.
- **2 marks** — Correct seven-versus-fourteen-day noninferiority interpretation.
- **2 marks** — Identifies major exclusions.
- **2 marks** — Reviews response, dosing and selective repeat cultures/oral switch.
- **2 marks** — Documents duration, safety review and stewardship benefits.

items.title: 27. When should haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis be considered in apparent sepsis
items.q: When should haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis be considered in apparent sepsis?
items.a:
HLH is a life-threatening hyperinflammatory syndrome caused by dysregulated immune activation. Adult secondary HLH may follow infection, malignancy or rheumatological disease (macrophage activation syndrome). Infection can trigger HLH and coexist with it, so this is not a simple choice between sepsis and inflammation.

Consider it in persistent or rapidly progressive apparent sepsis, especially with the “three Fs”: fever, falling blood counts and raised ferritin. Look for hepatosplenomegaly, hepatitis, coagulopathy, neurological dysfunction and multi-organ failure. Ferritin is a useful clue and trend, but even a very high result is not diagnostic in adults; severe infection, liver injury and malignancy also elevate it. Falling fibrinogen and rising triglycerides strengthen suspicion.

Send serial FBC/film, ferritin, fibrinogen, triglycerides, coagulation, liver/renal tests and LDH; investigate triggers including EBV/other infection, lymphoma and autoimmune disease with specialist advice. The HScore estimates probability using clinical/laboratory features and marrow findings; HLH-2004 criteria also provide a framework but neither should delay treatment of a deteriorating patient. Bone-marrow haemophagocytosis is neither necessary nor specific and can be absent early. Soluble CD25/NK-cell assays may help where available, but are not rapid prerequisite tests.

Call haematology/rheumatology, infectious diseases and ICU urgently. Continue appropriate antimicrobial treatment and organ support while seeking source control and the underlying trigger. Immunomodulation is individualised, commonly corticosteroids with agents such as anakinra in selected secondary HLH; malignancy/EBV-associated disease may require specific cytotoxic or other specialist regimens. Do not indiscriminately apply a paediatric etoposide protocol to every adult septic patient.

Monitor organ function and serial inflammatory/cytopenia trends to judge response. Re-evaluate the trigger and diagnosis if treatment fails. The exam-relevant message is to recognise a treatable sepsis mimic/overlap early and activate specialist management without waiting for all criteria, rather than memorising an unsupported ferritin cut-off or presenting anakinra as routine sepsis treatment.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Recognises triggers and sepsis overlap.
- **2 marks** — Three Fs with additional features and ferritin limitations.
- **2 marks** — Appropriate tests, HScore and marrow limitations.
- **2 marks** — Urgent multidisciplinary trigger-specific treatment.
- **2 marks** — Continues infection/organ support and tracks response.

items.title: 28. Outline perioperative considerations for patients with bloodborne viral infectio
items.q: Outline perioperative considerations for patients with bloodborne viral infection.
items.a:
Assess the patient’s illness and organ function, not just the infection label. Maintain confidentiality, explain the plan respectfully and use standard precautions for every patient. HBV, HCV or HIV alone does not require airborne isolation, a separate anaesthetic machine or cancellation. Add transmission-based precautions for a coexisting infection such as pulmonary TB when indicated.

For HBV/HCV determine whether there is active hepatitis, fibrosis/cirrhosis or decompensation. Review jaundice, ascites, encephalopathy, variceal bleeding, renal dysfunction, platelet count, coagulation and relevant treatment. Elective surgery during acute hepatitis or significant decompensation may need deferral and specialist optimisation; urgent surgery requires risk-aware support. Coagulation tests in cirrhosis incompletely describe haemostasis, so neither assume protection from thrombosis nor transfuse simply to normalise a number. Tailor drug choice/dose to liver/renal function and check antiviral interactions. Viral load and treatment status inform specialist management but do not remove the requirement for standard precautions.

For HIV review ART adherence, latest viral load/CD4, opportunistic infections, malignancy and cardiopulmonary, renal, neurological and haematological disease. A well-controlled patient often has perioperative risk comparable to other patients with similar comorbidity. Do not delay urgent surgery to obtain CD4 or viral-load results. In elective uncontrolled disease seek HIV-team advice on whether feasible optimisation will change risk without harmful delay.

Continue ART and indicated opportunistic-infection prophylaxis where possible, planning fasting/enteral access with the specialist. Check interactions particularly with ritonavir/cobicistat and CYP-metabolised anaesthetic, sedative and analgesic drugs; titrate and monitor respiratory effects. Do not stop selected components and leave an ineffective partial regimen without expert advice. Assess active infection, nutrition, anaemia and thrombosis risk; use aseptic devices and standard procedure-specific antibiotic prophylaxis, not blanket broad antibiotics for the HIV label.

Protect staff using safe sharps handling, eye/face protection where splash is possible, appropriate gloves and immediate exposure reporting. Following exposure, wash without squeezing, seek urgent occupational assessment and assess source/recipient status with consent. HIV PEP is time critical, HBV action depends on immunity/source, and HCV has surveillance rather than proven PEP. Keep patient care and staff exposure protocols distinct.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Respectful risk assessment and correct precautions.
- **2 marks** — HBV/HCV disease severity and hepatic/renal implications.
- **2 marks** — HIV control, opportunistic disease and urgency.
- **2 marks** — ART/prophylaxis continuation and interactions.
- **2 marks** — Safe staff practices and pathogen-specific exposure response.

items.title: 29. How do you plan perioperative management of DMARDs and other immunosuppressants
items.q: How do you plan perioperative management of DMARDs and other immunosuppressants?
items.a:
Balance infection and wound-healing risk against disease flare, graft rejection and adrenal insufficiency. Identify the exact medicine, indication, dose, dosing interval, last dose and planned procedure. Rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease and organ transplantation do not share a single interruption protocol. Assess active infection, previous infections, neutropenia, renal/liver function, disease activity, steroid exposure and the consequences of flare.

Conventional synthetic DMARDs such as methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are often continued for elective surgery. Methotrexate requires particular review with AKI, toxicity, cytopenia or active significant infection; check interacting drugs and avoid nitrous oxide because of combined antifolate effects. “Immunosuppressant” does not automatically mean stop treatment. Conversely, safety in one procedure does not establish safety in every septic emergency.

Biologics require a disease- and procedure-specific plan. Some rheumatology/arthroplasty pathways withhold for a dosing interval and restart after satisfactory wound healing and no infection; some IBD abdominal-surgery recommendations favour continuation of selected biologics. Consider agent half-life, immune effect, flare risk and urgency with the treating team. JAK inhibitors may need a short planned interruption under the relevant current guideline; also consider thrombosis and infection risk. Do not present a universal three- or seven-day rule independent of agent and guidance.

For transplant recipients coordinate with the transplant service: preserve effective immunosuppression and route, monitor levels when relevant, and check renal function, potassium and interacting antibiotics/azoles. Some agents, especially mTOR inhibitors, may need special wound-healing plans. Significant sepsis may justify a tailored reduction, but abrupt cessation of all agents risks rejection. Continue baseline corticosteroid and assess adrenal-suppression/surgical-stress supplementation rather than automatically giving high doses to everyone.

Document who makes the interruption/restart decision, the planned date/criteria, and how flare, rejection or infection will be recognised. Restart requires assessment of healing, infection and physiological recovery, not merely discharge from theatre. Communicate to surgery, nursing, pharmacy and the patient. Use standard SSI prevention and targeted antimicrobial/antiviral prophylaxis where indicated rather than an indiscriminate prolonged antibiotic course.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Balances infection, flare/rejection and adrenal risk.
- **2 marks** — Conventional DMARD continuation with exceptions.
- **2 marks** — Biologic/JAK disease-specific interruption/restart.
- **2 marks** — Transplant levels/interactions and steroid plan.
- **2 marks** — Clear multidisciplinary documentation and surveillance.

items.title: 30. Evaluate antimicrobial prophylaxis strategies in intensive care
items.q: Evaluate antimicrobial prophylaxis strategies in intensive care.
items.a:
First apply reliable non-antimicrobial prevention: hand hygiene, aseptic drug/line care, minimal device use, daily removal review, oral hygiene, aspiration precautions, appropriate ventilation liberation, nutrition and mobilisation. Antimicrobial prophylaxis is for a defined risk/indication, not a replacement for source control or routine device care.

Selective digestive decontamination (SDD) uses oral and gastric non-absorbed antimicrobials with a short systemic component; selective oropharyngeal decontamination omits the gastric/systemic elements. The aim is to reduce potentially pathogenic colonisation and subsequent infection in ventilated patients. Potential advantages must be weighed against local resistance ecology, selection pressure, adherence, cost and uncertainty about long-term unit effects. It is a unit-level policy with microbiology surveillance, not an ad hoc prescription for every ventilated individual.

The full international SuDDICU trial, published online in 2025 and in a 2026 issue, did not demonstrate lower in-hospital mortality with SDD. Some microbiological outcomes favoured intervention; ecological noninferiority for new resistant organisms was not established. Therefore neither “proven survival benefit” nor “proven absence of resistance harm” is a justified summary. SSC 2026 conditionally suggests SDD in ventilated adults in units with low resistance, which requires local stewardship consideration rather than a universal mandate.

Use targeted prophylaxis for patients with specific immune defects or treatment risks: for example PJP, CMV or invasive-fungal prophylaxis in selected transplant/haematology populations under the relevant specialist pathway. Distinguish prophylaxis from pre-emptive treatment triggered by surveillance and from empirical treatment of suspected infection. Routine systemic antifungals, IVIG or probiotics for all ICU/sepsis patients are not established beneficial strategies. Review toxicities, drug interactions, organ function and breakthrough organisms.

Surgical prophylaxis generally ends at closure according to procedure policy; a drain, central line or ventilator alone does not justify continuing antibiotics. Stress-ulcer prophylaxis is for GI-bleeding risk rather than infection prevention and should be stopped when its indication resolves. Audit infection rates, resistance, C. difficile, adverse effects and antibiotic exposure. De-escalate/stop therapies as risk changes and record the indication and review date.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Reliable non-antimicrobial prevention.
- **2 marks** — Defines SDD/SOD and unit-level benefits/risks.
- **2 marks** — Accurate full SuDDICU and conditional guideline interpretation.
- **2 marks** — Targeted immune-specific prophylaxis versus routine treatment.
- **2 marks** — Stop rules, adverse effects and ecological audit.

items.title: 31. Outline diagnosis and management of suspected catheter-related bloodstream infec
items.q: Outline diagnosis and management of suspected catheter-related bloodstream infection.
items.a:
Suspect a line source with new fever, rigors during line use, unexplained sepsis, local inflammation, purulence, tunnel infection or persistent bacteraemia. Examine all devices and other sources. A central line in situ plus a positive culture is not automatically catheter-related bloodstream infection; distinguish surveillance CLABSI from a clinical causal diagnosis and assess contaminants in context.

In an unstable patient begin shock management and appropriate empirical IV antibiotics promptly after cultures if this causes no meaningful delay. Obtain paired peripheral and line cultures, labelled by time and lumen, before antibiotics when feasible. Differential time to positivity (line culture becoming positive at least about two hours earlier with comparable sampling) can support catheter origin; it is not valid when sampling is unreliable and is not a prerequisite for removal in severe illness. Culture a removed tip when infection is suspected, not routinely every removed line.

Choose empirical cover according to illness severity, local MRSA/Gram-negative risk, immune state and prior isolates; consider Candida only with relevant risk. Tailor dosing and narrow to organism/susceptibility. Remove an unnecessary or implicated catheter when appropriate and establish alternative access at a clean site if needed. Severe sepsis, tunnel/pocket infection, persistent bacteraemia, S. aureus, fungal infection or complications generally favour removal. Do not exchange an infected line over a guidewire as routine source control.

Assess for endocarditis, septic thrombosis and metastatic infection when suggested by organism, persistent positive cultures or focal signs. Repeat cultures to document clearance where indicated, particularly S. aureus/fungaemia. Duration is organism- and complication-specific, counted using the relevant treatment/clearance convention; do not give every patient a fixed seven-day course. Long-term-line salvage is a specialist decision for selected uncomplicated infections and may combine systemic therapy with a lock; it is unsuitable for many high-risk organisms or complications.

Review the insertion and maintenance bundle: aseptic technique, appropriate skin preparation and drying, hub disinfection, intact dressings, minimal handling and daily removal. Communicate the organism, source-control decision, culture clearance, ongoing treatment and follow-up. Investigate clusters with infection prevention rather than blaming a single insertion event without evidence.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Differentiates clinical infection, surveillance definition and contamination.
- **2 marks** — Paired cultures and correctly qualified time-to-positivity.
- **2 marks** — Prompt appropriate antibiotics and source control.
- **2 marks** — Organism/complication-specific follow-up and duration.
- **2 marks** — Prevention bundle and clear handover.

items.title: 32. Describe the approach to refractory perioperative anaphylaxis
items.q: Describe the approach to refractory perioperative anaphylaxis.
items.a:
Refractory collapse needs simultaneous escalation, reliable adrenaline delivery, volume resuscitation and diagnostic reassessment. Call for expert help and use the current ANZAAG/ANZCA cognitive aid. Stop likely triggers and non-essential administration, inform the surgeon, give 100% oxygen initially, secure ventilation and position to support venous return. Check that IV access is patent and that drug concentration, pump, connections and dose are correct.

In a monitored anaesthetised adult, titrated IV adrenaline doses depend on severity: grade 2 commonly 10–20 micrograms, grade 3 50–100 micrograms, followed by an infusion for persistent instability under the card/local protocol. Give rapid assessed crystalloid boluses because profound capillary leak and venodilation create relative/absolute hypovolaemia. Do not confuse micrograms with milligrams. IM adrenaline is appropriate when IV access/expertise is unavailable; arrest-dose IV boluses are not given routinely to a patient with a pulse.

Reassess airway pressure, capnography, oxygenation, blood pressure, ECG and surgical field. Consider haemorrhage, high neuraxial block, airway/circuit obstruction, tension pneumothorax, embolism, myocardial ischaemia and drug error. Echo can identify severe underfilling, myocardial dysfunction or dynamic LV outflow obstruction; escalating inotropy in an underfilled hyperdynamic ventricle may worsen obstruction. Kounis syndrome is an allergic coronary syndrome, not proof that adrenaline should be withheld in life-threatening anaphylaxis.

For ongoing vasoplegia despite adequate adrenaline and volume, use a titrated second vasopressor such as noradrenaline/vasopressin with expert input and monitoring. Consider glucagon in a beta-blocked patient with resistant cardiovascular compromise, recognising limited evidence and vomiting/hyperglycaemia risk. Bronchodilators treat persistent bronchospasm as adjuncts. Sugammadex is not reliable rescue for rocuronium anaphylaxis and can itself cause anaphylaxis. Methylene blue is not routine first-line therapy; any exceptional rescue use needs expert risk assessment.

Start chest compressions for arrest and, under the perioperative guideline, consider them with SBP <50 mmHg in an anaesthetised patient despite treatment. Do not wait for a tryptase result. After stabilisation take the local serial tryptase samples, plan appropriate monitored care and communicate all exposures and treatment to the allergy service. Steroids and antihistamines do not reverse life-threatening shock and must not delay adrenaline.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Escalates, removes triggers and checks delivery/airway.
- **2 marks** — Severity-appropriate adrenaline with fluid and infusion.
- **2 marks** — Reassesses differential and echo physiology.
- **2 marks** — Reasoned rescue options with limitations.
- **2 marks** — Compression threshold and post-crisis pathway.

items.title: 33. How do you prevent infection during trauma resuscitation and urgent anaesthesia
items.q: How do you prevent infection during trauma resuscitation and urgent anaesthesia?
items.a:
Use standard precautions from first contact despite time pressure: hand hygiene, gloves, eye/face protection and fluid-resistant clothing matched to splash risk. Bloodborne infection status may be unknown and should not determine whether precautions are used. Coordinate tasks and a sharps-safe work area; announce sharps, avoid hand-to-hand passing where feasible, never recap used needles and dispose immediately into nearby containers. Protect rescuers during haemorrhage control and invasive airway/access procedures without delaying life-saving care.

Maintain aseptic IV/arterial/central access and airway equipment handling as far as the emergency allows. Separate clean drug preparation from contaminated gloves and equipment, disinfect hubs and vial septa, and use single-patient syringes/ampoules. Ultrasound probe covers do not replace cleaning/disinfection; use sterile gel/cover for the relevant invasive procedure and follow device reprocessing requirements. Document when full asepsis could not be ensured and replace emergency vascular devices as soon as practicable under the local policy, rather than quietly leaving them indefinitely.

Give early procedure/injury-specific antibiotics for open fractures and contaminated penetrating injuries according to local trauma protocols; arrange irrigation, debridement and definitive source control. Review allergies, weight, renal function, tetanus immunisation and the need for tetanus prophylaxis. Antibiotics do not compensate for delayed debridement or retained devitalised tissue. Do not automatically give prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics to every closed injury.

Prevent hypothermia, maintain perfusion and oxygenation, and manage glucose appropriately. Use clean wound handling, minimise unnecessary urinary/vascular devices and reassess them daily. Consider transmission-based precautions when a concurrent infection is suspected, but organise PPE and isolation so urgent trauma care can proceed safely.

After exposure to blood/body fluid, wash or irrigate immediately, report promptly and activate occupational-health assessment. HIV PEP is time critical; HBV action depends on vaccination/anti-HBs and source status; HCV needs baseline and follow-up testing rather than PEP. Document and hand over breaches, antibiotic doses/redosing, device insertion conditions, wound/tetanus plans and unresolved risks. Clean the environment and reprocess reusable equipment before the next patient.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Risk-matched PPE and safe sharps/team practice.
- **2 marks** — Aseptic access/drugs/equipment with documented emergency exceptions.
- **2 marks** — Targeted antibiotics, debridement and tetanus.
- **2 marks** — Physiology, device minimisation and relevant additional precautions.
- **2 marks** — Exposure response, handover and environmental cleaning.

items.title: 34. Summarise current sepsis priorities and care after the acute resuscitation phase
items.q: Summarise current sepsis priorities and care after the acute resuscitation phase.
items.a:
Recognise infection-associated organ dysfunction early using clinical assessment and a suitable deterioration screen. NEWS/NEWS2, MEWS or SIRS may support screening; qSOFA must not be the sole rule-out tool. SOFA describes organ dysfunction and risk, but a complete score is not a prerequisite to treatment. Differentiate legacy “severe sepsis” terminology from current Sepsis-3 sepsis/septic shock definitions.

For shock or probable/definite sepsis give effective antimicrobials urgently, ideally within one hour of recognition, after cultures if this causes no meaningful delay. For possible sepsis without shock undertake a rapid assessment and, if concern persists, treat within three hours; reassess alternatives and stop unnecessary antibiotics. Do not use procalcitonin alone to decide whether to start urgent antibiotics. Identify the source and achieve control ideally within six hours when intervention is required, accelerating with deterioration.

Use assessed crystalloid and early noradrenaline for shock, with an initial MAP around 65 mmHg in most adults and individual adjustment. Peripheral initiation is reasonable with a suitable site, monitoring and escalation plan. Evaluate perfusion, capillary refill, lactate trajectory, urine and cardiac function together. Consider low-dose IV corticosteroid in ongoing vasopressor-dependent shock. Prolonged beta-lactam maintenance follows a loading dose; review de-escalation and duration daily. Avoid routine IV vitamin C, IVIG, blood purification or beta-blockers as sepsis therapies.

After rescue reassess analgesia/sedation, delirium, sleep, ventilation liberation, fluid removal when overloaded, renal/drug dosing, nutrition and mobilisation. Use appropriate VTE and GI-bleeding prophylaxis with daily indication review. Screen for ICU-acquired weakness, swallowing problems and new functional/cognitive deficits. Discuss prognosis and goals with the patient/family, acknowledging uncertainty rather than presenting a score as destiny.

At discharge reconcile medicines, document the infection/source, cultures, treatment duration and pending results, and remove unnecessary devices. Arrange follow-up for physical weakness, cognition, mood, recurrent infection and deterioration of chronic disease; provide safety-net advice and rehabilitation/support. The 2026 paediatric guideline and maternal-sepsis literature require population-specific adjustments; an adult fluid or oxygen target must not be transplanted uncritically into children or pregnancy. These are shared boundaries, not additional whole paediatric/obstetric syllabuses in this set.

## Self-marking checklist

- **2 marks** — Recognition/screening versus diagnosis and legacy terminology.
- **2 marks** — Risk-dependent antibiotic timing and urgent source control.
- **2 marks** — Individualised haemodynamics and appropriate adjuncts.
- **2 marks** — Post-resuscitation organ support and rehabilitation.
- **2 marks** — Medication/results handover and post-sepsis follow-up.

items.title: 2025.2 Q2: A patient was successfully resuscitated in an operating theatre with a
items.q: A patient was successfully resuscitated in an operating theatre with a suspected anaphylactic crisis shortly after anaesthetic induction drugs were given. Outline the post-crisis management and follow up for a suspected intraoperative anaphylactic reaction.
items.model:
## Immediate decisions (the priorities)

- **1.** **Stabilise and reassess** briefly: adrenaline requirement, airway oedema, bronchospasm, haemodynamics. Keep the team informed.
- **2.** **Proceed or abandon surgery?** Decide with the surgeon. If the reaction was severe (grade 3–4, adrenaline infusion needed, cardiovascular collapse), **abandon or postpone** unless the surgery is life-saving; mild, rapidly resolved reactions may allow cautious continuation with the culprit removed and invasive monitoring.
- **3.** **Disposition**: ICU or HDU for a severe reaction or ongoing infusion; otherwise monitored recovery. Observe for **biphasic reactions** (recurrence after initial resolution; risk is higher with severe initial reaction and delayed adrenaline). Keep a monitored bed for at least 6 hours, longer (often 24 hours) after severe reactions. Consider airway oedema and whether to leave the patient intubated.
- **4.** **Ongoing therapy**: adrenaline infusion if required, fluids, bronchodilators; antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts only.

## Investigations: tryptase

**ANZAAG–ANZCA post-crisis card (2022): serum tryptase immediately once feasible without delaying resuscitation, at 1 hour, at 4 hours, and a baseline after 24 hours.** Record onset and sample times; a later outpatient baseline may be needed. A peak exceeding 1.2 × baseline + 2 micrograms/L supports mast-cell activation but neither proves IgE mediation nor identifies the culprit; a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.

## Documentation and communication

- **Record** the timeline, all drugs and agents given (neuromuscular blocker, antibiotic, chlorhexidine, latex, dye, sugammadex, gelatin), their order and timing, treatment and response.
- **Open disclosure** with the patient and family; give written information and an **interim letter** to the GP and surgeon; **adverse event** reporting (TGA/ Medsafe/ CARM) and incident reporting.
- Alert in the medical record and a **medical alert bracelet** until the culprit is established.

## Follow up

Refer to an **allergy and immunology clinic** (anaesthetic allergy service) for testing **4–6 weeks after** the reaction: skin prick and intradermal tests, specific IgE (where available), and drug challenge where indicated. Supply every exposure for specialist assessment; the clinic selects validated tests and relevant alternatives rather than performing indiscriminate testing. The patient should receive a final letter with the culprit and safe alternatives.

## Debrief

Team debrief after the clinical priorities are addressed.

> **Examiner's point:** shorter, structured answers that decide on surgery, disposition (biphasic risk), correct tryptase timing and detailed follow-up scored best.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Use the four sampling points above rather than the previous three-sample UK-style schedule. The official local post-crisis card advises close monitoring for 6 hours and consideration of 24-hour ICU/HDU observation for moderate–severe reactions; ongoing instability requires continued critical care. Persistent and biphasic reactions differ, and a generic “20% biphasic” estimate should not dictate disposition. Oral non-sedating antihistamine is for residual skin symptoms; corticosteroids do not reliably prevent biphasic anaphylaxis. The treating anaesthetist should ensure referral is actually made and received, with anaesthetic/surgical/nursing charts, all exposures, exact timeline, treatment and tryptase values. Source: ANZAAG card 6; ANZCA PG69 (2025), referral and follow-up sections.
rubric: Decides whether to proceed with or abandon surgery
Disposition with rationale and biphasic risk
Tryptase timing (immediate, 1 h, 4 h, baseline >24 h)
Communication with the patient, GP and surgeon
Referral to an allergy service for testing at 4–6 weeks

items.title: 2023.2 Q10: Discuss the potential benefits and risks of supranormal oxygen levels
items.q: Discuss the potential benefits and risks of supranormal oxygen levels in the perioperative setting.
items.model:
## Frame the trade-off

Supranormal oxygen means arterial/tissue oxygen exposure above that required for adequate oxygenation. Distinguish increasing FiO2 from the resulting PaO2, and brief rescue/preoxygenation from sustained hyperoxaemia. The benefit is context dependent; a high saturation does not guarantee adequate oxygen delivery when haemoglobin or cardiac output is low. With saturated haemoglobin, additional oxygen mostly increases the small dissolved component (CaO2 ≈ 1.34 × Hb × SaO2 + 0.003 × PaO2, with Hb in g/dL and PaO2 in mmHg).

## Potential benefits with mechanisms

Preoxygenation denitrogenates the FRC, increasing the alveolar oxygen reservoir and extending safe apnoea time for induction, difficult airway management and interruption of ventilation. High FiO2 is appropriate during major hypoxaemia, peri-arrest care and anaphylaxis while correcting the cause. It may offset shunt-related hypoxaemia to a limited degree and increases dissolved oxygen; the effect is greater under hyperbaric pressure, relevant to selected CO poisoning/decompression/gas embolism contexts.

Improved wound tissue oxygen tension may facilitate neutrophil oxidative killing and collagen formation. Trials/guidelines on high perioperative FiO2 for SSI have been inconsistent; this is a potential benefit rather than a universal mandate for 80% oxygen. High oxygen can accelerate absorption of some gas collections (e.g. nitrogen washout), but never replaces urgent drainage of tension pneumothorax. It has a specific role in CO poisoning even when ordinary pulse oximetry appears reassuring.

## Risks with mechanisms

High alveolar oxygen washes out nitrogen, permitting absorption atelectasis in poorly ventilated units and increasing shunt. Prolonged exposure generates reactive oxygen species, epithelial/endothelial injury and inflammatory lung damage; toxicity depends on dose, duration and susceptibility. Hyperoxia causes coronary/cerebral vasoconstriction and may reduce regional flow despite a higher PaO2. In normoxaemic acute coronary syndromes, routine oxygen has no established benefit; titrate to need rather than treating chest pain itself with maximal oxygen.

In susceptible COPD patients, excessive oxygen may worsen hypercapnia predominantly through V/Q redistribution and the Haldane effect, with ventilatory effects also possible. Oxygen can mask hypoventilation/opioid toxicity by preserving SpO2 while CO2 rises; assess respiratory effort and capnography. It supports combustion and increases airway-fire risk during laser/diathermy procedures. Neonatal retinopathy and harm in some resuscitation/brain-injury contexts demonstrate that oxygen is a drug with population-specific targets; do not extrapolate adult goals to neonates.

## Apply the evidence

Use high oxygen when immediately required for safety, then titrate after stabilisation to an appropriate saturation/PaO2 range for the patient and setting. Check ABG when needed in shock or suspected CO2 retention; avoid both hypoxaemia and unnecessary sustained hyperoxia. Sepsis oxygen-target trials do not justify asserting that an ultra-conservative target improves survival in every patient. The 2023 examiner wanted at least five significant risks/benefits with explanation, including the reservoir-versus-masked-deterioration balance and changing myocardial-ischaemia practice. This is a shared mapped answer, not a claim that respiratory oxygen therapy has moved to Set 4.

**Sources and review basis:** Official 2023.2 report; explicit shared Master mapping (primarily Set 3); oxygen physiology and current sepsis/respiratory guidance. The present Set 4 reason for inclusion is SSI/host-defence overlap, clearly labelled.
rubric: **2 marks** — Defines exposure and differentiates brief reservoir/rescue from prolonged use.
**3 marks** — At least three contextual benefits with mechanisms.
**3 marks** — At least three harms with mechanisms.
**1 mark** — SSI/myocardial and other evidence uncertainty.
**1 mark** — Individual titration, ABG/ventilation assessment and avoidance of both extremes.

items.title: 2019.2 Q10: Describe the role of the anaesthetist in minimising surgical site infe
items.q: Describe the role of the anaesthetist in minimising surgical site infection.
items.model:
## Lead a perioperative prevention plan

Surgical-site infection arises through patient, provider and environmental reservoirs. The anaesthetist has a leadership role in institutional protocols, safe medication handling, physiological optimisation and effective antibiotic prophylaxis. The answer must focus on infection of the operative wound rather than only the anaesthetist’s own sharps safety.

Before surgery identify diabetes/hyperglycaemia, obesity, smoking, malnutrition, immune suppression, existing infection and colonisation. Optimise what time and surgical urgency allow; avoid unnecessary delay in urgent source-control surgery. Participate in targeted MRSA screening/decolonisation where indicated. Avoid routine shaving; clip only if hair removal is needed. Plan warming, antibiotic dose/timing and glucose monitoring at the team brief. Clarify allergy rather than automatically replacing cefazolin for a vague penicillin label.

## Prevent transfer of organisms

Perform hand hygiene at the relevant moments and remove contaminated airway gloves before touching IV access, syringes, drug preparation or the clean work area. Use aseptic preparation and administration: disinfect vial septa and injection hubs, single-patient syringes/ampoules, no shared propofol or reused syringes. Protect the sterile field and use appropriate mask/barrier precautions for lines and neuraxial catheters. Clean contaminated high-touch surfaces and reusable equipment between patients; reprocessing must match device risk and manufacturer instructions.

Work with theatre staff to keep doors closed, limit unnecessary traffic and maintain ventilation/cleaning standards. Ensure appropriate skin preparation is applied safely and allowed to dry, without contaminating injection equipment or causing pooling/fire risk. Communicate a chlorhexidine allergy across the entire pathway and use an effective alternative.

## Antibiotics and physiology

Confirm the right antibiotic, weight-adjusted dose and actual administration before incision/tourniquet; allow slow infusions sufficient time and redose during prolonged surgery or major blood loss. Document and communicate stop rules. Treatment for a dirty/infected field is different from prophylaxis.

Avoid hypothermia: reliable temperature monitoring, prewarming where appropriate, forced-air warming and warmed fluids, with a usual goal ≥36 °C. Prevent marked hyperglycaemia without causing hypoglycaemia; use local monitoring/insulin protocols. Maintain adequate perfusion, oxygenation and volume status without excessive fluids or unnecessary transfusion. Additional oxygen for an actual oxygenation requirement is appropriate; routine fixed 80% FiO2 solely to prevent SSI has uncertain benefit and potential pulmonary harms, so follow the agreed institutional policy rather than claiming a settled mortality benefit.

## Follow-through

Provide a recovery handover including antibiotic timing/redosing, temperature, glucose and identified infection risks. Audit SSI outcomes and process compliance, review sources of contamination with infection control, and improve team behaviour and systems. Prophylactic dexamethasone is not automatically contraindicated: PADDI found noninferiority for SSI with a single 8-mg dose, while transient hyperglycaemia needs consideration.

**Sources and review basis:** Official 2019.2 report: leadership, three reservoirs, appropriate antibiotics and avoidance of hypothermia. Current PG28 (2025); PADDI primary trial; oxygen risks/benefits addressed in the explicitly shared 2023.2 Q10 model.

**2 marks** — Antibiotic choice, dose, timing, redosing and duration.
**2 marks** — Avoids hypothermia with practical measures.
**2 marks** — Aseptic drug/line/equipment practice and clean environment.
**1 mark** — Glucose, perfusion/oxygen and transfusion balance.
**1 mark** — Leadership, handover, audit and feedback.

items.title: 2018.2 Q2: A 30-year-old woman requires a laparoscopic appendicectomy. She report
items.q: A 30-year-old woman requires a laparoscopic appendicectomy. She reports a "severe allergic reaction" during a laparoscopy five years ago. Outline your strategy for managing this case, given her history.
items.model:
## Gather information first

The history decides everything, so I would obtain the old anaesthetic chart, hospital notes, any allergy clinic letter and test results, and ask the patient. Key points: the drugs given just before the reaction (induction agents, muscle relaxant, antibiotic, chlorhexidine skin prep, latex, patent blue dye, gelatin colloid, opioid), onset time, the features (rash, bronchospasm, hypotension, adrenaline use, ICU admission), whether tryptase was taken, any later testing, and other allergies (latex, antibiotics, food, atopy). The likely culprits are neuromuscular blockers (rocuronium, suxamethonium), antibiotics (cefazolin), chlorhexidine, latex, patent blue and gelatin.

## Timing and testing

Appendicectomy is urgent, so I would not delay surgery for allergy testing. If the records cannot be found, I treat her as allergic to something unknown and use a low-trigger plan. If the surgeon can wait a short time, I would involve the allergy service, but never at the risk of a perforated appendix. The original event was five years ago, so there is no biological need to wait another 4–6 weeks to investigate it. Arrange specialist assessment at the earliest feasible time; if a new reaction occurs, the usual testing interval is 4–6 weeks, with urgent exceptions directed by the specialist.

## Plan

- **Discuss and consent:** tell her and the surgeon the risk, and keep the number of drugs given to a minimum.
- **Low-trigger anaesthetic:** a latex-free environment; avoid chlorhexidine if the cause is unknown (use povidone-iodine); select an appropriate antibiotic with low cross-reactivity to suspected agents and administer under monitoring at the correct surgical prophylaxis time; use alternative induction and opioid agents selected from the previous exposure history rather than assuming propofol or remifentanil is safe. Avoid NMBAs if one may have caused the earlier event; discuss an alternative technique with an anaesthetic allergist. If paralysis is essential, make an explicit specialist-informed risk decision. Sugammadex availability does not make rocuronium safe and is not established anaphylaxis treatment.
- **Prepared to treat:** invasive monitoring, adrenaline ready (grade 2 adult IV aliquots 10–20 micrograms; grade 3 50–100 micrograms, titrated) with an infusion ready, fluids, a second anaesthetist and the anaphylaxis kit.
- **After:** if a new reaction occurs, arrange monitored care appropriate to severity and sample tryptase immediately when feasible, at 1 hour, at 4 hours and baseline after 24 hours; document and refer. Without a new reaction, arrange retrospective allergy assessment rather than acute serial sampling for the remote event.

## Evidence

Management follows ANZAAG-ANZCA guidance; most perioperative anaphylaxis is to neuromuscular blockers and antibiotics (NAP6).

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

PG69 (2025) Appendix 2 is directly applicable to time-sensitive surgery after an uninvestigated reaction: seek anaesthetic-allergy advice, avoid suspected previous exposures and known cross-reactants, plan chlorhexidine- and latex-free care, and consider an NMBA-free technique where feasible. The urgency, airway and surgical requirements still matter; “low trigger” is not a guarantee. Inhalational maintenance can be considered. Do not omit effective surgical prophylaxis or administer it too late. If there is no new reaction, fresh acute tryptase samples are not useful for the episode five years ago; arrange retrospective allergy assessment and a future anaesthetic plan. Sugammadex can itself trigger anaphylaxis. Prepare severity-appropriate adrenaline, fluids and monitoring; an arterial line/HDU bed is individualised, not mandatory in every stable patient.
rubric: Consent and discussion with the surgeon
Avoids or selects drugs for a low-trigger plan

items.title: 2017.2 Q9: A 50-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) presents for
items.q: A 50-year-old woman with systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) presents for laparoscopic appendicectomy. She is currently treated with folate supplements and weekly methotrexate. Describe how your anaesthetic plan is modified by the presence of scleroderma in this patient.
items.model:
## Assess the manifestations that change this anaesthetic

Scleroderma can cause a difficult airway, oesophageal dysfunction/aspiration, restrictive interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension, myocardial disease, renal impairment and difficult vascular access/monitoring. Establish the extent rather than assuming every feature is present. Assess mouth opening/microstomia, jaw movement, neck mobility and dentition; dysphagia, reflux, regurgitation and gastric symptoms; dyspnoea, exercise tolerance, oxygen use, PFTs and echo where available; hypertension/renal function and digital/Raynaud disease. Obtain focused investigations without delaying necessary appendicitis source control. Consider sepsis, fasting/vomiting and perioperative risk with the surgeon and patient.

## Airway and aspiration

Reflux/oesophageal dysmotility may persist despite fasting, so plan aspiration prophylaxis where appropriate, ready suction and a cuffed tracheal tube. A standard rapid-sequence induction is not automatically safe if mouth opening or ventilation is difficult: consider awake intubation with an expert operator when indicated, topicalisation and a rescue airway plan. Select an oral/nasal route from anatomy and bleeding risk; avoid traumatic repeated attempts and protect fragile mucosa. Gastric decompression is individualised because instrumentation may be difficult or traumatic.

## Ventilation and circulation

Use tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, limit plateau/driving pressure and individualise PEEP in fibrotic low-compliance lungs; avoid aggressive recruitment of poorly recruitable lung. Avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia and acidosis, especially with pulmonary hypertension; preserve RV coronary perfusion and avoid abrupt increases in pulmonary vascular resistance. Monitor pneumoperitoneum/position effects and discuss lower insufflation pressures or conversion if poorly tolerated.

Titrate induction to cardiovascular reserve and sepsis. Assess need for an arterial line from disease severity; peripheral vasospasm can make pulse oximetry/NIBP inaccurate, so change site, warm the limb and verify the signal rather than chasing artefactual numbers. Ultrasound may help difficult IV access. Avoid unnecessary cannulation of ischaemic digits, maintain normothermia and padding, and balance perfusion against overload. Review renal function and pressure because scleroderma renal crisis is an important concern. Treat actual hypotension appropriately; Raynaud disease is not a reason to withhold necessary vasopressors in shock.

## Medication, infection and recovery

Confirm the weekly methotrexate dose/day, blood counts and hepatic/renal toxicity; folate supplementation does not remove toxicity risk. Conventional low-dose methotrexate is often continued for uncomplicated elective surgery, but AKI, serious infection or poor oral intake warrant specialist review before the next dose. **Avoid nitrous oxide in patients receiving methotrexate** because it can potentiate antifolate toxicity; check other interactions, notably trimethoprim/co-trimoxazole. Do not assume routine high-dose steroid cover if she takes no steroids; unnecessary high-dose steroids are particularly undesirable in systemic sclerosis.

Provide multimodal analgesia with renal/respiratory caution, thorough antiemesis and aspiration precautions at emergence, quantitative reversal and awake extubation once oxygenation/ventilation are adequate. Decide on enhanced monitoring/ICU from respiratory, RV and septic severity. Document handover of organ risks and medication plan. This full shared model is included because it is explicitly mapped, while its main disease ownership remains outside infection.

**Sources and review basis:** Official 2017.2 report: aspiration, limited mouth opening, safe ventilation and circulation/monitoring were central. Blue Book 2023 DMARD chapter (targeted reading) supplements medication decisions. Explicit shared mapping, not a new reassignment of the multisystem set.
rubric: **2 marks** — Specific airway assessment and feasible rescue/awake plan.
**2 marks** — Restrictive lung/PH ventilation and haemodynamic implications.
**1 mark** — Safe emergence and appropriate postoperative disposition.

items.title: 2017.1 Q12: Outline the factors relevant to selection of a perioperative antibioti
items.q: Outline the factors relevant to selection of a perioperative antibiotic prophylaxis regimen for a surgical patient. (50%) Discuss strategies to ensure appropriate implementation of antibiotic prophylaxis regimens. (50%)
items.model:
## Regimen selection (50%)

First distinguish prophylaxis from treatment: an established infected/dirty operative field requires a therapeutic course and source control. For prophylaxis assess the procedure, wound class, likely organisms, implant use and consequences of infection. Use the institutional procedure-specific regimen based on local susceptibility data. Most prophylaxis targets skin staphylococci/streptococci; colorectal procedures also require enteric Gram-negative and anaerobic activity. A prosthetic joint and a colorectal resection do not need the same spectrum.

Review allergy phenotype, previous tolerated antibiotics, MRSA/MDR carriage, recent infection/antibiotics, renal function, body weight, pregnancy and potential interactions. Cefazolin is often first line (typical adult 2 g IV; 3 g at ≥120 kg where the local protocol specifies). Its distinct side chain means a penicillin label alone usually does not require substitution. Prior cefazolin anaphylaxis or severe delayed beta-lactam reactions require an alternative specialist-informed plan. Add MRSA coverage only when indicated; vancomycin is not automatically equivalent MSSA prophylaxis and may need other procedure-specific cover.

The drug must achieve adequate tissue concentrations before contamination: give most IV agents within 60 minutes before incision and before tourniquet inflation. Start vancomycin early enough for the required slow infusion (usually within a 120-minute window). Plan redosing for prolonged surgery (e.g. cefazolin around four hours, adjusted to protocol/renal function), major haemorrhage or marked dilution. Use the shortest effective duration, usually finishing at wound closure; an indwelling drain alone is not an indication to continue prophylaxis.

## Implementation (50%)

Create a readily accessible, agreed surgical/anaesthetic/pharmacy policy with standard procedure-specific orders, doses, infusion times, redosing and stop rules. Make appropriate drugs immediately available in theatre, including alternatives. Allocate who prescribes, administers, documents and redoses: “the surgeon will do it” is not a reliable process.

At the preoperative review and team brief confirm the indication, allergy phenotype, chosen agent and dose. At WHO Sign In/Time Out verify actual administration time and infusion completion rather than merely whether a prescription exists. Document the dose, route and time on the anaesthetic chart; use timer/electronic reminders for redosing and specify the stop time in handover. If prophylaxis is missed, administer promptly, inform the surgeon and document the deviation without implying that post-incision dosing was optimal.

Educate staff, provide feedback on local SSI organisms/resistance, and audit appropriate indication, selection, dose, timing, redosing and discontinuation. Review infections and near misses with the multidisciplinary team and update the pathway when evidence changes. Balance efficacy with C. difficile, toxicity and resistance; broader and longer are not necessarily better.

**Sources and review basis:** Official 2017.1 report: relevance to patient/procedure, allergy and an implementation strategy/checklist were required. Current update: ANZCA PG28/PG69 (2025) and local procedure-specific prophylaxis guidance; see audit source links.
rubric: **2 marks** — Procedure/organisms and patient-specific selection, including allergy.
**1 mark** — Correct dose and timing before incision/tourniquet.
**1 mark** — Reasoned distinction between prophylaxis and therapy.
**2 marks** — Agreed policy, resources, education and allocated responsibility.
**2 marks** — Checklist confirms actual administration, documentation and reminders.
**1 mark** — Audit, feedback and stop-rule handover.

items.title: 2016.2 Q12: Evaluate the use of 10% povidone-iodine compared to 0.5% chlorhexidine
items.q: Evaluate the use of 10% povidone-iodine compared to 0.5% chlorhexidine/70% isopropyl alcohol as skin preparation prior to the institution of lumbar epidural analgesia.
items.model:
## Povidone-iodine 10%

- **Mechanism and activity**: releases free iodine; broad spectrum (bacteria, fungi, spores slowly, viruses). **Bacteriostatic at low concentration and bactericidal after 1–3 minutes' contact**.
- **Advantages**: long clinical use, aqueous (non-flammable), avoids chlorhexidine exposure, although no antiseptic is safe for inadvertent neuraxial injection, and low cost.
- **Disadvantages**: slower onset, **inactivated by blood and organic matter**, requires time to dry (otherwise ineffective), little residual activity, contact dermatitis, thyroid absorption in neonates, and rare **anaphylaxis** (iodine allergy is a myth; reactions are to povidone).

## Chlorhexidine 0.5% in 70% isopropyl alcohol

- **Mechanism**: disrupts cell membrane; **bactericidal** with rapid action (alcohol) and **persistent residual activity** (hours), less affected than iodine by organic material, although gross contamination still requires removal.
- **Advantages**: superior skin antisepsis in trials (Darouiche, surgical site infection; lower catheter colonisation and CRBSI), recommended by ANZCA PG28 (2025), ASRA and the UK guidance for neuraxial blocks.
- **Disadvantages**: **neurotoxicity if it enters the CSF or epidural space** (arachnoiditis, meningitis; case reports), flammability (alcohol must dry before diathermy), contact dermatitis, ocular injury, and **anaphylaxis** (rare, increasing recognition, particularly chlorhexidine in lines and catheters).

## Practical points

- **Allow it to dry completely** (for the manufacturer-specified contact/drying time; do not substitute a universal 30–60-second rule), avoid pooling, and ensure none contacts the needle, catheter, gloved fingers or equipment; use a separate sterile applicator.
- **Concentration**: current ANZCA PG28 permits 0.5–2% chlorhexidine in alcohol for neuraxial skin preparation. Concentration does not remove the need for complete drying and strict separation from injection equipment. The question compares 0.5% chlorhexidine/alcohol with aqueous 10% povidone-iodine; it does not isolate the chlorhexidine effect from the alcohol effect.
- If the patient is allergic to one, use the other; use alcohol-based preparations carefully in neonates.

## Conclusion

Chlorhexidine in alcohol is the preferred agent because of its efficacy and persistence, provided it is dry and precautions are taken. Povidone-iodine remains an acceptable alternative.

> **Examiner's point:** advantages and disadvantages of both, bacteriostatic versus bactericidal action, and the incidence of anaphylaxis.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. Use the question’s stated percentage split to guide emphasis/time; this domain checklist is a separate completeness score, not a published analytic mark scheme. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Distinguish rapid alcohol action, chlorhexidine persistence and organic-matter interference from outcomes: evidence of less bacterial colonisation is stronger than direct evidence of fewer rare epidural abscesses. Surgical/CVC trials cannot be presented as head-to-head epidural-infection proof. Neither preparation is a safe injectable solution. Use a single-use applicator away from the drug tray; avoid pooling, splashes and soaked materials, allow complete drying, use a spinal introducer as appropriate, and label/separate all solutions. Povidone-iodine allergy is distinct from seafood or contrast reactions. Source: PG28 (2025) regional-anaesthesia section and ASRA infection-control consensus (2025).
rubric: Mechanism and speed of action of both
Neurotoxicity concern and need to dry

items.title: 2015.2 Q8: A 20 year old patient has been successfully resuscitated from suspecte
items.q: A 20 year old patient has been successfully resuscitated from suspected anaphylaxis. Describe your immediate and longer term post crisis management.
items.model:
## Immediate post-crisis management

- **Reassess** airway, breathing and circulation: persistent bronchospasm, upper airway oedema (consider keeping the airway secured, with a cuff-leak test before extubation), and adrenaline requirement.
- **Environment and monitoring**: ICU or HDU for severe reactions; continuous ECG, SpO2, arterial pressure; observe for **biphasic reaction** (minimum 6 hours, 24 hours for severe reactions or when ongoing treatment).
- **Treatment**: adrenaline infusion if needed, fluid, bronchodilators; remove the possible trigger (stop infusions, replace latex, stop the antibiotic/blood).
- **Surgery**: decide whether to proceed (see severity and urgency).

## Blood investigations

**ANZAAG–ANZCA post-crisis card (2022): serum tryptase immediately once feasible without delaying resuscitation, at 1 hour, at 4 hours, and a baseline after 24 hours.** Record onset and sample times; a later outpatient baseline may be needed. A peak exceeding 1.2 × baseline + 2 micrograms/L supports mast-cell activation but neither proves IgE mediation nor identifies the culprit; a normal result does not exclude anaphylaxis.

## Longer-term management

- **Allergy referral**: skin prick and intradermal testing, specific IgE, and drug challenge at **4–6 weeks** (usually delayed to reduce false negatives; urgent earlier testing is specialist-directed and negative early tests may need repeating), using the complete exposure list to select relevant investigations and safe alternatives.
- **Communication**: tell the patient what happened and the agents suspected, provide an **interim letter** before discharge, a final letter after testing for the GP, surgeon and patient, and document in the medical record and alert system.
- **Medical alert identification** and individualised advice. An adrenaline autoinjector is not routinely required for an isolated anaesthetic-drug trigger; the allergy service assesses community exposure risk and any separate indication.
- **Reporting**: incident report and regulatory reporting (TGA/ Medsafe).
- **Future anaesthetics**: prior information to avoid the culprit and its cross-reacting group.
- **Support**: debrief for staff and the patient.

> **Examiner's point:** serial tryptase with correct time frame, an appropriate monitored environment, referral for allergy testing, and communication (interim and final letters).

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Use the four sampling points above rather than the previous three-sample UK-style schedule. The official local post-crisis card advises close monitoring for 6 hours and consideration of 24-hour ICU/HDU observation for moderate–severe reactions; ongoing instability requires continued critical care. Persistent and biphasic reactions differ, and a generic “20% biphasic” estimate should not dictate disposition. Oral non-sedating antihistamine is for residual skin symptoms; corticosteroids do not reliably prevent biphasic anaphylaxis. The treating anaesthetist should ensure referral is actually made and received, with anaesthetic/surgical/nursing charts, all exposures, exact timeline, treatment and tryptase values. Source: ANZAAG card 6; ANZCA PG69 (2025), referral and follow-up sections.
rubric: Reassesses and monitors for biphasic reaction
Serial tryptase with timing and trends
Referral for allergy testing at 4–6 weeks
Interim and final letters to GP and patient

items.title: 2014.1 Q7: You are inserting a central venous line (CVL) as part of your anaesthe
items.q: You are inserting a central venous line (CVL) as part of your anaesthetic management for a laparotomy. Outline the perioperative measures you should consider to minimise central venous line sepsis.
items.model:
## Decide whether it is needed

Weigh the **indication** (inotropes, CVP, access, TPN) against the risk of line infection, pneumothorax and thrombosis; consider peripheral access, ultrasound-guided PICC, or delaying insertion.

## Before insertion

- **Hand hygiene** (alcohol rub or surgical scrub), **maximal sterile barrier precautions**: sterile gown, gloves, mask, cap, and full-body drape (the patient).
- **Skin antisepsis**: **chlorhexidine 2% in alcohol 70%** (or 0.5%), allowed to dry fully.
- **Insertion bundle/checklist** with a trained observer empowered to stop the procedure; **ultrasound guidance** reduces attempts and complications; use all-in-one kits.
- **Site selection**: **subclavian** has the lowest infection risk but higher mechanical risk; internal jugular is common; **femoral** carries important infection/thrombosis concerns; relative risks depend on patient, site care and duration. Avoid sites near infection, burns or tracheostomy.
- Use the minimum number of lumens; consider **antimicrobial-impregnated catheters** (chlorhexidine–silver sulfadiazine, or minocycline–rifampicin) where rates remain high.
- **Antibiotic prophylaxis for insertion is not recommended**; no routine antibiotic lock.

## After insertion

- **Dressing**: sterile transparent semi-permeable dressing or **chlorhexidine-impregnated dressing**; change when soiled or every 7 days (gauze every 2 days).
- **Port disinfection** with alcohol/chlorhexidine for 15 seconds before each access; use closed systems; change administration sets at the correct intervals (blood and lipids within 24 hours; other continuous sets follow current local/manufacturer intervals; do not treat 96 hours as a universal maximum).
- **Daily review of need** and **prompt removal** when no longer required; **avoid routine line replacement**.
- Lines inserted in an emergency without full aseptic technique should be replaced within 48 hours.
- **Education, audit and surveillance** of CLABSI rates, with feedback; staff competency, and compliance with local protocol.

## Recognition

Unexplained fever or sepsis, local erythema or pus: take paired blood cultures (line and peripheral), and remove or replace the line if septic.

> **Examiner's point:** risks versus benefits, aseptic technique, protocols, hand hygiene, skin antiseptic, site choice, port disinfection, staff education, and early removal.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. 
## Audit clarification and extension

PICC insertion is not an intrinsically infection-free alternative to a CVC. Avoid routine prophylactic antibiotics, scheduled guidewire exchanges and replacement based solely on fever. If CRBSI is suspected, take paired peripheral/line cultures before treatment if feasible; shock, tunnel infection, persistent bacteraemia or pathogens such as S. aureus/Candida usually require prompt removal after alternative access, with organism-specific treatment and assessment for metastatic infection. A subclavian site may reduce infection but threatens future dialysis access and carries mechanical risk. Source: PG28 2025; CDC catheter prevention guidance and contemporary CLABSI bundles. The historical examiner requires prevention across insertion and subsequent care, not merely a sterile insertion recipe.
rubric: Considers risks and benefits of the line
Hand hygiene and full barrier precautions

items.title: 2012.1 Q14: a. What do the terms decontamination, disinfection and sterilisation m
items.q: a. What do the terms decontamination, disinfection and sterilisation mean? (30%) b. What measures should be in place to minimise the risk of transmission of infection to the respiratory tract of patients via anaesthetic equipment? (70%)
items.model:
## Definitions (30%)

- **Decontamination:** the process of making an item safe to handle/use through appropriate removal or inactivation of contamination; cleaning physically removes soil and precedes further reprocessing. Cleaning is the essential first reprocessing step, because organic matter protects organisms; decontamination is the wider process.
- **Disinfection:** inactivation of non-sporing microorganisms by thermal (pasteurisation at 70 to 90 degrees C) or chemical means (glutaraldehyde, peracetic acid, alcohol), at low, intermediate or high level.
- **Sterilisation:** complete destruction of all microorganisms including spores (steam autoclave, ethylene oxide, gamma radiation, hydrogen peroxide plasma).

## Measures to protect the patient's airway (70%)

The examiners want the focus on transmission to the patient via equipment, not staff protection alone.

- **Staff:** hand hygiene before each patient and after contact, gloves, masks if potentially infectious, vaccination, and not working while unwell.
- **Single-use items** for anything that touches the airway wherever possible (masks, airways, tracheal tubes, suction catheters, laryngeal masks), kept in their supplied clean/sterile packaging until use.
- **Laryngoscopes:** blades are single-use or cleaned and then high-level disinfected or sterilised, handles cleaned and disinfected between patients, and used blades kept separate from clean ones.
- **Breathing system:** a bacterial/viral filter at the patient end protects the circuit, absorber and ventilator; items between the patient and filter are discarded; circuits without effective patient-end filtration require between-patient replacement or validated manufacturer-specified reprocessing; gas sampling is taken on the machine side of the bacterial/viral filter where the equipment permits; unfiltered sampled gas must not be returned to the breathing system.
- **Machine:** disinfect external surfaces between cases; CO2 absorber, bellows and ventilator reprocessed per manufacturer.
- **Flexible scopes and videolaryngoscopes:** cleaned and high-level disinfected with tracked reprocessing, or single-use scopes.
- **Special patients:** tuberculosis needs airborne staff/room precautions and effective bacterial/viral filtration; suspected CJD requires procedure/tissue-specific specialist advice, with single-use/quarantine where indicated rather than treating every airway exposure as high-risk neurosurgery.
- **Systems:** follow current PG28 (2025) and Australian/NZ standards (AS 5369:2023 (accepted by HealthCERT New Zealand)), involve infection control, train staff, audit and report incidents.

## Evidence

Transmission through anaesthetic equipment is rare but documented (hepatitis C via shared syringes and vials; contaminated circuits); filters reduce circuit contamination.

This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. Use the question’s stated percentage split to guide emphasis/time; this domain checklist is a separate completeness score, not a published analytic mark scheme. 
## Audit clarification and extension

Use current PG28 (2025) and AS 5369:2023, rather than relying on superseded PS28/AS4187 terminology. Clean reusable laryngoscope handles then at least low-level disinfect after every use; blades need high-level disinfection or sterilisation. Device labelling/manufacturer instructions govern whether an item is reusable. HME alone is not necessarily a bacterial/viral filter. Filtered circuits still need inspection, change if contaminated/damaged and a defined validated change policy; filtration is not indefinite permission to reuse. Reprocess reusable masks as semi-critical devices and protect all clean airway equipment from handling/environmental contamination. A sterile probe cover does not replace the required cleaning/disinfection level.

items.title: 2010.1 Q13: a. What do you understand by the term "Universal Precautions"? (40%) b
items.q: a. What do you understand by the term "Universal Precautions"? (40%) b. Describe how you apply these precautions in your daily anaesthesia practice. (60%)
items.model:
## a. Universal precautions (40%)

**Universal precautions** are infection-control practices designed to **minimise transmission of blood-borne pathogens (HIV, hepatitis B and C)** to staff and patients. **Every patient is treated as potentially infectious** regardless of known status. They apply to **blood and body fluids** (semen, vaginal secretions, CSF, pleural, peritoneal, pericardial and synovial fluids, and amniotic fluid) but not to faeces, nasal secretions, sputum, sweat, tears, urine or vomit unless visibly bloody.

They are now incorporated into **standard precautions**, which add respiratory hygiene and apply to all body fluids. They are distinct from **additional (transmission-based) precautions** for known or suspected infections such as TB, MRSA, CJD and influenza (airborne, droplet, contact).

## b. Application in anaesthetic practice (60%)

- **Hand hygiene** with alcohol rub or washing: before and after each patient and procedure (five moments).
- **Personal protective equipment**: gloves for IV cannulation, airway management and handling secretions; **mask and eye protection** during intubation, extubation, suction and regional procedures; gowns when contamination is likely; **cover cuts** with waterproof dressings.
- **Sharps safety**: do not recap needles, immediate disposal in a rigid sharps container at the point of use, and avoid passing sharps by hand (neutral zone). Report needlestick injuries and follow the exposure protocol (wash, report, baseline serology, post-exposure prophylaxis within hours).
- **Disposal of waste** (clinical waste bag for soiled materials) and **spills** (clean promptly with appropriate disinfectant).
- **Equipment**: single-use airway devices and syringes, one needle and syringe per patient, single-dose ampoules, decontamination and disinfection of reusable items (laryngoscope blades and handles, bronchoscopes), filters on breathing circuits.
- **Staff and system**: vaccination against hepatitis B, education, supervising theatre staff and ensuring compliance as **team leader**, and audit.

> **Examiner's point:** hand hygiene and sharps handling were often omitted; distinguish universal, standard and additional precautions.

**Scoring (/ 8, educator-created):** 1 mark for each checklist domain explained accurately and applied to this case, 0.5 for incomplete coverage, 0 if absent/unsafe. This is not an official ANZCA scheme. Include the audit clarification in the relevant domain. Use the question’s stated percentage split to guide emphasis/time; this domain checklist is a separate completeness score, not a published analytic mark scheme.
